Read text file `.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md`.
1|---
2|name: muse-round
3|description: Run one round of the Muse agent on the MobileMoE-S decode kernels as a swarm. Explorers map the code and measurements into a shared analysis; then competing builders write and grade fused Metal kernels for the top inefficiencies. From round 2 on, the round starts from the previous rounds' results and must beat their best attempts. Both phases are tracked in shared documents.
4|---
5|
6|# One round of the Muse agent: a swarm explores, then builds
7|
8|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed on main and tagged `muse-code-era` before the first Muse Code session; each later version is committed before the round that uses it. [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
9|
10|**Skill version 5.** This file, the role cards and tracking.md are versioned together; [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) lists every version. Each round records the version it ran (see *Versions* in tracking.md).
11|
12|You are the **lead** of a Muse Code session in your own worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. The first prompt names the Meta model you run as, the name your commit subjects start with, and the co-author line every commit ends with. `claude/muse-agent-brief.md` fixes the task, the slots, the tools and limits, the grader command and the pass criteria (G1, G2). Four ADRs change it in five ways:
13|
14|1. **Harness** ([ADR 0006](../../../claude/adr/0006-muse-spark-in-muse-code.md)). You are a Muse Code session, not a Claude Code one. Muse Code adds no trailer, so you write the first prompt's co-author line on every commit yourself (see *Commits*).
15|2. **No attempt limit and no stop rule** (ADR 0006). The brief's *When a slot stops* no longer applies: you decide when a slot is done. Every graded attempt is committed, so the history shows every try.
16|3. **A swarm** ([ADR 0007](../../../claude/adr/0007-muse-spark-swarm.md)). Helpers explore and build; you coordinate and commit.
17|4. **Files** (ADR 0007, [ADR 0009](../../../claude/adr/0009-rounds-build-on-each-other.md)). Each round writes in its own **round folder**: round 1 at the top of `muse-spark/`, round N from 2 on in `muse-spark/round-<N>/`. It holds `exploration/` and `implementation/`, the round's shared documents, which replace `strategy.md`; `kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<M>/`; and `summary.md`. tracking.md writes it `<round>/`.
18|5. **Rounds build on each other** (ADR 0009). A finished round's files are frozen: read them and cite them, and the hooks refuse any change to them. From round 2 on, a slot may have a **baseline**, the best attempt so far that passes the current G2, and a new attempt must beat it in the same grader run. A slot without one has a **starting point** instead: an earlier attempt to build from, which Claude's measurement names.
19|
20|The rest of the brief stands. The goal: kernels that pass G1 and G2, beat the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 rows and, where the slot has a baseline, beat it too, faster because they remove a cause you can name. The Muse agent was Muse Spark in round 1 and is Muse Wonder from round 2 ([ADR 0008](../../../claude/adr/0008-muse-wonder.md)); documents written in earlier rounds say "Muse Spark".
21|
22|## The swarm
23|
24|| Role | Name | Task | Card |
25||---|---|---|---|
26|| **Lead** (you) | | Start the helpers, keep the two READMEs, settle clashes, commit | this file |
27|| **Explorer** | `explorer-<territory>` | Map one territory into entries, and find where it loses time | [explorer.md](explorer.md) |
28|| **Verifier** | `verifier` | Check every inefficiency against its sources | [verifier.md](verifier.md) |
29|| **Builder** | `builder-<n>-<letter>` | Write and grade one solution for one hypothesis: one attempt | [builder.md](builder.md) |
30|| **Boundary agent** | `boundary-<n>` | Write what a hypothesis's solution must keep identical, and check passing attempts against it | [boundary.md](boundary.md) |
31|
32|You don't explore, build or grade yourself. Start each helper with a prompt of this shape:
33|
34|> You are `<name>`, a `<role>` in round `<N>`'s swarm; this round writes in `<round folder>`. Read `.agents/skills/muse-round/<card>` and `.agents/skills/muse-round/tracking.md`, then: `<task>`.
35|
36|[tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the shared documents (the two phase folders, their READMEs, entries and logs) and the rules every agent keeps. Read it before starting anyone. Up to 12 agents run at once, you included.
37|
38|**A checkpoint** is what you do each time a helper returns, and whenever the log shows something to settle:
39|1. **Read the log.** Read the phase log since your last checkpoint.
40|2. **Settle clashes.** When two entries describe one cause, keep the fuller one and set the other's status to `superseded by <entry>`. When two helpers work on one item, redirect one of them (`subagent_send_message`). Log what you decided.
41|3. **Refresh the tracker.** Update the phase README's tracker table, and raise the version of each hypothesis entry that changed.
42|4. **Raise the version.** Raise the phase README to its next version, and add its line to `## Versions`, naming the entries that changed and their versions (see *Versions* in tracking.md).
43|5. **Commit** the phase folder, plus any attempt that came back, as that version (see *Commits*).

45|## The round
46|
47|### 0. Find where you are
48|
49|- Run `git log --oneline main -1`, then `git tag --list -n1 'muse-round-*'`, which lists the finished rounds. **This round** is one more than the highest; with none, it is round 1. Its folder is `muse-spark/round-<N>/` (round 1: `muse-spark/`).
50|- `git log --oneline --grep '^Muse ' muse-code-era..HEAD` lists the Muse agent's commits of every round.
51|- **From round 2 on,** read Claude's measurement of the previous round, `claude/findings/muse-round-<N-1>.md`. It has the G3 results and names each slot's baseline or starting point. If it is missing, stop and reply "Claude's measurement of round <N-1> is missing": this round builds on it.
52|- If this round's folder already exists, a session stopped partway: carry on from its READMEs' last versions.
53|- Read the brief.
54|
55|**Done** when you can name the round number and its folder, and from round 2 on each slot's baseline or starting point and the latest G3 results.

57|### 1. The starting point (from round 2 on)

60|- the previous rounds' final exploration and implementation READMEs and `summary.md`;
61|- the `notes.md` of each baseline or starting-point attempt;
62|- Claude's measurement.

64|Then write the opening of this round's `exploration/README.md` (set up as in step 2.1), a section **Starting point**:
65|- **Per slot:**
66|  - the baseline, or the starting point where there is none, and its piece timing;
67|  - its G3 effect, and how that compares with what was predicted, with the reason where Claude's measurement gives one;
68|  - what keeps a starting point from passing G2, and where the attempt still spends its time.
69|- **What is left:**
70|  - the confirmed inefficiencies not yet built or not fully removed, ranked by predicted saving against the baselines, or the reference where a slot has none;
71|  - the slots not yet tried, for example `routing+combine`;
72|  - the recommendations outside the slots.
73|- **Refuted claims,** which no one chases again.

78|### 2. Exploration
79|
80|1. **Set up the folder.** Write `<round>/exploration/README.md` with a heading, its version line (v1, with skill version 5), the tracker (one row per territory) and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`.
81|2. **Start the explorers and the verifier,** all at once.
82|   - **Round 1** starts with these territories:
83|
84|     | Territory | Covers |
85|     |---|---|
86|     | `model` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py`: the decoder layer, `MoE.__call__` and everything around the slots |
87|     | `switch-layers` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/switch_layers.py`: the routed experts' path, `gather_qmm`, the sort from 16 rows |
88|     | `quantized-kernels` | `quantized.h` and `quantized_utils.h` in `.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/`: the `affine_gather_*` kernels behind `gather_qmm` |
89|     | `other-kernels` | the other Metal kernels in the same folder that the routing and combine slots launch: sort, softmax, reductions, elementwise, copies |
90|     | `vllm-metal` | `third_party/vllm-metal/vllm_metal/`: how the engine runs a decode step around the model |
91|     | `grader` | `bench/grader/`: the slot interface, what G1, G2 and the piece timing measure, and so the boundary every solution keeps |
92|     | `findings` | `claude/findings/` and `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/` |
93|     | `runs` | `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/`, `2026-10-29-baseline/` and `2026-10-30-micro/` |
94|
95|   - **From round 2 on,** the starting point lists the territories:
96|     - `baseline-<slot>` for each slot: its baseline's kernels and `spec.json`, which are now the code in the slot, or its starting point's. Map them with the checklist, and find where they still lose time and, for a starting point, why it fails G2;
97|     - `g3`: Claude's measurement of the previous round, where the end-to-end change differs from the piece timing, and why;
98|     - of round 1's territories, only those the starting point reopens. An explorer starts from that territory's earlier entries and writes only what is new.

Merge or close a territory that turns out to hold nothing, and add one when an inefficiency points somewhere no one covers. Log each change and update the tracker.

104|### 3. The analysis
105|
106|Write the final `<round>/exploration/README.md`. It is the round's report on the code, for this round's builders and for future improvements:
107|
108|- **Tracker:** the final table.
109|- **Starting point** (from round 2 on), as written in step 1, with any correction exploration made.
110|- **Context:** the decode step, the MoE block and its slots, and what the measurements say about where the time goes.
111|- **Territory map:** how the territories feed each other. For each territory: what it receives, what it passes on, and its measured cost.
112|- **Inefficiencies, ranked:**
113|  - the confirmed ones inside the slots, ranked by predicted saving as a share of the decode step, averaged over 1, 8 and 32 rows; from round 2 on, the saving is against the baseline where the slot has one;
114|  - each with its cost, kind and entry;
115|  - Claude's findings marked as Claude's, earlier rounds' entries linked as theirs, and this round's own reading marked as yours.
116|- **Recommendations:** the confirmed inefficiencies outside the slots, with their evidence. They're for surucuonur's team.
117|- **Refuted claims,** in one line each, so no one chases them again.
118|- **Files read:** links to each territory entry's list.
119|
120|Commit it. **Done** when every ranked item links a confirmed entry and every number in the README has its source.
121|
122|### 4. Implementation
123|
124|Take the ranked inefficiencies in order, at most two at a time, in different slots so their attempts never touch. Write `<round>/implementation/README.md` with a heading, its version line, the tracker and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`. For each hypothesis:
125|
126|1. **Open the hypothesis.** Write `<round>/implementation/hyp-<n>-<slug>.md`, with status `boundary`, the inefficiency, the slot and, from round 2 on, the slot's baseline folder or `none`. Add its tracker row and log it.
127|2. **Draw its boundary.** Start `boundary-<n>` to write the boundary, and wait for it.
128|3. **Compete.**
129|   - Set the status to `building`.
130|   - Start 2 or 3 builders, `builder-<n>-a`, `-b` and `-c`. Give each a different direction drawn from the analysis: for example, fusing kernels, reading each weight byte once, or a different threadgroup shape. From round 2 on, a direction may start from the baseline's or starting point's kernels, or from scratch.
131|4. **Collect.** Each time a builder returns:
132|   - checkpoint, committing its attempt folder with the hypothesis entry, the README and the log;
133|   - if the attempt passed G2, start `boundary-<n>` to check it.
134|5. **Harden.**
135|   - Pick the best attempt: it passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, and it is the fastest across the three row counts against the compiled reference and, where the slot has one, the baseline.
136|   - Set the status to `hardening`, and start a builder for that attempt's next single change.
137|   - Repeat while the attempt still has a cause you can name and remove.
138|6. **Close.**
139|   - **`ready`:** the best attempt passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, beats the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 rows and, where the slot has a baseline, has `beats_baseline` true, and you can name no further change worth making. Write the **Decision**: the attempt, why it is best, and what G3 should show.
140|   - **`dropped`:** say why. A slot whose hypotheses are all dropped keeps its baseline, or the reference where it has none.
141|
142|Then open the next-ranked inefficiency. **Done** when no confirmed inefficiency is left that you judge will pay. Write why in the implementation README.
143|
144|### 5. Finish
145|
146|1. **The implementation README:** the final tracker, one paragraph per hypothesis, and a **Ready to test** section. It names the attempt per slot that goes to G3, this round's, the baseline kept, or the reference, and the change in decode step period you expect at 1, 8 and 32 requests against the previous round's, with how you worked it out.
147|2. **The exploration README:** add *What building taught*, the analysis corrected by what the attempts showed.
148|3. **`<round>/summary.md`:** a `## Round N` section with:
149|   - the model, the skill version this round ran, and the final versions of both READMEs;
150|   - the final attempt per slot;
151|   - the number of graded attempts per slot, this round and over all rounds;
152|   - the expected G3 change;
153|   - what you'd try next;
154|   - your recommendations outside the slots.
155|4. **Commit,** then reply with this round's commits and the words "Round N finished".
156|
157|## Your own rules
158|
159|- **Writes:**
160|  - you write the two READMEs, the hypothesis entries' status blocks and decisions, and `summary.md`;
161|  - every helper writes only what its card names;
162|  - all of it stays in this round's folder.
163|- **G3 and vLLM belong to surucuonur's team,** who run them after merging your branch.
164|- **The rules every agent keeps** are in tracking.md.
165|
166|## Commits
167|
168|You are the only agent that commits. Commit only on `muse-agent`.
169|- **What to add:** this round's phase folders that exist so far (only `exploration` until implementation starts) and the attempt folders that came back. An attempt another builder is still writing waits for its own commit. An entry that is mid-edit is committed as it stands, and finished in a later commit.
170|- **The message:**
171|  - every subject starts with the name the first prompt gives you, then a colon;
172|  - a checkpoint's subject is `<name>: <phase> v<N>: <what changed>`, the version it records;
173|  - every message ends with the first prompt's co-author line, exactly.
174|
175|For example, in round 2 as Muse Wonder:
176|
177|```bash
178|git add muse-spark/round-2/exploration muse-spark/round-2/implementation muse-spark/round-2/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<M>
179|git commit -m "Muse Wonder: implementation v4: experts attempt 3 graded, beats baseline" \
180|  -m "Co-Authored-By: Muse Wonder (Meta Model API) <muse-wonder@meta-model-api.invalid>"
181|```
182|
183|Use no other co-author. The hooks refuse a commit without a Muse agent's co-author, a commit outside `muse-spark/`, a change to a finished round's files, a new file outside this round's folder, and any merge. Push, merge, rebase, tags, git config and hook skipping stay with surucuonur.

1|# Round 1 of the Muse agent, measured
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|In round 1 (2026-11-03), the Muse agent (Muse Spark, `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`) explored the decode step as a swarm, then wrote fused Metal kernels for three slots of the mixture-of-experts block. Its summary, [muse-spark/summary.md](../../muse-spark/summary.md), names one final attempt per slot. Each one passed the grader, and the summary predicted, from the per-slot timing, that together they would shorten the decode step by 0.54, 1.81 and 5.72 ms at 1, 8 and 32 requests.
6|
7|This is Claude's independent measurement of those three attempts, done on main after merging round 1 (`a4995e4`), on 2026-11-04:
8|- **re-grading** them with the grader;
9|- **checking them end to end** in the model, in plain MLX and in vLLM;
10|- **timing the decode step (G3)** with each slot alone and with all three together.
11|
12|It is the measurement that round 2's skill reads first: the last section names what round 2 starts from in each slot.
13|
14|**Where everything is.** The raw data is in [results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/). The scripts are:
15|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py`, the grader;
16|- `bench/grader/time_candidates.py`, the end-to-end check and G3;
17|- `bench/micro/chain_timing.py`, the chained-timing experiment.
18|
19|**The machine.** The M1 Pro measured the baseline ([method](../benchmark/method.md)). Docker was quit for these runs, with surucuonur's permission. Another job of surucuonur's was running, and 21.3 to 22.7 GB of the 22.5 to 23.5 GB of swap were in use (`machine-*.txt`). vLLM ran with `VLLM_METAL_KV_COMMIT_PROBE=0`, as in earlier runs.
20|
21|## Summary
22|
23|- **All three attempts pass the grader as round 1 ran it.** On main, each one compiles, matches the reference within G2's tolerances at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and beats the compiled reference in the per-slot timing.
24|- **In the model, all three together make the decode step slower with 1 and 8 requests.** In vLLM:
25|  - +0.98 ms (+18%) with 1 request;
26|  - +0.16 ms (+1%) with 8;
27|  - −1.76 ms (−6%) with 32.
28|
29|  Round 1 predicted −0.54, −1.81 and −5.72 ms.

22|## The slots
23|
24|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the step: 1 to 32 in decode. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
25|
26|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
27|
28|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
29|
30|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
31||---|---|---|---|
32|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
33|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
34|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
35|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
36|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
37|
38|Reference:
39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
69|
70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.

190|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
191|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
192|3. **G3, faster.** The decode step's period is the median over 3 repeats in shuffled order, with 128-token prompts, at 1, 8 and 32 requests. It must be lower than both the original model's and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code. The gap must exceed the spread between repeats.
193|
194|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
195|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
196|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
197|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer`: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, and `beats_compiled`.
198|
199|**The piece timing** runs the slot on all 20 layers' captured decode inputs, at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and waits for the GPU once at the end. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row. It takes the median of 30 repeats, per layer. It is a guide; G3 decides.
200|
201|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and beats the compiled reference in the piece timing at all three row counts, or after 5 attempts. Name your final attempt per slot in `muse-spark/summary.md`; it goes to the end-to-end and G3 checks, which surucuonur's team runs after merging your branch.

76|The analysis corrected by what the attempts showed (see `../implementation/README.md`):

79|2. **The piece harness prices kernels differently from in-step knock-outs.** A fused kernel costs a ~24 µs/layer floor with barriers/serial tails (routing) and ~17 µs/layer streaming elementwise (combine) — not 6.81 µs per launch; the reference's 12 routing kernels cost ~3 µs each when pipelined 20 deep. 2|

12|elements/row; the weights-norm sum runs on 1 thread at 1 row). This attempt

5|# From round 2, a kernel must be bit-exact at every size it runs at, prefill included, and the piece timing chains the layers
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|**The change.** Claude's measurement of round 1 ([findings](../findings/muse-round-1.md)) found that round 1's final attempts, which passed the grader, broke the brief's end-to-end rule in the model, and that one of them slowed the decode step it was meant to speed up. The grader missed three things:
10|
11|1. **Sizes.** It tested a slot on a decode step's inputs only, at 1, 8 and 32 rows. The same `MoE.__call__` runs the prefill, at 127 to 2,048 rows with 128-token prompts. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes, from `gather_qvm` to `gather_qmm_rhs`, and so does its rounding. Round 1's experts kernel copied `gather_qvm` bit for bit, and differed in 62% of its outputs at each prefill size.
12|2. **Exactness.** G2 allowed small differences: 2 bfloat16 units in the last place, and 10⁻⁴ for routing weights. End to end, the brief asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. Round 1's routing weights, within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences in 24 tokens.
13|3. **Latency.** The piece timing ran 20 layers' calls with no data between them, so the GPU could overlap them. At 1 row, round 1's experts kernel was 29% faster than the reference on overlapped calls and 66% slower on chained ones (`bench/micro/chain_timing.py`). In the model it slowed the decode step by 1.2 ms (22% in vLLM, 25% in plain MLX).
14|
15|On 2026-11-04 surucuonur chose, before round 2:
16|- **every call:** the kernels run wherever `MoE.__call__` runs, the prefill included;
17|- **bit-exact** outputs;
18|- **chained** piece timing.
19|
20|## How it works
21|
22|- **G2 at two kinds of size.** `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` checks every layer at:
23|  - the captured decode inputs, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
24|  - the first prefill chunk at 1, 8 and 32 requests (127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows), recorded while it runs (`slots.capture_prefill`), with the prompts `time_candidates.py` uses.
25|- **Bit-exact.** An output passes only if it equals the reference's:
26|  - for routing, the 4 experts and their weights, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order;
27|  - for combine and experts, every element.
28|
29|  The grader still reports the largest gap, in units in the last place, to help find the cause. The reference checked against itself shows no difference at any size.
30|- **Chained timing.** Each layer's call takes one input through `link`, a single fused kernel that adds 0 × one value of the previous call's output, so the call can't start before the previous one finishes. Every function timed (reference, compiled, candidate and baseline) gets the same link. The chained times match those of a real data chain within 10%.
31|  - **Why not `mx.depends`:** it orders only the graph. In a test on 2026-11-04, round 1's experts kernel took 46 µs per layer with it at 1 row, as fast as with no dependency, against 133 to 195 µs with a real data dependency in three runs.
32|- **The end-to-end check and G3 are unchanged.**
33|  - `bench/grader/time_candidates.py` now takes several `SLOT=FOLDER` attempts.
34|  - It times each slot alone, against its own compiled reference, and all of them together.
35|
36|## Consequences
37|
38|- **No round-1 attempt passes the new G2,** so round 2 has no baseline in any slot. Its bar is the compiled reference. Round 1's final attempts are its starting points, named in Claude's findings.
39|- **The experts slot needs a kernel exact at prefill sizes,** matching `gather_qmm_rhs`'s rounding from 60 rows on, or a single design whose rounding matches both of MLX's kernels.
40|- **A grader run takes longer.** It loads the model (760 MB) for every slot and runs three prefill chunks.
41|- **The piece timing now includes one small link kernel per layer** for every function timed. That brings the reference and the candidate closer in relative terms, but not in µs.
42|- **Not covered:** prefill speed. G3 times decode steps only, so a kernel slower at prefill sizes would go unnoticed, apart from the time to first token.
43|
44|## Considered options
45|
46|- **Decode calls only,** with MLX's code in the prefill. The kernels would need to be exact only at decode sizes, but they would no longer replace the whole MoE block. Not chosen: surucuonur asked for every call.
47|- **Keep the tolerances, and relax the token rule** to counting the sequences that differ. Simpler kernels, but the claim would become "the same model up to rounding", with a threshold to pick.
48|- **Keep independent timing,** and rely on G3 to catch latency. Round 2's builders would again rank attempts by a number that hid a 22% slowdown.
49|- **`mx.depends` for the chain.** No extra kernel, but it doesn't make the GPU wait.

1|"""Grade one kernel attempt: compile it, test it on captured inputs, time it.
2|
3|The independent grader for the Muse agent's kernels (claude/muse-agent-brief.md).
4|G2 tests it on the inputs `slots.py capture` recorded from a real decode step
5|(1, 8 and 32 rows), and on every layer's inputs in a prefill, recorded as
6|it runs (127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows): every output must be identical to the
7|reference's, bit for bit, since only then are the model's tokens identical
8|(claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md). The timing chains the 20 layers, so
9|each call waits for the one before, as in a decode step. The grader prints
10|its verdict as JSON, and writes it to --out when given. It never writes into
11|the attempt folder, which holds only the Muse agent's files.
12|
13|  .venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_candidate.py <attempt folder> <slot> [--out FILE]
14|      [--baseline [SLOT=]FOLDER ...]
15|
16|--baseline times an earlier, already graded attempt in the same run as the
17|candidate, and adds `beats_baseline`. From round 2 on, the bar is the previous
18|round's final attempt for the slot (claude/adr/0009-rounds-build-on-each-other.md).
19|The two are timed in alternating repeats, so drift in the GPU's clocks reaches
20|both alike, and the candidate beats the baseline at a row count only if it is
21|faster in at least WINS_NEEDED of the REPEATS paired repeats: a one-sided sign
22|test at p < 0.01. The same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5% between
23|medians, so comparing medians alone would pass on noise. FOLDER alone is an
24|attempt for the same slot. For routing+combine, give either one
25|routing+combine attempt or `routing=FOLDER` and `combine=FOLDER`.
26|"""
27|
28|import argparse
29|import json
30|import math
31|import statistics
32|import sys
33|import time
34|import traceback
35|from pathlib import Path
36|
37|import mlx.core as mx
38|import numpy as np
39|
40|sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent))
41|import gpu_lock  # noqa: E402
42|import slots  # noqa: E402
43|
44|ROWS = (1, 8, 32)
45|REPEATS = 30
46|WINS_NEEDED = next(  # 22 of 30
47|    k
48|    for k in range(REPEATS + 1)
49|    if sum(math.comb(REPEATS, i) for i in range(k, REPEATS + 1)) / 2**REPEATS < 0.01
50|)
51|
52|
53|def parts(slot):
54|    return ["routing", "combine"] if slot == "routing+combine" else [slot]
55|
56|
57|def load(attempt, slot):
58|    spec = json.loads((attempt / "spec.json").read_text())
59|    sources = [
60|        p.read_text()
61|        for p in sorted(attempt.glob("block-*.metal"), key=lambda p: int(p.stem[6:]))
62|    ]
63|    specs = spec if slot == "routing+combine" else {slot: spec}
64|    return {p: slots.build(specs[p], sources, p) for p in parts(slot)}
65|
66|
67|def baselines(values, slot):
68|    """The --baseline attempts' functions by part; they must cover the slot's parts."""
69|    fns = {}
70|    for value in values:
71|        name, sep, folder = value.rpartition("=")
72|        name = name if sep else slot
73|        if name not in slots.SLOTS:
74|            sys.exit(f"--baseline {value}: unknown slot {name!r}")
75|        try:
76|            fns |= load(Path(folder), name)
77|        except Exception as e:
78|            sys.exit(f"--baseline {value}: can't load it: {short_error(e)}")
79|    if sorted(fns) != sorted(parts(slot)):
80|        sys.exit(f"--baseline must cover {parts(slot)}, not {sorted(fns)}")
81|    return fns
82|
83|
84|def ulp_bf16(r):
85|    """bfloat16's unit in the last place at |r|, floored at |r| = 0.001 (brief, G2)."""
86|    exp = np.floor(np.log2(np.maximum(np.abs(r), 1e-3)))
87|    return 2.0 ** (exp - 7)
88|
89|
90|def differences(g, r):
91|    """Elements of *g* that aren't *r*'s bit for bit, and the largest gap in units
92|    in the last place (floored at |r| = 0.001); "at" is the flat index of it."""
93|    differ = (g != r) & ~(np.isnan(g) & np.isnan(r))
94|    out = {"differ": int(differ.sum()), "max_ulp": 0.0}
95|    if out["differ"]:
96|        with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
97|            over = np.nan_to_num(np.abs(g - r) / ulp_bf16(r), nan=1e9, posinf=1e9)
98|        out |= {"max_ulp": float(min(over.max(), 1e9)), "at": int(over.argmax())}
99|    return out
100|
101|
102|def check_routing(fn, layer):
103|    ref_inds, ref_w = slots.ref_routing(layer["x"], layer["w_router"], layer["bias"])
104|    got = fn(x=layer["x"], w_router=layer["w_router"], bias=layer["bias"])
105|    inds, w = got["inds"], got["weights"]
106|    rows = layer["x"].shape[0]
107|    if inds.shape != (rows, slots.K) or w.shape != (rows, slots.K):
108|        return {
109|            "error": f"shapes inds {inds.shape}, weights {w.shape}; want ({rows}, 4)"
110|        }
111|    if inds.dtype != mx.uint32 or w.dtype != mx.float32:
112|        return {
113|            "error": f"dtypes inds {inds.dtype}, weights {w.dtype}; want uint32, float32"
114|        }
115|    inds, w = np.array(inds), np.array(w)
116|    ref_inds, ref_w = np.array(ref_inds), np.array(ref_w)
117|    if inds.max() >= slots.E:
118|        return {"error": f"expert index {int(inds.max())} out of range (60 experts)"}
119|    # Exact, in order: combine sums the 4 pairs in this order.
120|    differ = (inds != ref_inds).any(axis=1) | (w != ref_w).any(axis=1)
121|    same_order = (inds == ref_inds).all(axis=1)
122|    rel = np.abs(w - ref_w)[same_order] / np.maximum(np.abs(ref_w[same_order]), 1e-12)
123|    out = {
124|        "rows_differ": int(differ.sum()),
125|        "rows_other_experts": int(
126|            sum(set(a) != set(b) for a, b in zip(inds.tolist(), ref_inds.tolist()))
127|        ),
128|        "max_rel_err": float(rel.max()) if rel.size else 0.0,
129|    }
130|    if out["rows_differ"]:
131|        r = int(differ.argmax())
132|        out["example"] = (
133|            f"row {r}: experts {inds[r].tolist()}, weights {w[r].tolist()}; "
134|            f"want {ref_inds[r].tolist()}, {ref_w[r].tolist()}"
135|        )
136|    return out
137|
138|
139|def check_combine(fn, layer):

179|def link(a, prev):

184|def chained(fn, layers, names):
185|    """All 20 layers' calls, each one waiting for the one before, as in a decode step.
186|
187|    A call's smallest input is linked to the previous call's last output, the
188|    same for every function timed. Without the wait, the GPU overlaps the
189|    calls and hides a slow call's latency; mx.depends orders only the graph.
190|    """
191|    small = min(names, key=lambda n: layers[0][n].size)
192|    outs = []
193|    for layer in layers:
194|        args = {n: layer[n] for n in names}
195|        if outs:
196|            args[small] = link(args[small], outs[-1][-1])
197|        out = fn(**args)
198|        if isinstance(out, dict):
199|            out = list(out.values())
200|        outs.append(list(out) if isinstance(out, (tuple, list)) else [out])
201|    return outs

204|def timed(fn, layers, names):
205|    """Median µs per layer: the 20 layers' chained calls, then one wait for the GPU."""
206|    for _ in range(3):
207|        mx.eval(chained(fn, layers, names))
208|    times = []
209|    for _ in range(REPEATS):
210|        t0 = time.perf_counter()
211|        mx.eval(chained(fn, layers, names))
212|        times.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(layers))
213|    return round(statistics.median(times) * 1e6, 1)

216|def paired_times(fns, layers, names):
217|    """Per-repeat µs per layer of each function, in rotating order within each repeat."""
218|    calls = [lambda f=f: mx.eval(chained(f, layers, names)) for f in fns]
219|    for _ in range(3):
220|        for call in calls:
221|            call()
222|    times = [[] for _ in fns]
223|    for i in range(REPEATS):
224|        for j in [(i + k) % len(fns) for k in range(len(fns))]:
225|            t0 = time.perf_counter()
226|            calls[j]()
227|            times[j].append((time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(layers) * 1e6)
228|    return times

231|def short_error(e):
232|    """The exception, keeping only the compiler's error lines from Metal builds."""
233|    text = "".join(traceback.format_exception_only(type(e), e)).strip()
234|    lines = text.splitlines()
235|    if len(lines) > 1 and "Unable to build metal library" in lines[0]:
236|        keep = [lines[0]]
237|        for i, line in enumerate(lines):
238|            if "error:" in line:
239|                keep += lines[i : i + 3]
240|        text = "\n".join(keep)
241|    return text[:4000]

44|def ref_routing(x, w_router, bias):
45|    scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)
46|    inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=K - 1, axis=-1)[:, :K]
47|    w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)
48|    return inds, w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * SCALE

51|def ref_combine(y, weights, shared):
52|    return (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared

55|def ref_experts(x, inds, *weights):
56|    """The port's SwitchGLU on flat rows: [rows, D] and [rows, K] -> [rows, K, D]."""
57|    from mlx_lm.models.activations import swiglu
58|    from mlx_lm.models.switch_layers import _gather_sort, _scatter_unsort
59|
60|    gate, up, down = weights[0:3], weights[3:6], weights[6:9]
61|    xx = mx.expand_dims(x, (-2, -3))
62|    do_sort = inds.size >= 64
63|    idx, inv = inds, None
64|    if do_sort:
65|        xx, idx, inv = _gather_sort(xx, inds)
66|
67|    def qmm(a, w):
68|        return mx.gather_qmm(
69|            a,
70|            *w,
71|            rhs_indices=idx,
72|            transpose=False,
73|            group_size=32,
74|            bits=4,
75|            mode="affine",
76|            sorted_indices=do_sort,
77|        )
78|
79|    y = qmm(swiglu(qmm(xx, gate), qmm(xx, up)), down)
80|    if do_sort:
81|        y = _scatter_unsort(y, inv, inds.shape)
82|    return y.squeeze(-2)

97|def make_moe_call(routing=ref_routing, combine=ref_combine, experts=None):
98|    """MoE.__call__ with its slots swapped for *routing*, *combine*, *experts*.
99|
100|    With the references it gives the port's outputs bit for bit (checked by
101|    check_identity), so any difference comes from the swapped slot. With
102|    experts=None the port's own SwitchGLU runs.
103|    """

105|    def moe_call(self, x):
106|        lead = x.shape[:-1]
107|        flat = x.reshape(-1, D)
108|        bias = self.expert_bias.astype(mx.float32)
109|        inds, weights = routing(flat, self.router.weight, bias)
110|        if experts is None:
111|            y = self.experts(x, inds.reshape(*lead, K))
112|        else:
113|            w = expert_weights(self.experts)
114|            y = experts(flat, inds, *[w[n] for n in EXPERT_WEIGHTS])
115|        shared = self.shared_expert(x)
116|        out = combine(y.reshape(-1, K, D), weights, shared.reshape(-1, D))
117|        return out.reshape(*lead, D)

119|    return moe_call

303|def build(spec, sources, slot):
304|    """A function slot_inputs -> slot_outputs from Muse Spark's spec and Metal blocks."""
305|    slot_in, slot_out = SLOTS[slot]
306|    kernels = []
307|    for k in spec["kernels"]:
308|        header = "" if k.get("header_block") is None else sources[k["header_block"]]
309|        fn = mx.fast.metal_kernel(
310|            name=re.sub(r"\W", "_", str(k["name"])),
311|            input_names=list(k["inputs"]),
312|            output_names=[o["name"] for o in k["outputs"]],
313|            source=sources[k["source_block"]],
314|            header=header,
315|            atomic_outputs=bool(k.get("atomic_outputs", False)),
316|        )
317|        kernels.append((k, fn))
318|    missing = set(slot_out) - set(spec["slot_outputs"])
319|    if missing:
320|        raise ValueError(f"slot_outputs is missing {sorted(missing)}")
321|

9|## What it does
10|
11|`bench/grader/` is the contract every solution keeps: `slots.py` defines the three
12|slots (inputs, outputs, reference code) and turns a candidate's launch spec into
13|`mx.fast.metal_kernel` calls; `check_candidate.py` grades one attempt (G1 runs, G2
14|correct on captured inputs, piece timing vs reference and compiled); `time_candidates.py`
15|runs the deciding checks after merge (G2 end-to-end greedy tokens, G3 step period);
16|`gpu_lock.py` serializes all GPU jobs. It contributes no decode-step kernels itself —
17|its time costs are the reference slot costs it measures (the headroom) and the
18|slot-edge traffic it mandates (the floor).

219|- **Boundary floor — traffic the slots mandate** (unremovable within the
220|  interface, so it caps every saving): per layer, experts must write
221|  y [rows,4,768] bf16 (rows×6144 B) and combine must re-read it; routing must
222|  write inds+weights [rows,4] (rows×32 B) for experts/combine to read. Per step
223|  @32 rows: y 196 KB × 2 (write+read) × 20 layers = 7.9 MB → 0.04 ms at
224|  200 GB/s; inds/weights ≈ 41 KB → negligible. Saving floor ≈ 0.04 ms @32 rows
225|  (≈ 0.001 ms @1 row): fusing *within* slots captures essentially all of each
226|  slot's cost; cross-slot fusion is not expressible (`routing+combine` still
227|  runs the reference experts + shared expert between the parts, brief:171).
228|- **Piece timing vs G3 (builder warning):** the piece timing medians 30 repeats
229|  of 20-layer evals per part and sums the parts; G3 medians 3 full steps. A
230|  candidate can win the piece timing yet lose G3 (e.g. via cache/overlap effects
231|  the isolated evals don't see). The gap must exceed the repeat spread.

57|- **G2 combine** checks exact shape [rows,768] and bf16 dtype, and every element within 2 bf16 ULP of the reference with the ULP floored at |r| = 0.001 (`check_candidate.py:44-47,96-109`); `pass` iff all 20 layers pass (`check_candidate.py:133-138,192-197`). Inputs are captured from all 20 layers of one real decode step per row count (`slots.py:137-171`). In a `routing+combine` candidate each part is checked on its own and combine receives the captured reference weights, never the candidate's (brief:171, `check_candidate.py:96-98,181-187`). Piece timing (median of 30 × all-20-layers eval ÷ 20) must beat `mx.compile(ref_combine)` at all three row counts to stop the slot (brief:193,195, `check_candidate.py:209-226`).
58|- **What it can't see:** row counts other than 1, 8 and 32 — a decode step can have any row count from 1 to 32 (brief:24); inputs other than the captured ones (other prompts, later decode steps, non-reference weights from a fused routing kernel); threadgroup-memory use near the 32 KB limit (`slots.build` enforces only the 1024-thread cap, `slots.py:275`); results that depend on thread timing; the end-to-end greedy-token check (24 tokens at 1 and 32 requests, plain MLX and vLLM) and G3 full-step timing, which the team runs after merging (brief:185-186,195). Boundary checks will probe exactly these.
59|
60|### The GPU limits
61|
62|At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory (brief:98); `grid` counts threads, not threadgroups (brief:175). Hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 16 cores, SIMD width 32, `bfloat` available in Metal (brief:99).
63|
64|## Builders
65|
66|### builder-3-a — direction (a): single kernel, thread-per-output grid
67|
68|- **attempt-1** (`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1`): one thread per
69|  output element, grid rows×768, threadgroup 256; each thread weights 4 bf16
70|  values in fp32, rounds once, adds shared. Predicted 24 / 24 / 25, measured
71|  **17.2 / 17.0 / 18.5** µs per layer at 1/8/32 rows (compiled 22.9 / 26.2 /
72|  28.0). G1 pass, G2 pass (0 bad, max ULP 0.0/2.0/1.0). Beats compiled at all
73|  three row counts — stops the slot per the brief rule. Taught: the hyp-2
74|  ~24 µs "floor" was routing-specific (barriers + serial scan); a barrier-free
75|  streaming kernel's floor is ~17 µs (see notes.md).
76|
77|### builder-3-b — direction (b): single kernel, threadgroup-per-row with staged weights/shared
78|
79|- **attempt-2** (`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-2`): one threadgroup
80|  (192 threads) per row; weights + shared staged to ~3.1 KB threadgroup
81|  memory with vectorized u64 loads, y streamed with vectorized u64 loads,
82|  fp32 weight+sum (j = 0..3), `bfloat(acc)` + single-rounding bf16 add.
83|  Predicted 21 / 19 / 20, measured **17.9 / 16.1 / 18.1** µs per layer at
84|  1/8/32 rows vs compiled 20.9 / 23.0 / 27.9 (reference 24.8 / 24.0 /
85|  43.3). G1 pass, G2 pass (0 bad, max ULP 0.0 / 2.0 / 1.0, worst case the
86|  8-row 2-ULP touch — identical margins to attempt-1). Beats compiled at
87|  all rows. Taught: staging + one barrier cost nothing measurable vs
88|  direction (a) — both sit on the ~17 µs dispatch floor; first grading
89|  failed G2 on a 96-vs-192 u64/expert stride bug, fixed before the
90|  verdict (see notes.md). Slot already stopped at attempt-1; this is the
91|  direction-(b) datapoint, attempt-1 stays the pick.
92|
93|## Boundary checks
94|
95|*checked by boundary-3, 2026-11-03T22:11Z. Verdict: both attempts **pass** —
96|no defects. The 8-row 2.0-ULP touch is compiler FMA contraction, identified
97|and validated below; it saturates at 2.0 ULP on realistic inputs.*
98|
99|### attempt-1 (`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1`) — pass
100|
101|- **Row counts 1–32:** grid is `rows*768` threads, threadgroup 256
102|  (`spec.json:1`); `rows*768/256 = 3*rows` groups exactly for every integer
103|  row count, and `row = idx/768, d = idx - row*768` (`block-0.metal:12-14`)
104|  is exact for all `idx`. No row-dependent branches or constants. Max index
105|  `31*3072+767+2304 = 98303 < 32*3072` (`block-0.metal:17-23`); 256 threads
106|  ≤ 1024.
107|- **Threadgroup memory:** none used — no unwritten reads possible, 0 B of
108|  32 KB.
109|- **Thread timing:** threads are fully independent (no threadgroup memory,
110|  no atomics, disjoint outputs) — the result is deterministic.
111|- **Input assumptions:** none. Weights are used as arbitrary f32 with no
112|  range/sum/nonneg assumption (`block-0.metal:20-23`); `weights[r,j]` pairs
113|  with `y[r,j,:]` strictly positionally; both bf16 rounding points are kept
114|  (`bfloat(acc)` then the bf16 `+ shared`, `block-0.metal:25`).
115|
116|### attempt-2 (`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-2`) — pass
117|
118|- **Row counts 1–32:** grid `rows*192`, threadgroup 192 (`spec.json:1`) is
119|  exactly `rows` groups for every row count; `row = threadgroup id`
120|  (`block-0.metal:14`), each thread owns outputs `tid*4..tid*4+3`. All
121|  loops/bounds are row-independent constants. 192 threads ≤ 1024.
122|- **Unwritten reads:** none. `wsh[0..3]` is written by `tid < 4` and
123|  `shsh[0..767]` by all 192 threads (disjoint `tid*4` quads) before the
124|  single barrier (`block-0.metal:20-35`); all reads (`block-0.metal:37-40,62-65`)
125|  come after it. The barrier is unconditional and reached by every thread
126|  (the `tid<4` branch holds only a write).
127|- **Near the limit:** `4*4 + 768*4 = 3088 B`, 9.4% of 32 KB.
128|- **Thread timing:** all sharing is barrier-guarded disjoint writes plus
129|  read-only broadcast — deterministic.
130|- **Input assumptions:** none. Weights arbitrary f32, positional pairing
131|  (expert-`j` u64 block with `wj`, `block-0.metal:52-58`), both rounding
132|  points kept (`block-0.metal:62-65`); `bfloat(shsh[…])` is exact because
133|  `shsh` holds exact bf16 values, so the add is identical to attempt-1's.
134|  u64 loads are aligned and exact: shared row base `row*1536 B`, y row base
135|  `row*6144 B` (both 8-B aligned for all rows), sizes exactly 192/768 u64 —
136|  no overread (`block-0.metal:27-28,47,53`). Bit-exactness of the staging
137|  is corroborated by the identical G2 fingerprints (0.0/2.0/1.0) of both
138|  attempts: any staging error would move the touch.
139|
140|### The 2.0-ULP touch (both attempts): FMA contraction, not a defect
141|
142|CPU emulation (pure numpy, no GPU/model; bf16 RNE validated 0/20006 vs an
143|exact rational oracle) of candidate-vs-reference on all 629,760 captured
144|elements:
145|
146|- The reference is the pure mul-then-add chain: MLX v0.32.4
147|  `col_reduce_small` computes `op(new, totals) = new + totals`
148|  (`reduce_col.h`), and with the (32,4,1) strided-small dispatch
149|  (`reduce.cpp`, `threadgroup_y = min(8, …, 4) = 4`) each element lands on
150|  its own thread, so the reference association is the linear chain —
151|  bit-identical to an uncontracted candidate (IEEE add commutes).
152|- The Metal compiler FP-contracts the candidate's mul+add chain into FMA:
153|  the FMA-chain evaluation reproduces the grader fingerprint **exactly**,
154|  (0.0, 2.0, 1.0) at 1/8/32 rows, in two contraction shapes; all 120 pure
155|  mul association trees give ≤1.0 on rows8 with zero fingerprint matches —
156|  ruling out sum order as the source.
157|- Realistic risk: 0 bad elements in 20M triplet-resampled captured elements
158|  (true y/weights/shared joint distribution) for the FMA evaluations and
159|  trees alike; max exactly 2.0. Exceedance needs adversarially constructed
160|  cancellation (`shared ≈ −acc` to <2%): max 8.0 there, a construction
161|  absent from real data. The brief's G2 note (brief:184) budgets exactly
162|  this class of difference, and the remaining gates (captured-only G2,
163|  greedy-token end-to-end, G3 timing) are insensitive to it.
164|
165|Optional, not required: if the team wants nonzero margin at rows8, qualify
166|the accumulator `precise` (inhibits FMA contraction) and re-grade; both
167|attempts pass the gates as they stand.
168|
169|## Decision
170|
171|Best: `muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1` (builder-3-a, thread-per-output). Why: beats compiled at all three row counts by the wider relative margin (17.2 / 17.0 / 18.5 vs 22.9 / 26.2 / 28.0: −25 / −35 / −34%, against attempt-2's −14 / −30 / −35%); simpler (no threadgroup memory, fully independent threads); builder-3-b concedes it stays the pick. Both pass G1, G2 and boundary checks. No hardening round: both kernels sit on the ~17 µs/layer dispatch floor, flat across row counts with traffic ≤1.4 µs — no speed change worth making. The 8-row 2.0-ULP touch is FMA contraction, proven max exactly 2.0 on realistic inputs with zero exceedances (only adversarial `shared ≈ −acc` cancellation exceeds it); boundary-3's optional `precise`-accumulator margin-buy is noted for a later round, not worth a re-grade now. G3 should show: a faster step at all three concurrencies. Knock-out basis predicts −0.47 / −0.30 / −0.19 ms/step; the piece timing shows −0.10 / −0.10 / −0.24 ms/step ((22.4−17.2), (22.1−17.0), (30.7−18.5) µs/layer × 20 layers); the truth is between and G3 decides.

{"path":"muse-spark/round-2/exploration/README.md","content":"# Exploration: round 2 — analysis

**Version:** v1 · 2026-11-04T03:14:21Z · skill version 5

## Tracker

| Territory | Agent | Status | Inefficiencies | Updated |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `baseline-experts` | `explorer-baseline-experts` | exploring | — | 2026-11-04 03:14Z |
| `baseline-routing` | `explorer-baseline-routing` | exploring | — | 2026-11-04 03:14Z |
| `baseline-combine` | `explorer-baseline-combine` | exploring | — | 2026-11-04 03:14Z |
| `g3` | `explorer-g3` | exploring | — | 2026-11-04 03:14Z |
| `quantized-kernels` | `explorer-quantized-kernels` | exploring | — | 2026-11-04 03:14Z |
| `grader` | `explorer-grader` | exploring | — | 2026-11-04 03:14Z |

## Starting point

Round 2 builds on round 1 (`muse-spark/`, frozen, tagged `muse-round-1`) as measured independently by Claude in `claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` (2026-11-04, on `main` after merging round 1 at `a4995e4`). The grader changed for round 2 (ADR 0010, `claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md`): G2 is now bit-exact at decode sizes 1, 8, 32 rows and at prefill sizes 127, 1,016, 2,048 rows, and the piece timing chains the 20 layers through a link kernel. **No slot has a baseline.** No earlier attempt passes the current G2. A new attempt must pass G1 and the new G2 and beat the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 rows in the chained timing; there is no `--baseline` to pass. Each slot's starting point below is the attempt to build from, named in Claude's measurement (`claude/findings/muse-round-1.md`, *For round 2: baselines and starting points*).

Round 1's final attempts, their piece timings and G3 effects are summarised per slot. Piece timings are given in both forms where Claude measured them: the old independent timing (20 layers overlapped, `grade-<slot>.json`) and the new chained timing (`bench/micro/chain_timing.py`, `console-chain.txt`). G3 is the decode-step period change against the unchanged model in vLLM (median of 3 shuffled repeats, 128-token prompts; `console-vllm.txt`), the gate the brief decides on. Round 1's own prediction was from the piece timing (piece basis × 20 layers) and from knock-outs; both are quoted so the gap can be seen.

### Per slot

#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4`

- **What it is.** One fused per-pair kernel (256 threads per (row, expert-slot) pair, `rows*4` threadgroups), gate/up/down plus silu-mul fused, intermediates in threadgroup memory (3,840 B). Per-block numerics replicate MLX's `affine_gather_qvm` bitwise: strided-lane K accumulation plus `simd_sum` per 32-output block, silu computed entirely in bfloat16 (round after every op). See `muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4/notes.md` and `muse-spark/implementation/hyp-1-fused-experts.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Old grader, independent (Claude re-grade, `claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` §1): candidate 92.1 / 165.4 / 529.9 µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows against compiled reference 139.5 / 221.4 / 762.4 and reference 143.8 / 222.5 / 770.1 — beats both everywhere when overlapped. Chained (`console-chain.txt`): candidate 132.9 / 175.9 / 587.6 µs per layer against reference 80.3 / 239.6 / 797.6 — **66% slower than the reference at 1 row when chained** (52.6 µs × 20 layers ≈ 1.05 ms per step), faster at 8 and 32 rows. Round 1's own run gave 50.0 / 157.8 / 515.4 µs (independent); the 1-row figure is the outlier Claude already flagged as shifting between runs.
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Alone in vLLM: +1.16 ms (+21.6%) at 1 request, −0.82 ms (−5.7%) at 8, −4.15 ms (−13.9%) at 32 (`claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` §3). Round 1 predicted (piece basis) −0.29 / −1.22 / −5.01 ms and (knock-out basis) −0.40 / −1.30 / −3.67 ms to −0.5 / −2.5 / −8.6 ms (`muse-spark/summary.md`, `muse-spark/implementation/README.md` *Ready to test*). At 1 request the sign flips: predicted faster, measured slower. At 8 and 32 requests the measured saving is real but smaller than the piece basis. The compiled reference alone changes the step by +0.07 / +0.02 / −0.10 ms, so the attempt beats the compiled reference at 8 and 32 requests and loses to both at 1 request (brief's G3 rule).
  - **Reason (measured).** The old piece timing overlapped the 20 layers' calls, hiding one call's latency. Chained, the kernel's latency shows. Claude's estimate from the code: at 1 row the grid is 4 threadgroups (one per pair), too few to fill the 16-core GPU, so one call takes long even when many calls together go fast. Round 1 called this occupancy starvation; attempt-4 doubled threads per pair to 256 to fight it and still chains slower than the reference at 1 row.
- **What keeps it from passing G2.** Exact at decode sizes only. Under the new grader (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/grade-exact-experts.json`): decode 1 / 8 / 32 rows differ 0 / 0 / 0 (pass); prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows differ 4,868,667 / 39,078,912 / 78,741,557 elements, up to 43 / 65 / 110.5 units in the last place (fail). Cause: the kernel copies `gather_qvm`'s arithmetic exactly, which is why it is bit-exact at decode sizes. From 60 rows on MLX switches its experts kernel from `gather_qvm` to `gather_qmm_rhs`, which rounds differently (`claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` §2, §6; dispatch in `muse-spark/exploration/territory-switch-layers.md` §G and `territory-quantized-kernels.md` §C). The grader never tested more than 32 rows in round 1.
- **Where it still spends its time.** The 1-row chained latency above (132.9 vs 80.3 µs per layer). Per-pair weight reads remain: at 32 rows the experts read 908 MB against 443 MB for the distinct experts (GPU counters, `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md` via round 1's analysis), half the bytes repeat reads, and even so the path runs at only 62 GB/s (31% of peak), so most of the cost is kernel efficiency, not bytes. Grouped designs that read each expert once lost in round 1's piece harness (duty-cycle ceiling ~55 GB/s; scan/chunk/barrier overhead) — see *What building taught* in `muse-spark/exploration/README.md`.

#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** One fused kernel per layer: router scores (matmul + sigmoid + bias), top-4 selection, weight normalise/scale. One 32-thread threadgroup per row; thread `t` computes experts `t` and `t+32`; thread 0 does the serial top-4 scan. See `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/notes.md` and `muse-spark/implementation/hyp-2-fused-routing.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Old grader, independent (Claude re-grade): candidate 25.3 / 24.3 / 68.9 µs per layer against compiled 31.5 / 42.7 / 87.6 and reference 39.9 / 83.5 / 101.2 — beats compiled everywhere. Round 1's own run: 28.5 / 23.6 / 41.8 µs. No chained figure was published for this slot; the new grader's chained timing is what round 2 must beat.
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Alone in vLLM: +0.19 ms (+3.4%) at 1 request, −0.40 ms (−2.8%) at 8, −0.49 ms (−1.6%) at 32. Round 1 predicted (piece basis) −0.15 / −0.49 / −0.47 ms and (knock-out basis) −0.9 / −1.2 / −1.4 ms. At 8 and 32 requests the measured saving tracks the piece basis, far below the knock-out basis. At 1 request the sign flips. Against the brief's G3 rule the attempt beats both the unchanged model and the compiled reference only at 32 requests; at 8 requests its range ends 0.05 ms below the compiled reference's; at 1 request it is slower than both. The compiled reference alone saves 0.22 / 0.18 / 0.16 ms, so part of the headroom is already taken by compiling the reference.
  - **Reason.** Round 1's builders found the piece harness prices a fused kernel at a ~24 µs per layer floor (dispatch/eval plus, for routing, two barriers and a serial 60-element scan on thread 0), not at one 6.81 µs launch; the reference's 12 kernels cost ~3 µs each when pipelined 20 deep. The knock-out and the piece harness therefore disagree on the slot's standalone cost, and G3 sides closer to the piece harness at 8/32 rows. The 1-row case has a single threadgroup wavefront on a 16-core GPU, so fixed cost amortises worst there.
- **What keeps it from passing G2.** Experts and order match; weights differ in the last bits at every size. Under the new grader (`grade-exact-routing.json`): rows differing 20 / 159 / 638 at decode 1 / 8 / 32 rows (of 20 / 160 / 640 rows summed over 20 layers) and 2,518 / 16,187 / 32,743 at prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows; rows with other experts 0 at every size; max relative error 2.6×10⁻⁶ at decode, up to 8.7×10⁻⁶ in the prefill. The old G2 allowed 10⁻⁴ relative, so this passed with ~40× margin in round 1; the new G2 asks for equality in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. Cause (Claude's reading): the reference's order of operations and rounding points for the router product and the weight sum — for example the float32 sum order of `x @ w_router.T` and of `w.sum(...)` — differ from the kernel's serial 768-term accumulation and left-to-right 4-term sum. Greedy decoding turns any such difference into different tokens: within G2's old tolerances this attempt still changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences in 24 tokens.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Traffic is negligible (~4 MB per step; w_router 184 KB per layer per row read once). The cost is the fused kernel's fixed floor (~24 µs per layer in the old harness) plus the serial top-4 scan. Compute (92k FLOP per row) is negligible either way.

#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** One fused kernel per layer: weight the 4 experts' bfloat16 outputs by the float32 weights, sum in float32, round once to bfloat16, add the shared expert. One thread per output element on a `rows×768` grid, threadgroup 256, no threadgroup memory. See `muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1/notes.md` and `muse-spark/implementation/hyp-3-fused-combine.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Old grader, independent (Claude re-grade): candidate 18.6 / 17.0 / 18.9 µs per layer against compiled 23.8 / 26.1 / 32.0 and reference 23.1 / 22.5 / 39.5 — beats compiled everywhere. Round 1's own run: 17.2 / 17.0 / 18.5 µs.
- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Alone in vLLM: −0.51 ms (−9.6%) at 1 request, −0.71 ms (−4.9%) at 8, −0.39 ms (−1.3%) at 32. Round 1 predicted (piece basis) −0.10 / −0.10 / −0.24 ms and (knock-out basis) −0.47 / −0.30 / −0.19 ms. The measured saving exceeds the piece basis at 1 and 8 requests and sits between the two bases at 32. Against the brief's G3 rule the attempt beats both the unchanged model and the compiled reference at 8 requests; at 1 request its range overlaps the compiled reference's; at 32 requests it is 0.12 ms ahead, within the spread. The compiled reference alone saves 0.29 / 0.26 / 0.27 ms.
- **What keeps it from passing G2.** A handful of elements differ from 8 rows on. Under the new grader (`grade-exact-combine.json`): decode 1 row differ 0 (pass), 8 rows differ 2 (max 2.0 ULP), 32 rows differ 2 (max 1.0 ULP); prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows differ 6 / 50 / 130 elements, up to 1 / 16 / 32 ULP (fail). The old G2 allowed 2 ULP, so this passed in round 1 (the 8-row 2.0-ULP touch was proven to be Metal FMA contraction of the mul+add chain, max exactly 2.0 on realistic inputs). The new G2 asks for every element equal. Cause (Claude's reading): the reference's order of operations for the sum over the 4 pairs — the candidate's left-to-right chain contracts to FMAs while MLX's `col_reduce_small` reduction associates differently — so a few elements round differently. The fix must reproduce the reference's association and rounding points, and suppress contraction where it changes the result.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At the bare dispatch floor (~17 µs per layer, flat across row counts; traffic ≤1.4 µs at 200 GB/s). Both round-1 combine directions sit on this floor; no kernel-body change in round 1 moved it.

#### All three together

In vLLM all three attempts together change the step by +0.98 ms (+18.3%) at 1 request, +0.16 ms (+1.1%) at 8, −1.76 ms (−5.9%) at 32, against round 1's prediction of −0.54 / −1.81 / −5.72 ms. The parts do not add: at 8 requests the three alone save 0.82, 0.40 and 0.71 ms but together cost 0.16 ms; at 32 requests the experts kernel alone saves 4.15 ms and all three together save 1.76 ms. Together they launch 567 kernels per step at 1 request against 967 unchanged, so a shorter list of kernels runs slower. **Measured but not explained** in Claude's measurement; the cause is an open question for round 2 (see territory `g3` below). The three compiled references together save 0.50 / 0.56 / 0.24 ms in vLLM (0.62 / 0.52 / 0.26 ms in plain MLX) without any new kernel.

In the model every attempt changes tokens: with 32 requests in vLLM each one alone changes 7 to 12 of the 32 sequences from the first generated token, and all three together change 13. The compiled references change none, so the unchanged model is deterministic and every difference comes from the attempts. The experts cause is the prefill (above); routing's and combine's small rounding differences, within the old G2 tolerances, are enough to flip greedy tokens on these near-tie prompts.

Round 1 ran the grader 29 times on the experts slot for the 4 attempts its summary counts, 18 of those on attempt-1 (editing the same folder between runs). Skill version 5 keeps the rule that one grader run is one attempt.

### What is left

Confirmed inefficiencies not yet built or not fully removed, ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar). Savings are the headroom the starting point leaves: the chained piece gap where Claude measured it, otherwise the G3 gap to the compiled reference. Exactness is listed first where it blocks the slot entirely — a faster kernel that fails G2 saves nothing.

1. **Experts: exact at prefill sizes, and faster chained at 1 row.** The slot is 0.92 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 row and 14.67 ms of 28.19 ms (52%) at 32 rows (Claude's knock-outs, round 1 analysis). The starting point already beats the compiled reference when overlapped at all rows and chained at 8/32 rows, but it (a) fails G2 at every prefill size because it matches `gather_qvm` while MLX runs `gather_qmm_rhs` from 60 rows on, and (b) loses 52.6 µs per layer chained at 1 row (≈1.05 ms per step, matching G3's +1.16 ms). Removing (a) is a correctness gate, not a saving; removing (b) is worth up to ~1.1 ms per step at 1 request against the reference, on top of keeping the 8/32-row chained wins (63.7 and 210.0 µs per layer against the reference). This is Claude's questions 1 and 2 for round 2.
2. **Routing: exact float32 arithmetic.** The slot costs 1.02 ms at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 (knock-outs); the starting point's G3 headroom over the compiled reference is negative at 1 request (+0.19 against the compiled reference's −0.22 ms) and small at 8/32. The blocker is exactness: every row's weights differ in the last bits while the experts and their order already match. Reproducing the reference's sum orders and rounding points (the router product, the sigmoid, the 4-term normalise sum) makes the slot pass G2; only then can a chained-timing win over the compiled reference be banked. Claude's question 3 (routing half).
3. **Combine: exact 4-term sum.** The slot costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32. The starting point differs in only 2 elements at decode 8/32 rows and 130 at the largest prefill size — the smallest exactness gap of the three — from FMA contraction against the reference's reduction order. Reproducing that order (and suppressing contraction, e.g. with a `precise` accumulator, an option round 1's boundary check already named) should make the slot pass G2 with the kernel otherwise unchanged, keeping its G3 win at 8 requests and contesting 1 and 32. Claude's question 3 (combine half).
4. **Why the three together lose time each saves alone.** At 8 requests in vLLM the three alone save 1.93 ms in sum and together cost 0.16 ms; at 32 requests the experts alone save 4.15 ms and together 1.76 ms. No slot's kernel explains the interaction; it is measured but not explained. Until it is understood, per-slot piece wins may not compose into a G3 win. Claude's question 4.

**Slots not yet tried.** `routing+combine` (brief: both slots, each with its own kernels, in one candidate; the grader tests each part on its own and the combine part receives the reference routing weights). Round 1 graded routing and combine as separate candidates and never as one `routing-combine` folder. It remains available; since the parts are graded independently it is packaging unless a shared design emerges, but it is the only slot combination no round has attempted.

**Recommendations outside the slots** stand as written in `muse-spark/summary.md` (round 1) and `muse-spark/exploration/README.md` *Recommendations*; Claude's measurement did not test them. In brief: attention K/V re-read per query head (GQA layout miss, up to ~2 ms at 32 rows); split-K partial traffic from 14 rows (rough upper bound ≈2.4 ms at 32 rows, unmeasured); 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers + 60 contiguous copies per step (−0.21 ms measured at 8 rows, `squeeze(0)` fix); ~2 ms engine CPU per 1-row step while CPU-bound (≈0.5 ms of small Python fixes). They are for surucuonur's team; no hypothesis targets them.

### Refuted claims

No one chases these again.

- `ineff-runs-3` (round 1, refuted): the micro sorted/unsorted gaps (5.08→3.82, 8.12→5.65, 15.02→9.63 ms) measure per-pair vs grouped kernel choice on identically ordered pairs, not pair order — sorting serving's pairs at 8 rows cannot yield 1.3 ms, and the 32-row gap was never collected. See `muse-spark/exploration/README.md` *Refuted claims*.
- Round 1's implicit timing claim — that the old independent piece timing ranks attempts as the model does — is refuted by Claude's chained measurement: the experts starting point was 29% faster than the reference overlapped and 66% slower chained at 1 row. Round 2 ranks by the chained timing only.

# Territory: baseline-routing — the routing slot's starting point under bit-exact G2

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
- **Status:** exploring
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T03:18:47Z
- **Next:** post ineff-baseline-routing-1..4, then fold any notes

## What it does

In every decode step and every prefill chunk, each of the 20 layers runs
`MoE.__call__` (`third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:217-232`): cast the
layer input to float32, multiply by the router weight transposed, sigmoid, add the
expert bias only for selection, take the top-4 experts per row, gather their
*unbiased* scores, normalise them (divide by their sum + 1e-20) and scale by 2.5.
The slot outputs `inds` [rows,4] uint32 and `weights` [rows,4] float32; `inds`
feeds the experts slot, `weights` feeds combine, which sums the 4 (expert,
weight) pairs *in the emitted order* — which is why round 2's G2 requires the
same experts, the same weights and the same order, bit for bit
(`claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:25-27`,
`bench/grader/check_candidate.py:119-121`).

The starting point is round 1's `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1`: one fused
Metal kernel per layer (`block-0.metal`, 78 lines; `spec.json`: one kernel
`fused_routing`, grid `rows*32`, threadgroup 32). One threadgroup per row stages
`x[row]` (768 bfloat16→float32) in threadgroup memory, each of the 32 threads
computes 1–2 experts' 768-term dot products serially, writes
`sigmoid(acc)` to `scores[60]`, and thread 0 alone does a serial insertion
top-4 scan over the biased scores and writes `inds`/`weights`
(`block-0.metal:10-78`).

## The headline finding (details in ineff-baseline-routing-1 and -2)

Under the new grader the starting point fails G2 at **every** size while the
experts and their order always match (`rows_other_experts` 0 everywhere):
rows differing 20/159/638 at decode 1/8/32 rows (of 20/160/640 rows summed over
20 layers — 100% / 99.4% / 99.7% of rows) and 2,518/16,187/32,743 at prefill
127/1,016/2,048 rows (of 2,540/20,320/40,960 — 99.1% / 79.7% / 79.9%), max
relative error 2.6e-06 at decode and up to 8.7e-06 in the prefill
(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/grade-exact-routing.json`, quoted in
`muse-spark/round-2/exploration/README.md:39`). The experts match because
selection is insensitive to last-bit score differences (no captured row is a
near-tie at the 4th/5th place); the weights expose every last-bit difference
in the 4 selected scores. Section 3 below pins down, op by op, which of the
reference's operations the kernel reproduces exactly and which it does not:
**the divergence is in the scores — the router matmul's float32 accumulation
order (which changes with `rows`) and MLX's sigmoid formula — not in the
4-term weight sum, whose order the kernel already matches.**

## Checklist

### 1. The starting-point kernel — `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/{block-0.metal,spec.json,notes.md}`

- **Callers:** the grader builds it via `slots.build` into one
  `mx.fast.metal_kernel` (`bench/grader/slots.py:303-345`) and calls it once per
  layer per size in G2 (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py:286`) and in the
  chained piece timing (`check_candidate.py:184-213`). In the model it would
  replace the routing part of `make_moe_call` (`slots.py:97-119`). Shapes:
  rows = 1/8/32 (decode), 127/1,016/2,048 (prefill); grid `rows*32` threads,
  one 32-thread threadgroup per row at every size (`spec.json`, block-0:10-11).
- **Callees:** none — one Metal kernel. It launches 1 kernel/layer (20/step)
  where the reference launches ~12/layer (240/step; brief:47).
- **Data:** in: `x` [rows,768] bfloat16, `w_router` [60,768] float32, `bias`
  [60] float32; out: `inds` [rows,4] uint32, `weights` [rows,4] float32
  (`spec.json`; brief:30-36). Threadgroup memory: `xsh[768]` float +
  `scores[60]` float = 3,312 B of 32 KB (`block-0.metal:13-14`).
- **Neighbours:** before: post-attention layernorm output reshaped to
  [rows,768] (`mobilemoe.py:258`, `slots.py:107`); after: experts gather by
  `inds`, combine sums `(y * weights[...,None])` in emitted order
  (`mobilemoe.py:230-231`). A replacement must keep shapes, dtypes, the
  unbiased-score rule and — new in round 2 — the reference's exact per-row
  order (see Invariants).
- **Cost:** measured (old, independent timing; Claude re-grade,
  `claude/findings/muse-round-1.md:47`): candidate 25.3/24.3/68.9 µs per layer
  at 1/8/32 rows vs compiled reference 31.5/42.7/87.6 and reference
  39.9/83.5/101.2. Round 1's own run: 28.5/23.6/41.8 (`notes.md:33-37`).
  No chained figure exists for this slot yet (round-2 README:36) — the chained
  timing is the bar a round-2 attempt must beat. End to end (G3, vLLM,
  `muse-round-1.md:85-86`): attempt alone +0.185/−0.397/−0.490 ms/step vs the
  compiled reference's −0.220/−0.183/−0.157, i.e. the attempt is ~0.41 ms/step
