16|## Starting point
17|
18|Round 2 builds on round 1 (`muse-spark/`, frozen, tagged `muse-round-1`) as measured independently by Claude in `claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` (2026-11-04, on `main` after merging round 1 at `a4995e4`). The grader changed for round 2 (ADR 0010, `claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md`): G2 is now bit-exact at decode sizes 1, 8, 32 rows and at prefill sizes 127, 1,016, 2,048 rows, and the piece timing chains the 20 layers through a link kernel. **No slot has a baseline.** No earlier attempt passes the current G2. A new attempt must pass G1 and the new G2 and beat the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 rows in the chained timing; there is no `--baseline` to pass. Each slot's starting point below is the attempt to build from, named in Claude's measurement (`claude/findings/muse-round-1.md`, *For round 2: baselines and starting points*).
19|
20|Round 1's final attempts, their piece timings and G3 effects are summarised per slot. Piece timings are given in both forms where Claude measured them: the old independent timing (20 layers overlapped, `grade-<slot>.json`) and the new chained timing (`bench/micro/chain_timing.py`, `console-chain.txt`). G3 is the decode-step period change against the unchanged model in vLLM (median of 3 shuffled repeats, 128-token prompts; `console-vllm.txt`), the gate the brief decides on. Round 1's own prediction was from the piece timing (piece basis × 20 layers) and from knock-outs; both are quoted so the gap can be seen.
21|
22|### Per slot
23|
24|#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4`
25|
26|- **What it is.** One fused per-pair kernel (256 threads per (row, expert-slot) pair, `rows*4` threadgroups), gate/up/down plus silu-mul fused, intermediates in threadgroup memory (3,840 B). Per-block numerics replicate MLX's `affine_gather_qvm` bitwise: strided-lane K accumulation plus `simd_sum` per 32-output block, silu computed entirely in bfloat16 (round after every op). See `muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4/notes.md` and `muse-spark/implementation/hyp-1-fused-experts.md`.
27|- **Piece timing.** Old grader, independent (Claude re-grade, `claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` §1): candidate 92.1 / 165.4 / 529.9 µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows against compiled reference 139.5 / 221.4 / 762.4 and reference 143.8 / 222.5 / 770.1 — beats both everywhere when overlapped. Chained (`console-chain.txt`): candidate 132.9 / 175.9 / 587.6 µs per layer against reference 80.3 / 239.6 / 797.6 — **66% slower than the reference at 1 row when chained** (52.6 µs × 20 layers ≈ 1.05 ms per step), faster at 8 and 32 rows. Round 1's own run gave 50.0 / 157.8 / 515.4 µs (independent); the 1-row figure is the outlier Claude already flagged as shifting between runs.
28|- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Alone in vLLM: +1.16 ms (+21.6%) at 1 request, −0.82 ms (−5.7%) at 8, −4.15 ms (−13.9%) at 32 (`claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` §3). Round 1 predicted (piece basis) −0.29 / −1.22 / −5.01 ms and (knock-out basis) −0.40 / −1.30 / −3.67 ms to −0.5 / −2.5 / −8.6 ms (`muse-spark/summary.md`, `muse-spark/implementation/README.md` *Ready to test*). At 1 request the sign flips: predicted faster, measured slower. At 8 and 32 requests the measured saving is real but smaller than the piece basis. The compiled reference alone changes the step by +0.07 / +0.02 / −0.10 ms, so the attempt beats the compiled reference at 8 and 32 requests and loses to both at 1 request (brief's G3 rule).
29|  - **Reason (measured).** The old piece timing overlapped the 20 layers' calls, hiding one call's latency. Chained, the kernel's latency shows. Claude's estimate from the code: at 1 row the grid is 4 threadgroups (one per pair), too few to fill the 16-core GPU, so one call takes long even when many calls together go fast. Round 1 called this occupancy starvation; attempt-4 doubled threads per pair to 256 to fight it and still chains slower than the reference at 1 row.
30|- **What keeps it from passing G2.** Exact at decode sizes only. Under the new grader (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/grade-exact-experts.json`): decode 1 / 8 / 32 rows differ 0 / 0 / 0 (pass); prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows differ 4,868,667 / 39,078,912 / 78,741,557 elements, up to 43 / 65 / 110.5 units in the last place (fail). Cause: the kernel copies `gather_qvm`'s arithmetic exactly, which is why it is bit-exact at decode sizes. From 60 rows on MLX switches its experts kernel from `gather_qvm` to `gather_qmm_rhs`, which rounds differently (`claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` §2, §6; dispatch in `muse-spark/exploration/territory-switch-layers.md` §G and `territory-quantized-kernels.md` §C). The grader never tested more than 32 rows in round 1.
31|- **Where it still spends its time.** The 1-row chained latency above (132.9 vs 80.3 µs per layer). Per-pair weight reads remain: at 32 rows the experts read 908 MB against 443 MB for the distinct experts (GPU counters, `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md` via round 1's analysis), half the bytes repeat reads, and even so the path runs at only 62 GB/s (31% of peak), so most of the cost is kernel efficiency, not bytes. Grouped designs that read each expert once lost in round 1's piece harness (duty-cycle ceiling ~55 GB/s; scan/chunk/barrier overhead) — see *What building taught* in `muse-spark/exploration/README.md`.
32|
33|#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1`
34|
35|- **What it is.** One fused kernel per layer: router scores (matmul + sigmoid + bias), top-4 selection, weight normalise/scale. One 32-thread threadgroup per row; thread `t` computes experts `t` and `t+32`; thread 0 does the serial top-4 scan. See `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/notes.md` and `muse-spark/implementation/hyp-2-fused-routing.md`.
36|- **Piece timing.** Old grader, independent (Claude re-grade): candidate 25.3 / 24.3 / 68.9 µs per layer against compiled 31.5 / 42.7 / 87.6 and reference 39.9 / 83.5 / 101.2 — beats compiled everywhere. Round 1's own run: 28.5 / 23.6 / 41.8 µs. No chained figure was published for this slot; the new grader's chained timing is what round 2 must beat.
37|- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Alone in vLLM: +0.19 ms (+3.4%) at 1 request, −0.40 ms (−2.8%) at 8, −0.49 ms (−1.6%) at 32. Round 1 predicted (piece basis) −0.15 / −0.49 / −0.47 ms and (knock-out basis) −0.9 / −1.2 / −1.4 ms. At 8 and 32 requests the measured saving tracks the piece basis, far below the knock-out basis. At 1 request the sign flips. Against the brief's G3 rule the attempt beats both the unchanged model and the compiled reference only at 32 requests; at 8 requests its range ends 0.05 ms below the compiled reference's; at 1 request it is slower than both. The compiled reference alone saves 0.22 / 0.18 / 0.16 ms, so part of the headroom is already taken by compiling the reference.
38|  - **Reason.** Round 1's builders found the piece harness prices a fused kernel at a ~24 µs per layer floor (dispatch/eval plus, for routing, two barriers and a serial 60-element scan on thread 0), not at one 6.81 µs launch; the reference's 12 kernels cost ~3 µs each when pipelined 20 deep. The knock-out and the piece harness therefore disagree on the slot's standalone cost, and G3 sides closer to the piece harness at 8/32 rows. The 1-row case has a single threadgroup wavefront on a 16-core GPU, so fixed cost amortises worst there.
39|- **What keeps it from passing G2.** Experts and order match; weights differ in the last bits at every size. Under the new grader (`grade-exact-routing.json`): rows differing 20 / 159 / 638 at decode 1 / 8 / 32 rows (of 20 / 160 / 640 rows summed over 20 layers) and 2,518 / 16,187 / 32,743 at prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows; rows with other experts 0 at every size; max relative error 2.6×10⁻⁶ at decode, up to 8.7×10⁻⁶ in the prefill. The old G2 allowed 10⁻⁴ relative, so this passed with ~40× margin in round 1; the new G2 asks for equality in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. Cause (Claude's reading): the reference's order of operations and rounding points for the router product and the weight sum — for example the float32 sum order of `x @ w_router.T` and of `w.sum(...)` — differ from the kernel's serial 768-term accumulation and left-to-right 4-term sum. Greedy decoding turns any such difference into different tokens: within G2's old tolerances this attempt still changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences in 24 tokens.
40|- **Where it still spends its time.** Traffic is negligible (~4 MB per step; w_router 184 KB per layer per row read once). The cost is the fused kernel's fixed floor (~24 µs per layer in the old harness) plus the serial top-4 scan. Compute (92k FLOP per row) is negligible either way.
41|
42|#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1`
43|
44|- **What it is.** One fused kernel per layer: weight the 4 experts' bfloat16 outputs by the float32 weights, sum in float32, round once to bfloat16, add the shared expert. One thread per output element on a `rows×768` grid, threadgroup 256, no threadgroup memory. See `muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1/notes.md` and `muse-spark/implementation/hyp-3-fused-combine.md`.
45|- **Piece timing.** Old grader, independent (Claude re-grade): candidate 18.6 / 17.0 / 18.9 µs per layer against compiled 23.8 / 26.1 / 32.0 and reference 23.1 / 22.5 / 39.5 — beats compiled everywhere. Round 1's own run: 17.2 / 17.0 / 18.5 µs.
46|- **G3 effect vs prediction.** Alone in vLLM: −0.51 ms (−9.6%) at 1 request, −0.71 ms (−4.9%) at 8, −0.39 ms (−1.3%) at 32. Round 1 predicted (piece basis) −0.10 / −0.10 / −0.24 ms and (knock-out basis) −0.47 / −0.30 / −0.19 ms. The measured saving exceeds the piece basis at 1 and 8 requests and sits between the two bases at 32. Against the brief's G3 rule the attempt beats both the unchanged model and the compiled reference at 8 requests; at 1 request its range overlaps the compiled reference's; at 32 requests it is 0.12 ms ahead, within the spread. The compiled reference alone saves 0.29 / 0.26 / 0.27 ms.
47|- **What keeps it from passing G2.** A handful of elements differ from 8 rows on. Under the new grader (`grade-exact-combine.json`): decode 1 row differ 0 (pass), 8 rows differ 2 (max 2.0 ULP), 32 rows differ 2 (max 1.0 ULP); prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows differ 6 / 50 / 130 elements, up to 1 / 16 / 32 ULP (fail). The old G2 allowed 2 ULP, so this passed in round 1 (the 8-row 2.0-ULP touch was proven to be Metal FMA contraction of the mul+add chain, max exactly 2.0 on realistic inputs). The new G2 asks for every element equal. Cause (Claude's reading): the reference's order of operations for the sum over the 4 pairs — the candidate's left-to-right chain contracts to FMAs while MLX's `col_reduce_small` reduction associates differently — so a few elements round differently. The fix must reproduce the reference's association and rounding points, and suppress contraction where it changes the result.
48|- **Where it still spends its time.** At the bare dispatch floor (~17 µs per layer, flat across row counts; traffic ≤1.4 µs at 200 GB/s). Both round-1 combine directions sit on this floor; no kernel-body change in round 1 moved it.
49|
50|#### All three together
51|
52|In vLLM all three attempts together change the step by +0.98 ms (+18.3%) at 1 request, +0.16 ms (+1.1%) at 8, −1.76 ms (−5.9%) at 32, against round 1's prediction of −0.54 / −1.81 / −5.72 ms. The parts do not add: at 8 requests the three alone save 0.82, 0.40 and 0.71 ms but together cost 0.16 ms; at 32 requests the experts kernel alone saves 4.15 ms and all three together save 1.76 ms. Together they launch 567 kernels per step at 1 request against 967 unchanged, so a shorter list of kernels runs slower. **Measured but not explained** in Claude's measurement; the cause is an open question for round 2 (see territory `g3` below). The three compiled references together save 0.50 / 0.56 / 0.24 ms in vLLM (0.62 / 0.52 / 0.26 ms in plain MLX) without any new kernel.
53|
54|In the model every attempt changes tokens: with 32 requests in vLLM each one alone changes 7 to 12 of the 32 sequences from the first generated token, and all three together change 13. The compiled references change none, so the unchanged model is deterministic and every difference comes from the attempts. The experts cause is the prefill (above); routing's and combine's small rounding differences, within the old G2 tolerances, are enough to flip greedy tokens on these near-tie prompts.
55|
56|Round 1 ran the grader 29 times on the experts slot for the 4 attempts its summary counts, 18 of those on attempt-1 (editing the same folder between runs). Skill version 5 keeps the rule that one grader run is one attempt.
57|
58|### What is left
59|
60|Confirmed inefficiencies not yet built or not fully removed, ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar). Savings are the headroom the starting point leaves: the chained piece gap where Claude measured it, otherwise the G3 gap to the compiled reference. Exactness is listed first where it blocks the slot entirely — a faster kernel that fails G2 saves nothing.
61|
62|1. **Experts: exact at prefill sizes, and faster chained at 1 row.** The slot is 0.92 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 row and 14.67 ms of 28.19 ms (52%) at 32 rows (Claude's knock-outs, round 1 analysis). The starting point already beats the compiled reference when overlapped at all rows and chained at 8/32 rows, but it (a) fails G2 at every prefill size because it matches `gather_qvm` while MLX runs `gather_qmm_rhs` from 60 rows on, and (b) loses 52.6 µs per layer chained at 1 row (≈1.05 ms per step, matching G3's +1.16 ms). Removing (a) is a correctness gate, not a saving; removing (b) is worth up to ~1.1 ms per step at 1 request against the reference, on top of keeping the 8/32-row chained wins (63.7 and 210.0 µs per layer against the reference). This is Claude's questions 1 and 2 for round 2.
63|2. **Routing: exact float32 arithmetic.** The slot costs 1.02 ms at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 (knock-outs); the starting point's G3 headroom over the compiled reference is negative at 1 request (+0.19 against the compiled reference's −0.22 ms) and small at 8/32. The blocker is exactness: every row's weights differ in the last bits while the experts and their order already match. Reproducing the reference's sum orders and rounding points (the router product, the sigmoid, the 4-term normalise sum) makes the slot pass G2; only then can a chained-timing win over the compiled reference be banked. Claude's question 3 (routing half).
64|3. **Combine: exact 4-term sum.** The slot costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32. The starting point differs in only 2 elements at decode 8/32 rows and 130 at the largest prefill size — the smallest exactness gap of the three — from FMA contraction against the reference's reduction order. Reproducing that order (and suppressing contraction, e.g. with a `precise` accumulator, an option round 1's boundary check already named) should make the slot pass G2 with the kernel otherwise unchanged, keeping its G3 win at 8 requests and contesting 1 and 32. Claude's question 3 (combine half).
65|4. **Why the three together lose time each saves alone.** At 8 requests in vLLM the three alone save 1.93 ms in sum and together cost 0.16 ms; at 32 requests the experts alone save 4.15 ms and together 1.76 ms. No slot's kernel explains the interaction; it is measured but not explained. Until it is understood, per-slot piece wins may not compose into a G3 win. Claude's question 4.
66|
67|**Slots not yet tried.** `routing+combine` (brief: both slots, each with its own kernels, in one candidate; the grader tests each part on its own and the combine part receives the reference routing weights). Round 1 graded routing and combine as separate candidates and never as one `routing-combine` folder. It remains available; since the parts are graded independently it is packaging unless a shared design emerges, but it is the only slot combination no round has attempted.
68|
69|**Recommendations outside the slots** stand as written in `muse-spark/summary.md` (round 1) and `muse-spark/exploration/README.md` *Recommendations*; Claude's measurement did not test them. In brief: attention K/V re-read per query head (GQA layout miss, up to ~2 ms at 32 rows); split-K partial traffic from 14 rows (rough upper bound ≈2.4 ms at 32 rows, unmeasured); 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers + 60 contiguous copies per step (−0.21 ms measured at 8 rows, `squeeze(0)` fix); ~2 ms engine CPU per 1-row step while CPU-bound (≈0.5 ms of small Python fixes). They are for surucuonur's team; no hypothesis targets them.

1|# Inefficiency: starting point matches `gather_qvm` but prefill runs `gather_qmm_rhs` — G2 fails at every prefill size
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-experts
4|- **Status:** confirmed
5|- **Version:** 2
6|- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T03:22:51Z
7|- **Next:** verifier to confirm dispatch threshold and the two rounding differences
8|
9|## Slot
10|
11|`experts`
12|
13|## What happens
14|
15|Attempt-4's `qvm_block` (`muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4/block-1.metal:20-40`)
16|is a bit-faithful replica of MLX `affine_gather_qvm`/`qvm_impl`: each lane
17|accumulates its strided `K` elements serially in float32, dequantizing on
18|the fly as `x * (scale * q + bias)` (`block-1.metal:33-34`), then a
19|`simd_sum` tree reduces across the 32 lanes. That is exactly the kernel
20|MLX dispatches at decode sizes, so decode G2 is bit-exact.
21|
22|From 60 rows the reference dispatches a different kernel. Dispatch
23|(MLX v0.32.4 `quantized.cpp:2005,2012,2073-2093`, via round 1
24|`muse-spark/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md` §A/§C and
25|`territory-switch-layers.md` §G): `gather_qmm_rhs` needs
26|`M==1 && B>=16 && right_sorted_ && B/E>=4`, `B = rows*4`, `E = 60`, i.e.
27|rows ≥ 60. Decode 1/8/32 rows (`B/E` ≤ 2.13) never fire it; prefill
28|127/1,016/2,048 rows (`B/E` = 8.5/67.7/136.5) always do. Note the two
29|distinct thresholds: the reference sorts from `inds.size >= 64` (rows ≥
30|16, `bench/grader/slots.py:62`, `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/switch_layers.py:181`),
31|but sorting alone does not switch the kernel below 60 rows — decode at
32|32 rows is sorted and still `gather_qvm`.
33|
34|`affine_gather_qmm_rhs` (`quantized.h:2580-2718`, installed 0.32.4
35|headers) rounds differently in two independent ways, both new readings
36|this round (round 1 mapped the kernel as never-run and did not read its
37|arithmetic):
38|

13|## What happens
14|
15|The starting point (`muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:31-34`)
16|computes each of the 60 router scores as one thread's serial float32 chain,
17|`acc += xsh[d] * w_router[e*768 + d]` for d = 0..767 (compiler FMA contraction
18|does not change the left-to-right grouping). The reference,
19|`mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)` (`bench/grader/slots.py:45`),
20|never accumulates that way. In MLX 0.32.4's `Matmul::eval_gpu`
21|(`mlx/backend/metal/matmul.cpp`, tag v0.32.4) with M=rows, N=60, K=768,
22|A not transposed, B transposed, the accumulation order is chosen by `rows`:
23|
24|| rows | MLX kernel | float32 accumulation order |
25||---|---|---|
26|| 1 | GEMV `gemv_float32_bm4_bn1_sm1_sn32_tm4_tn4` (`min(M,N)==1` → `gemv`; `gemv_wide` skipped, f32 out) | 32 lanes × serial 24 products (lane l: d = i*128 + l*4 + 0..3, i=0..5, `kernels/gemv.h:162-182`), then shuffle tree sn=16,8,4,2,1 (`gemv.h:202-208`) |
27|| 8, 32, 127 | steel split-K GEMM (Case 1: `_tm*_tn <= 2048` on this `…s` device, `_tk=48 >= 8`, `K >= max(M,N)`) | 32 K-partitions (8/32 rows) or 8 (127 rows); each partition: simdgroup 8×8 MMA over BK=16 chunks (BM=16/32, BN=32); partials summed sequentially in partition order (`steel_gemm_splitk.h:186-189`); last partition absorbs the remainder iterations (`splitk.h:140-155`) |
28|| 1,016, 2,048 | regular steel GEMM (split-K off: 768 < M) | BM=64/BN=64/BK=16 tiles (`GEMM_TPARAM_MACRO` fallback for `…s`), K walked in BK=16 chunks, simdgroup MMA accumulation chunk after chunk |
29|
30|A serial scalar loop cannot reproduce the two MMA regimes' rounding by
31|reordering: the 8-product accumulation inside each `simdgroup_float8x8`
32|multiply-accumulate is the hardware's. Bit-exactness therefore needs either
33|the same simdgroup matrix ops with the same tiling and K-order per regime
34|(branch on `rows`, or separate spec kernels), or a proof that another order
35|rounds identically (none known). Full derivation:
36|`territory-baseline-routing.md` section 3.1.

13|## What happens
14|
15|The starting point (`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1/block-0.metal:20-25`)
16|writes the 4-term f32 sum as one expression,
17|`float(y0)·w0 + float(y1)·w1 + float(y2)·w2 + float(y3)·w3`, then
18|`bfloat(acc) + shared`. Compiled as a single Metal kernel, the compiler
19|FP-contracts the mul+add pairs into FMAs, keeping each product unrounded
20|into its add. The reference can never do this: `ref_combine`
21|(`bench/grader/slots.py:51-52`) runs eagerly as separate kernels —
22|`binary_g` multiply (`Multiply` is plain `x * y`, product rounded once
23|to f32), then `col_reduce_small` (`Sum` is plain `a + b`, init 0) folding
24|((p₀+p₁)+p₂)+p₃ with a rounding after every add, then `copy_v` bf16
25|round, then `binary_vv` bf16 add (headers under
26|`.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/`;
27|full mapping in `territory-baseline-combine.md` checklist B–D). The
28|candidate's `acc` therefore differs from the reference fold by ~1 f32
29|ULP on some elements; the bf16 rounding absorbs it except when `acc`
30|sits at a rounding midpoint, and the following `+ shared` can magnify
31|the reported gap when it cancels toward zero (ULP floored at
32|`|r| = 0.001`, `bench/grader/check_candidate.py:84-99`).

35|already the reference's left fold, and round 1's CPU emulation showed

40|fingerprint, so neither loop form nor staging avoids contraction — the
41|fix must suppress it (the `precise` accumulator round 1's boundary
42|named there) while keeping the ((p₀+p₁)+p₂)+p₃ fold and both bf16
43|rounding points.

8|
9|## Slot
10|
11|`experts`
12|
13|## What happens
14|
15|MLX's prefill kernel `affine_gather_qmm_rhs`
16|(`quantized.h:2570-2718`, installed 0.32.4 headers) tiles sorted
17|pairs into `BM=16`-row tiles. The host over-provisions the grid:
18|`grid_y = min(B, ceil(B/16) + E - 1)` with `E = 60`
19|([quantized.cpp v0.32.4:1817-1819](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/v0.32.4/mlx/backend/metal/quantized.cpp#L1817-L1819)),
20|i.e. up to 59 tiles beyond the all-in-one-expert minimum, because
21|any expert may contribute a partial tile. Each threadgroup then
22|runs `schedule_row_tile<16>` (`utils.h:501-542`) to find its
23|expert; threadgroups past the real tile count return false and
24|exit (`quantized.h:2637-2640`) — launched, scheduled, discarded.
25|
26|Useful tiles are `T = Σ_e ceil(cnt_e/16)` over per-expert pair
27|counts `cnt_e`. Tiles that are real but partial
28|(`tgp_bm < 16`, `quantized.h:2636`) still run the full tile:
29|`BlockLoader::load_safe` zero-pads the missing `x` rows
30|(`steel/gemm/loader.h:83-128`), `BlockMMA::mma`
31|(`steel/gemm/mma.h:513-537`) multiplies them, and
32|`store_result_safe` discards them (`quantized.h:2687-2695`).
33|The weight tile is fully loaded and dequantized regardless
34|(`QuantizedBlockLoader`, `quantized.h:665-791`), so a partial
35|tile costs a full tile of load + MMA for a fraction of the rows.
36|
37|This is distinct from the G2 failure itself
38|(`ineff-baseline-experts-1`): even a bit-exact replica of this
39|kernel inherits the waste; a replica that regroups rows
40|(different `BM`, or per-row accumulation with the same per-row
41|arithmetic — territory §C invariant) avoids it without
42|changing any valid output bit.
43|
44|## Cost
45|
46|Decode 1/8/32 rows: **0 kernels, 0 bytes** — this kernel never
47|runs there (`B/E ≤ 2.13 < 4`, territory §A table). All figures
48|below are per product per layer at the prefill sizes, balanced-expert
49|model (`cnt_e` near the uniform mean `B/60`; grader prompts are
50|random tokens, territory §C). `N` tiles: gate/up 12, down 24
51|(`BN=32`).
52|
53|| prefill rows | B | dispatched `grid_y` | useful `T` | empty y-tiles | padded rows `T·16−B` |
54||---|---|---|---|---|---|
55|| 127 | 508 | 91 | 60 | 31 (34.1%) | 452 / 960 (47.1%) |
56|| 1,016 | 4,064 | 313 | 300 | 13 (4.2%) | 736 / 4,800 (15.3%) |
57|| 2,048 | 8,192 | 571 | 540 | 31 (5.4%) | 448 / 8,640 (5.2%) |
58|
59|Arithmetic: `grid_y` from the host formula; `T = 60·ceil((B/60)/16)`
60|in the balanced case (`ceil(8.47/16)=1`, `ceil(67.7/16)=5`,
61|`ceil(136.5/16)=9`). Empty threadgroups per gate/up call =
62|empty y-tiles × 12 (372 / 156 / 372), per down call × 24
63|(744 / 312 / 744), each 64 threads that only run the
64|`schedule_row_tile` scan over 60 experts (`utils.h:514-541`:
65|two 32-lane prefix iterations) and exit. Padded-row MMA work:
66|the kernel issues `2·T·16·K·N` flops for `2·B·K·N` useful
67|(`K·N = 294,912` for both products), so 47.1% / 15.3% / 5.2%
68|of issued row-work multiplies zero-padded rows. Weight bytes
69|are *not* wasted by padding (the tile's weights serve its valid
70|rows); the waste is issued MMA/load slots and threadgroup
71|occupancy. No measured prefill time exists: the grader times
72|decode only (`claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:42`), so
73|no µs figure is claimed from measurement.

75|## Kind
76|
77|Overhead-bound (`claude/GLOSSARY.md`): at prefill the path is far
78|below both peaks, and the padded fraction is pure overhead —
79|issued work with no output. The empty-tile part is launch/
80|scheduling overhead; the padded-row part is wasted compute
81|inside otherwise useful threadgroups.
82|
83|## Spans
84|
85|`quantized-kernels` (host grid formula + `schedule_row_tile` +
86|`BlockMMA` partial-tile path) → slot `experts`. Neighbour:
87|`baseline-experts` (any grouped prefill branch of a candidate
88|chooses its own tiling; this entry prices MLX's).
89|
90|## Predicted saving
91|
92|0 µs per decode step at 1, 8 and 32 rows (kernel never runs
93|there). At prefill, removing both parts saves the padded
94|fraction of the main kernel's row work — up to ~47% at
95|127 rows, ~15% at 1,016, ~5% at 2,048 — plus the empty
96|threadgroups above, in time-to-first-token only. Prefill
97|speed is not gated (G3 times decode;
98|`claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:42`), so this saving

100|if it comes free with the exact prefill branch (e.g. a
101|per-row `qmm_rhs`-arithmetic kernel has no tiles to pad).
102|In absolute terms the main kernel's useful MMA floors at
103|`2·B·K·N / 5.2 TFLOPS` ≈ 57.6 / 461.0 / 929.2 µs per
104|layer-product at peak (territory §E); issued MMA including
105|padding floors at 108.9 / 544.6 / 980.0 µs, so the padded
106|part alone floors at ≈51.3 / 83.5 / 50.8 µs per
107|layer-product *if* the kernel ran at peak compute — it
108|does not (two barriers per 32-K tile,
109|`quantized_utils.h:14-29`), so treat these as lower bounds
110|on the waste, not predictions.

*Corrections exploration made to this Starting point.* (1) Combine: the written 4-term order already matches the reference's left fold `((p₀+p₁)+p₂)+p₃`; the sole cause is Metal FMA contraction, not association (`ineff-baseline-combine-1`). The Starting point's "association differs" phrasing is superseded. (2) Routing: the 4-term normalise sum already matches and is not a cause; the causes are the router matmul order (three regimes by `rows`, `ineff-baseline-routing-1`) and the sigmoid formula (`ineff-baseline-routing-2`). (3) Experts prefill: two independent rounding differences (bfloat16-rounded dequantized tiles and `BK=32` MMA accumulation order), either alone breaks exactness (`ineff-baseline-experts-1`, `territory-quantized-kernels.md`). (4) The three-together loss is now quantified as an interaction term (+2.08 ms at 8 requests, +3.28 ms at 32 in vLLM) with kernel-count reductions additive, so kernel count is not the cost (`ineff-g3-1`).

## Context

A decode step produces one token per request. On plain MLX with 128-token prompts the bare step takes 4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (Claude: `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md`, via round 1); in vLLM the unchanged step Claude re-measured for round 1 takes 5.370 / 14.363 / 29.851 ms (`claude/findings/muse-round-1.md` §3). A step is 867 kernels at 1 row, 987 at 32 rows, far below both hardware limits (whole-step 24–41 GB/s against 200 GB/s peak, ≤9% of peak compute), so it is overhead-bound throughout. Each tiny kernel costs ~6.81 µs end to end in the whole-step accounting, but the piece harness prices kernels differently (see *Territory map*): a fused kernel's floor is ~17 µs per layer when barrier-free and ~24 µs with barriers/serial tails, while the reference's kernels cost ~3–4.5 µs each when pipelined 20 deep. Round 2 ranks by the chained piece timing (each layer's call waits for the previous through the grader's `link` kernel), which matches the model's real dependency; the old independent timing is retained only as history.

The MoE block (`MoE.__call__`, `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:217-232`) runs in all 20 layers of every step, in decode and in prefill chunks alike. Per layer it launches: routing, 12 kernels (router cast+matmul+sigmoid, bias add, negate, argpartition, gather, weight norm); the routed experts, 7 kernels at 1 row (3 products + activation + 3 off-chain index ranges) and 13 from 16 rows (6 sort/unsort glue kernels); combine, 5 kernels (cast, multiply, sum, cast, add with the shared expert); plus the shared expert, 4 kernels. The three slots mirror this split: `routing` (240 kernels/step), `experts` (140–260/step), `combine` (100/step). A candidate's exact prefill branch avoids it for free by construction; fixing MLX itself is upstream work, in time-to-first-token only.

15|  4 simd waves instead of 7, more blocks in flight per call. This is

20|  arithmetic — each weight dequantized to bfloat16 first
21|  (`bfloat(scale·q+bias)`, `qmm_accum` in block-1) and K accumulated
22|  contiguously in BK=32 tile order by a single thread per output (one
23|  output per lane, no `simd_sum`), mimicking BlockMMA's sequential
24|  tile order. Same silu (full-bfloat16, attempt-4's) and the same four
25|  bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden, down).

30|`simd_sum` order. ineff-baseline-experts-3 (per-pair re-reads) is
31|deliberately kept — round-1 evidence says grouped reads lose at this
32|duty cycle; per-pair reads at/above 60 rows are correctness-only cost

1|# attempt-2: size-branched block-split experts (builder-1-a, direction a)
2|
3|First attempt in direction (a) for `hyp-1-experts-exact`. Builds on the
4|starting point `muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4` (baseline: none;
5|attempt-4 fails the current G2 at every prefill size). One spec, two
6|kernels in list order, each branching on `rows` read from
7|`inds_shape[0]` (the dispatch threshold `rows >= 60`, pairs >= 240,
8|from `territory-quantized-kernels` §A/§F, not the tested sizes):
9|
10|- `experts_gate_up` (block-0): one 32-thread threadgroup per
11|  (pair, 32-output block) — grid `rows*1536` threads = `rows*4*12`
12|  groups. Computes gate and up for its block, applies the silu-mul,
13|  writes `hidden[pair, block*32 + lane]`.
14|- `experts_down` (block-1): one 32-thread threadgroup per
15|  (pair, 32-output block) — grid `rows*3072` threads = `rows*4*24`
16|  groups. Reads `hidden`, writes its 32 outputs of `y`.
17|
18|Shared header (block-2): `qvm_block` copied byte-identically from
19|attempt-4, a new `qmm_block`, and attempt-4's full-bfloat16 silu.
20|
21|## What changed since attempt-4, and which inefficiency it removes
22|
23|1. **Prefill arithmetic (`ineff-baseline-experts-1`, the G2 gate).**
24|   Below 60 rows both kernels keep attempt-4's bit-exact `gather_qvm`
25|   arithmetic (float32 dequant through the product, strided lanes
26|   `k == lane (mod 32)` + `simd_sum`, full-bf16 silu). At 60 rows and
27|   above, `qmm_block` replicates `gather_qmm_rhs`: dequantized
28|   weights rounded to bfloat16 before the multiply
29|   (`dequantize` bits=4, `s` / `s/16` nibble form), then BK=32 tiles
30|   in increasing K order, each four sequential 8-wide
31|   `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate` steps on float fragments — the
32|   `BlockMMA` order. Row grouping is per-pair (fragment row 0, seven
33|   zero-padded rows in separate accumulators), which the boundary
34|   allows; per-row K order is unchanged. Gate/up/down each still
35|   round once from float32 to bfloat16, and the silu is shared.
36|2. **Chained 1-row latency (`ineff-baseline-experts-2`).** Attempt-4
37|   exposes 4 threadgroups per call at 1 row (one per pair) with
38|   barrier-serialised waves. Here a 1-row call exposes 48 (gate/up)
39|   + 96 (down) threadgroups, each computing exactly one 32-output
40|   block with the identical strided-lane + `simd_sum` order, so the
41|   GPU's 16 cores all have work while no block's bits change. Cost:
42|   a second launch per layer and one `hidden` round-trip (3 KB per
43|   pair); `x` is re-read from cache once per block (12x per pair,
44|   18 KB vs 369 KB of gate/up weights per pair).
45|3. `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair weight re-reads) is **not**
46|   removed: weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B, as in attempt-4.
47|   The 8/32-row chained wins must therefore be kept by occupancy,
48|   not by fewer bytes.
49|
50|Boundary kept: bit-exact accumulation order per size regime as
51|above; all four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden, down);
52|positional `y[r,j]` for any `inds` order; valid at every `rows`
53|(grid and block counts scale with `rows*4` pairs, branch only on
54|the 60-row dispatch threshold); 32 threads/group <= 1024;
55|threadgroup memory by hand (grader does not check 32 KB): GU
56|1536 + 128 + (256+1024+256)*4 = 7,808 B; Down 768 + 6,144 =
57|6,912 B.
58|
59|## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, this grader)
60|
61|Weight bytes per layer (552,960 B/pair): 2.21 / 17.7 / 70.8 MB at
62|4 / 32 / 128 pairs. Attempt-4 chained (round-2 exploration,
63|`console-chain.txt`): 132.9 / 175.9 / 587.6; reference chained
64|80.3 / 239.6 / 797.6.
65|
66|- 1 row: 144 small groups fill 16 cores; gate/up 1.47 MB + down
67|  0.74 MB at an assumed ~55 GB/s effective for 32-thread groups
68|  gives ~40 µs including the extra launch → **40 µs**
69|  (attempt-4 chained 132.9; reference 80.3).
70|- 8 rows: 384 + 768 groups, streaming regime; 17.7 MB at
71|  ~110 GB/s ≈ 160 µs → **165 µs** (attempt-4 175.9).
72|- 32 rows: 1,536 + 3,072 groups; 70.8 MB at ~115 GB/s ≈ 615 µs
73|  → **610 µs** (attempt-4 587.6; the 4% block-split tax is the
74|  risk to the kept win).
75|
76|G2: expect `differ == 0` at all six sizes. Decode reuses
77|attempt-4's proven per-block math unchanged; prefill depends on
78|the hardware's 8-wide fragment dot matching `BlockMMA`'s when fed
79|the same bfloat16-rounded operands in the same tile order.
80|
81|## Verdict
82|
83|G1 pass; **G2 pass — `differ` 0, `max_ulp` 0.0 at all six sizes**
84|(decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048). The prefill branch is
85|bit-exact: bfloat16-rounded dequantized weights plus BK=32 tiles of
86|four sequential 8-wide `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate` steps, fed a
87|single row per threadgroup, reproduce `gather_qmm_rhs` bit for bit
88|on every tested layer. `beats_compiled` false. Chained
89|µs/layer (candidate vs reference vs compiled, same run):
90|**103.6 / 326.8 / 887.6** vs 76.1 / 244.6 / 797.1 and
91|73.1 / 232.0 / 804.5. Baseline `none` — no
92|`wins_vs_baseline`/`beats_baseline`. The attempt is correct at
93|every size but slower than the compiled reference at all three
94|decode sizes, and slower than the starting point's chained times
95|(132.9 / 175.9 / 587.6, other harness) at 8/32 rows.
96|
97|## Miss analysis (prediction 40 / 165 / 610; all misses > 20%)
98|
99|Measured is 2.6x / 2.0x / 1.5x the prediction. Effective bandwidth
100|from 552,960 B/pair: 21 / 54 / 80 GB/s chained, against attempt-4's
101|chained 17 / 101 / 121 GB/s. The split helped exactly where group
102|count was the binding limit (1 row: 103.6 vs 132.9) and hurt
103|wherever streaming mattered. Two causes, both in the split shape,
104|not the arithmetic:
105|
106|1. **One simdgroup per group has too little memory parallelism.**
107|   Each 32-thread group runs its block's 24-step strided K loop
108|   alone; attempt-4 runs 8 such blocks concurrently per group, so
109|   one stalled load hides behind seven others. More groups only
110|   partly compensate: at 8/32 rows the GPU was already saturated
111|   with groups, and the per-group latency chain became the limit.
112|2. **Threadgroup memory caps residency in the decode branch too.**
113|   The qmm tiles (6,144 B of floats) are allocated in both kernels
114|   at every size, so a decode gate/up group carries 7,808 B where
115|   attempt-4 carries 3,840 B. Resident groups per core fall, and
116|   with 32-thread groups the resident thread count falls with
117|   them — the opposite of the occupancy the split was meant to add.
118|
119|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: exposing threadgroups is
120|not sufficient; a block-split kernel must keep several blocks in
121|flight per group (or per core) and keep decode threadgroup memory
122|near attempt-4's, e.g. 128-thread groups of 4 simdgroups each
123|owning one block (12 + 24 groups at 1 row), with the prefill tiles
124|overlaid on the decode buffers instead of added to them.
125|
126|**Next change:** rebuild the decode branch as 4-simdgroup groups
127|(4 blocks per group, qvm_block unchanged), overlay the qmm tile
128|memory on the decode threadgroup buffers, keep `qmm_block` as is.

35|widens to 8 simdgroups/row (better 1-row occupancy) but the MMA path
36|stages 48 chunks x 2 barriers and wastes 7/8 of each 8x8 tile at decode
37|sizes, so I predict it lands near the starting point, not below the floor:
38|1 row ~ 24 floor + 0.9 traffic + ~2 MMA staging ~= **27 us**;
39|8 rows ~ 24 amortised + 7.4 traffic ~= **26 us**;
40|32 rows ~ 18 amortised + 29.5 traffic ~= **40 us**.
41|Compiled reference (starting point's run): 30.5 / 42.0 / 49.1 us, so a
42|chained win is plausible only if G2 passes.
43|
44|## Known limits (stated before grading)
45|
46|- MMA tile is 8 rows x 8 experts, not steel's BM=16/32 x BN=32 (split-K)
47|  or 64x64 (regular). Per-element K/chunk/partition order matches; if the
48|  hardware 8-product rounding depended on tile position it would still
49|  differ — no evidence it does, but this is the residual risk.
50|- GEMV per-lane products use the same `acc += x*w` form as MLX gemv.h;
51|  compiler FMA contraction is assumed to match MLX's build.
52|- The thread-0 top-4 scan remains serial (60 steps) by design for ties.
53|
54|## Verdict (2026-11-04T03:37:08Z, one grader run)
55|
56|G1 pass, **G2 pass at all six sizes** (rows_differ 0, max_rel_err 0.0 at
57|1/8/32 and 127/1016/2048). Chained us/layer (ref / compiled / candidate):
58|1 row 77.8 / 56.2 / **54.9** (beats compiled); 8 rows 113.1 / 91.2 / 91.4
59|(tie, +0.2); 32 rows 136.3 / 98.9 / 114.8 (loses). `beats_compiled` false.
60|Baseline none, so no `beats_baseline`.
61|
62|The pre-grading worry that the 8-row MMA tile might round differently
63|from steel's larger tiles did not bite: hardware 8-product rounding is
64|tile-position independent on this GPU, and the GEMV shuffle replica plus
65|verbatim sigmoid are bit-exact. The 8x8-per-row emulation is therefore
66|sufficient for G2; no scalar fallback was needed.
67|
68|## Why timings missed predictions by >20%
69|
70|Predicted 27/26/40 us, measured 54.9/91.4/114.8 us. Two causes. (1) The
71|prediction anchored on round 1's independent-timing floor (~24 us); the
72|chained harness floor is higher (compiled itself is 56.2 us at 1 row
73|here vs 30.5 us in round 1's run), so the anchor was wrong, not just the
74|kernel. (2) The MMA path pays 48 chunks x 2 threadgroup barriers per row
75|plus 7/8 wasted tile rows and a full 184 KB w_router re-read per row:
76|at 32 rows that staging dominates and the candidate loses to compiled
77|by 16 us, while at 1 row the single launch still wins by 1.3 us. Next
78|change: keep the exact orders but stage BK=32+ per barrier (or load
79|fragments without per-chunk threadgroup staging) and put real rows in
80|all 8 A-tile rows so w tiles are shared across rows.

  "output": "# Attempt 2 (round 2) — builder-2-b, direction (b): minimal-change scalar exact fix

Starting point: `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1` (single kernel, one
32-thread threadgroup per row). That starting point fails G2 at every size
under round 2's bit-exact grader (product accumulation order +
sigmoid formula; see `muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-baseline-routing.md`
§3.1–3.2). Baseline for this slot: `none`, so there is no `beats_baseline`
bar; the bar is the compiled reference.

## What changed (only the scores)

Kept exactly as attempt-1: one kernel, grid `rows*32`, threadgroup 32, one
threadgroup per row, `x` staged in threadgroup memory, thread `t` computes
experts `t` and `t+32`, thread 0's serial strictly-greater top-4 insertion
scan (same tie rule), and the weights sum `s0+s1+s2+s3 + 1e-20f`, divide,
×2.5 in `inds` order. Changed only how each expert's score is computed:

1. **Sigmoid, MLX verbatim** (`unary_ops.h:308-314`):
   `y = 1/(1 + metal::precise::exp(metal::abs(acc)))`,
   `scores[e] = (acc < 0) ? y : 1 - y`. Removes `ineff-baseline-routing-2`.
2. **Product accumulation reordered scalar-wise, no MMA intrinsics:**
   - `rows == 1` (GEMV regime): 32 lane partials, lane `l` serially sums
     `d = i*128 + l*4 + 0..3` for `i = 0..5` (`gemv.h:162-182`), then the
     shuffle tree `sn = 16,8,4,2,1` (`gemv.h:202-208`) emulated in place on
     the partial array (ascending `l` reads `lane_part[l+sn]` before it is
     overwritten in that round).
   - `rows > 1` (split-K regime): 32 partitions of BK=16 chunks —
     partitions 0..30 cover 16 elements each, partition 31 covers the
     remaining 272 (steel split-K at 8/32 rows: `gemm_k_iterations =
     (768/16)/32 = 1`, `split_k_partition_size = 16`, last partition absorbs
     the rest, `steel_gemm_splitk.h:140-155`). Each partial is summed
     scalar-wise in increasing `d`; partials are summed sequentially in
     partition order from 0, as in `gemm_splitk_accum`
     (`steel_gemm_splitk.h:186-189`).

This is the controlled test of whether scalar reordering can be bit-exact:
at 1 row the GEMV grouping is fully scalar (lane serial sums + shuffle
tree), so it should reproduce the reference if FMA contraction matches;
at 8/32 rows the partition boundaries and sequential partial sum are exact,
but each partition's internal accumulation in MLX is an 8×8 simdgroup MMA
whose 8-product hardware accumulation a scalar loop may not reproduce
(`ineff-baseline-routing-1`). Note this attempt deliberately does **not**
reproduce MLX's partition count at 127 rows (8 partitions) or the regular
steel GEMM at 1,016/2,048 rows — direction (b) fixes 32 partitions at all
larger rows, so those sizes test the same scalar question less cleanly.

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-routing-2` (sigmoid, fully) and, if scalar reordering
rounds identically, `ineff-baseline-routing-1` (product order). It does not
touch `ineff-baseline-routing-3` (one simdgroup per row + serial scan) or
`-4` (`w_router` re-read per row) — minimal change by design.

## Prediction (µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows)

Same flop count as attempt-1 (768 multiply-adds per expert) and same
traffic (`rows × 184 KB` of `w_router`). Extra work per expert: 32 partial
stores + 31 tree/partition adds (≈8% more adds) and one `precise::exp`
instead of fast `exp` (60 per row, negligible). Attempt-1 measured
28.5 / 23.6 / 41.8 µs per layer in its own (round-1, unchained) grader run
(`muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/notes.md:35-37`), so ×1.08:

- 1 row: **≈31 µs** (compiled reference 30.5 in that run)
- 8 rows: **≈25 µs** (compiled 42.0)
- 32 rows: **≈45 µs** (compiled 49.1)

Round 2's chained timing may shift all figures; the prediction is against
attempt-1's harness numbers. G2 prediction: pass at 1 row; fail at 8/32 if
(and only if) the MMA internal accumulation differs from a scalar serial
sum within each partition.

## Verdict

Graded 2026-11-04 (one grader run, `routing` slot; baseline `none`, so no
`beats_baseline` / `wins_vs_baseline`):

- **G1: pass.**
- **G2: fail overall — but pass at all three decode sizes.**
  - decode 1 row: `rows_differ` 0, `rows_other_experts` 0, max rel err 0.0 — **pass**
  - decode 8 rows: 0, 0, 0.0 — **pass**
  - decode 32 rows: 0, 0, 0.0 — **pass**
  - prefill 127 rows: `rows_differ` 2,453 (of 2,540), experts always match,
    max rel err 3.3e-06 — fail. First difference (layer 0, row 0): experts
    [59, 55, 13, 5] in both; weights [1.142134189605713, 0.663673996925354,
    0.3643006682395935, 0.3298913240432739] vs reference
    [1.142134189605713, 0.6636739373207092, 0.3643006384372711,
    0.32989129424095154].
  - prefill 1,016 rows: `rows_differ` 20,128 (of 20,320), max rel err
    1.41e-05 — fail (first difference layer 0, row 0, same experts).
  - prefill 2,048 rows: `rows_differ` 40,453 (of 40,960), max rel err
    1.39e-05 — fail (first difference layer 0, row 0, same experts).
- **Timing:** none. The grader prints `timing_us_per_layer` only for a
  correct attempt, and `beats_compiled` is false; so the predicted
  ≈31 / 25 / 45 µs per layer could not be checked (neither confirmed nor
  missed by >20% — unmeasured, not a prediction miss). For context from the
  same round: builder-2-a's MMA replica (attempt-1) measured chained
  54.9 / 91.4 / 114.8 vs compiled 56.2 / 91.2 / 98.9 µs per layer.

## What this proves and disproves

**Scalar reordering CAN be bit-exact at decode sizes.** At 1 row the scalar
GEMV emulation (32 lane partials in `gemv.h` lane order + shuffle-tree
association) plus the verbatim sigmoid reproduces every score bit for bit
on all 20 layers. At 8 and 32 rows the scalar split-K emulation — exact MLX
partition boundaries (31 × BK=16 + last partition absorbing the remaining
272) with each partial summed serially in increasing `d` and partials
summed sequentially — is also bit-exact on all 160 / 640 rows. So the
8-product accumulation inside `simdgroup_float8x8` MMA, at least as it
affects these outputs, rounds identically to a serial scalar sum over the
same K order; the claim in `ineff-baseline-routing-1` that a scalar
reordering cannot reproduce the MMA regimes' rounding is **disproved at
8/32 rows** (and the GEMV half at 1 row).

The prefill failures do not test that claim: by design (direction (b) fixed
32 partitions at all larger rows) this kernel uses the wrong accumulation
grouping there — MLX uses 8 partitions of 96 at 127 rows and the regular
steel GEMM (BK=16 chunks accumulated chunk after chunk into one
accumulator) at 1,016/2,048 rows. The failure pattern confirms grouping is
the whole story: experts and order match everywhere (`rows_other_experts`
0 at all six sizes), only last-bit weight differences remain.

**Next change (one):** branch the partition geometry on `rows` as MLX does
— 8 partitions of 96 at the 127-row split-K sub-regime and a single
chunk-after-chunk scalar accumulation (BK=16 chunks, one accumulator) in
the regular-GEMM regime above 768 rows — keeping everything else in this
kernel identical. If the decode result generalises (MMA ≡ serial scalar
over the same K order), that attempt passes G2 at all six sizes with a
far simpler and likely faster kernel than the MMA replica; the grader's
chained timing would then be the first timing measurement of the scalar
design.

  "output": "# attempt-3 (round 2): hardening — 4-block groups, scalar prefill (builder-1-c)

Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
`none`). Builds on the best attempt
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-1` (G2 pass all six,
104.3/193.3/535.7 µs/layer chained vs compiled 77.6/235.7/791.6 —
loses only at 1 row). Starting point for the decode arithmetic is
attempt-1's proven helpers; attempt-2's failure modes are the
constraint.

## The one main change

Split attempt-1's single fused per-pair kernel (4 threadgroups per
call at 1 row, 512 threads each) into two kernels with 4-block
threadgroups, exposing more threadgroups per call without
attempt-2's 1-simdgroup-per-group collapse:

- `experts_gate_up` (block-0): one 128-thread threadgroup (4
  simdgroups) owns 4 distinct 32-output blocks — simdgroup `s` of
  chunk `c = tg % 3` computes block `blk = c*4 + s` of pair
  `tg / 3` (12 blocks/pair ÷ 4 = 3 groups/pair). Grid
  `rows*1536` threads = `rows*12` groups: **12 groups at 1 row**
  (96 at 8, 384 at 32). Each simdgroup runs gate then up for its
  block, lane 0 (decode) or every lane (prefill) stores the
  bfloat16-rounded results to `tg_gate`/`tg_up`, one barrier, then
  every lane applies the shared full-bfloat16 silu-mul and writes
  `hidden[pair, blk*32 + lane]`.
- `experts_down` (block-1): same shape for the 24 down blocks —
  `blk = (tg % 6)*4 + simd`, pair `tg / 6` (24 ÷ 4 = 6 groups/pair).
  Grid `rows*3072` threads = `rows*24` groups: **24 groups at
  1 row** (192 at 8, 768 at 32).

Everything else is copied, not redesigned:

- **Decode (`rows < 60`):** `qvm_block` in block-2 is byte-identical
  to attempt-1's (verified by diff; itself attempt-4's proven
  helper) — strided lanes `k ≡ lane (mod 32)` serial in float32,
  float32 dequant `x·(scale·q+bias)`, `simd_sum` tree. Splitting
  blocks across threadgroups does not change any block's
  accumulation order, so decode bits are attempt-1's.
- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`):** `qmm_accum` in block-2 is
  byte-identical to attempt-1's scalar path (verified by diff) —
  weight rounded to bfloat16 first
  (`float(bfloat(scale·q+bias))`), then K accumulated contiguously
  in `BK=32` tile order by one thread per output, one output per
  lane. Attempt-2's MMA tiles (`qmm_block`,
  `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate`, 6,144 B of float tile buffers)
  are **not** used, so no tile memory is allocated in either branch
  and decode residency is not taxed for prefill.
- Same branch threshold (`rows >= 60` from `inds_shape[0]`, the
  `gather_qmm_rhs` dispatch threshold, not the tested sizes), same
  four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden via silu-mul,
  down — silu helper byte-identical to attempt-2's copy of
  attempt-4's full-bfloat16 lowering), fp32 accumulation, and
  positional `y[r,j]` (`pair = r*4 + j` throughout; `hidden` is
  indexed by the same flat pair).

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-1
  leaves 12 of 16 GPU cores idle per call (4 threadgroups). Here a
  1-row layer call exposes 12 (gate/up) then 24 (down)
  threadgroups, so up to 12/16 cores hold gate/up work and all 16
  hold down work, while each group keeps 4 blocks in flight —
  the in-group load overlap whose loss (1 block/group) cost
  attempt-2 its 8/32-row wins (326.8/887.6). Cost of the split:
  one extra launch per layer on the chain and a `hidden`
  round-trip (1.5 KB/pair written + re-read vs 552,960 B/pair of
  weights, 0.5%); `x` is re-read per chunk-group (3× per pair,
  4.5 KB vs 368 KB of gate/up weights).
- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
  attempt-1's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
  verbatim instead of attempt-2's MMA construction.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
  kept, as in attempt-1 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
  round-1 grouped evidence says removing them loses at this duty
  cycle.

## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)

128 threads/group ≤ 1,024. Threadgroup memory: gate/up
`tg_x[768] + tg_gate[128] + tg_up[128]` bfloat16 = **2,048 B**;
down `tg_h[384]` = **768 B** — both below attempt-1's 3,840 B and
far below the 32,768 B limit, at every row count (allocations are
rows-independent; no prefill-only buffers exist). Grids scale as
`rows*12` / `rows*24` groups, so the kernel is valid at every
`rows ≥ 1`, including untested counts on both sides of 60.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)

Weight bytes per layer (552,960 B/pair): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB
at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs. References: attempt-1 chained (this round's
grader) 104.3 / 193.3 / 535.7 (effective 21 / 92 / 132 GB/s);
attempt-2 chained 103.6 / 326.8 / 887.6 (21 / 54 / 80 GB/s);
compiled (attempt-1's run) 77.6 / 235.7 / 791.6.

- **1 row: 74.** Latency-bound, not byte-bound (floor 11.1 µs at
  peak). Attempt-1's 104.3 with 4 groups ≈ fixed cost (launch/link,
  `tg_x` load, barriers, lane-0 stores) + a wave-serial part only
  4 cores can work on. Gate/up now spreads over 12 groups and down
  over 24 (1.5 waves of 16), each group with 4 concurrent block
  K-chains instead of attempt-2's 1: assuming the serial part
  scales with cores busy (4 → 12) and adding ~6 µs for the second
  launch + `hidden` round-trip, 2.21 MB at ~33 GB/s effective
  (between attempt-2's 21 with 1 block/group and the 8-row
  streaming rate) ≈ 67 µs + ~7 µs fixed ≈ **74** — just under the
  compiled 77.6, with the launch overhead as the risk.
  Per step this is the ineff-2 headroom: (104.3 − 74) × 20 ≈
  0.61 ms/step recovered of the 1.05 ms gap.
- **8 rows: 162.** Streaming with 96 + 192 groups: resident groups
  per core are capped by 2,048/768 B threadgroup memory (vs
  attempt-2's 7,808/6,912 B), and each group hides loads behind
  4 blocks. 17.69 MB at ~115 GB/s (attempt-1's 92 GB/s at 32
  groups, raised by 3× the groups at lower memory) ≈ 154 µs +
  ~8 µs launch/hidden ≈ **162**, keeping attempt-1's win over
  compiled 235.7.
- **32 rows: 530.** 384 + 768 groups, already saturated:
  70.78 MB at ~135 GB/s (attempt-1 reached 132 GB/s with 128
  fused groups; the split's extra `x`/`hidden` traffic is <1% of
  weight bytes) ≈ 524 µs + ~6 µs ≈ **530**, keeping the win over
  compiled 791.6. Risk: if the second launch's serialization on
  the chain costs more than ~10 µs/layer at streaming sizes, this
  lands nearer attempt-1's 535.7 — still a win.

G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — decode
reuses attempt-1's per-block math unchanged (only the block→group
mapping moved), and prefill reuses attempt-1's `qmm_accum`
verbatim, which already matched `gather_qmm_rhs` bit for bit.

## Verdict

G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0
everywhere** (decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048) — the
split kept attempt-1's bits in both regimes: per-block
`qvm_block` order unchanged by the block→group remapping, and the
scalar `qmm_accum` prefill path matched `gather_qmm_rhs` again.
Chained timing µs/layer (this run; candidate vs reference vs
compiled): **1 row 109.5 / 93.1 / 86.9 (loses both)**; 8 rows
195.0 / 248.8 / 243.6 (wins); 32 rows 637.7 / 846.0 / 798.9
(wins). `beats_compiled` false — the 1-row size still misses, as
in attempt-1. Baseline `none` — no
`wins_vs_baseline`/`beats_baseline`.

Against attempt-1 (different run; 1-row baselines shifted
77.6 → 86.9 compiled between runs, so treat 1 row as indicative):
109.5 vs 104.3 at 1 row (no gain), 195.0 vs 193.3 at 8 rows
(flat), 637.7 vs 535.7 at 32 rows (**+19% regression**). The
hardening did not beat the best attempt at any size.

## Miss analysis (prediction 74 / 162 / 530; all misses > 20%)

Measured 109.5 / 195.0 / 637.7 is **+48% / +20% / +20%** over
prediction. Effective bandwidth on pair bytes: 20 / 91 / 111 GB/s
— the 1- and 8-row rates are attempt-1's (21 / 92 GB/s), and the
32-row rate falls between attempt-2's 80 and attempt-1's 132 GB/s.
Three facts together locate the error in the prediction's model,
not in the arithmetic:

1. **Group count is not the 1-row binding limit past 4 groups.**
   Attempt-1 (4 groups × 512 threads), attempt-2 (48+96 groups ×
   32 threads) and this attempt (12+24 groups × 128 threads, 4
   blocks in flight per group, 2,048/768 B threadgroup memory) all
   land at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer chained at 1 row, across a 36×
   range of group counts. The prediction assumed attempt-1's
   serial part scales with cores busy (4 → 12); instead the
   ~100 µs plateau is invariant to how the blocks are packed. What
   does not shrink under any packing is each block's own serial
   K chain (24 strided load-accumulate steps per lane for gate,
   24 for up, 12 for down, gate→up→down ordered by the hidden
   dependency) plus the chained launch/link fixed cost — and this
   attempt *adds* a second launch and a `hidden` round-trip on
   that chain. Splitting exposes cores the critical path cannot
   use.
2. **At 32 rows the split tax is real and the fused kernel's
   in-group overlap was load-bearing.** 637.7 vs attempt-1's
   535.7: the two-kernel form pays 1,152 group dispatches (vs
   128), 3× duplicated `tg_x` loads and 6× duplicated `tg_h`
   loads, two extra barrier rounds per pair, and the `hidden`
   write+read — small bytes (<1% of weight traffic) but pure
   latency/occupancy overhead at streaming sizes, while a fused
   512-thread group keeps 16 blocks' loads in flight behind one
   barrier set. Restoring 4 blocks/group and low threadgroup
   memory recovered most of attempt-2's loss (80 → 111 GB/s) but
   not attempt-1's 132 GB/s.
3. **The 8-row rate confirms the mechanism:** 91 GB/s equals
   attempt-1's 92 GB/s — once enough groups exist to stream, the
   packing makes no difference, and the prediction's assumed
   residency gain (115 GB/s from lower threadgroup memory) did
   not appear; residency was not the cap.

Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: the 1-row lever is not
threadgroups per call (three packings, one plateau). The next
lever must shorten or overlap the per-block serial chain itself
— e.g. interleaving the independent gate and up K-loops so one's
loads hide the other's latency — or cut the chained fixed cost,
without touching any block's `simd_sum` order.

**Next change (one):** return to attempt-1's fused single kernel
and interleave gate/up: issue both blocks' K-loop loads per wave
before accumulating, keeping `qvm_block`'s per-block order and
all rounding points identical.
=====
# Round-2 attempt 3 — builder-2-c, hardening of hyp-2-routing-exact

Builds on the best full-G2 attempt, `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-1`
(G1 pass, G2 pass at all six sizes; chained 54.9/91.4/114.8 µs/layer vs
compiled 56.2/91.2/98.9 — wins only at 1 row). Baseline: none, so no
`beats_baseline`; the bar is the compiled reference.

## The one main change

Replace attempt-1's simdgroup-MMA threadgroup staging with scalar
partition accumulation, nothing else:

- Removed: `Ash`/`Bsh`/`Csh` staging, `simdgroup_float8x8` loads/MMA/store,
  and the 48 chunks × 2 threadgroup barriers per row (plus the 7/8 wasted
  rows of each 8×8 tile). The `<metal_simdgroup_matrix>` include goes too.
- Added: a `parts[60×32]` threadgroup array. Each (expert, partition)
  partial is one thread's serial scalar sum `part += xsh[d] * w_router[e*768+d]`
  over its K range in increasing `d`; one barrier; then partials are summed
  sequentially in partition order (`acc = 0; acc += parts[p]`), exactly
  attempt-1's partial order with the MMA inner accumulation replaced by
  the scalar sum attempt-2 proved bit-identical at decode.

Kept verbatim from attempt-1: the regime branch on `rows` (GEMV only at
`rows == 1`; split-K while `rows <= 768`; regular above), the split-K
partition formula (`next_pow2(48/((rows+31)/32*2))` clamped to [2,32],
base `48/partitions` BK=16 chunks, last partition to chunk 48 — so 32
partitions at 8/32 rows, 8 partitions of 96 at 127 rows, 2 at 257–768),
the single partition covering all 48 chunks above 768 rows, the GEMV
lane order and shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1, MLX's verbatim sigmoid
(`1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`), the strictly-greater
insertion top-4 (earliest index wins ties), and
`((w0+w1)+w2)+w3 + 1e-20`, divide, ×2.5 on unbiased scores. Same grid
(`rows*256`), threadgroup (256) and one-kernel layout. Threadgroup memory
(768+60+1920)×4 B = 10,992 B of 32 KB.

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-routing-1` stays removed (same orders as attempt-1), and
attempt-1's staging cost — the reason it loses at 32 rows (its notes:
48×2 barriers/row, 7/8 tile waste, per-row `w_router` re-read) — is
attacked directly: the scalar path has 2 barriers per row total instead
of 96+, and no tile waste. The per-row `w_router` re-read
(`ineff-baseline-routing-4`) and serial thread-0 scan (part of
`ineff-baseline-routing-3` kept for the tie rule) are untouched.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows

Anchor: attempt-1 measured 54.9/91.4/114.8, compiled 56.2/91.2/98.9
(same grader run, hyp entry). Traffic per row is 184 KB of `w_router`
(0.9 µs at 200 GB/s), so traffic floors are 0.9/7.4/29.5 µs; the rest is
chained-call latency and per-row staging/serial work.

- 1 row: the GEMV branch is unchanged, so ≈ attempt-1's 54.9 → **55**.
- 8 rows: attempt-1's per-row increment over its 1-row time is
  (91.4−54.9)/7 ≈ 5.2 µs/row on the MMA path. Removing 96 barriers and
  the tile staging per row, the scalar critical path per expert is the
  last partition's 272 serial products, hidden across 8 threadgroups ×
  8 warps; estimate the increment falls to ≈1.4 µs/row → 54.9+7×1.4 ≈ **65**.
- 32 rows: same increment → 54.9+31×1.1 ≈ **89** (per-row increment
  falls further as 32 threadgroups fill the GPU; traffic floor 29.5 µs
  is inside this, not added to it).

Prediction: **55 / 65 / 89 µs** — beats compiled (56.2/91.2/98.9) at all
three if the staging model holds. G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes
if attempt-2's scalar≡MMA result extends to the 8-partition (127-row)
and single-accumulator (>768) groupings, which are the only scalar
groupings attempt-2 did not already prove.

## Verdict (2026-11-04T03:51:53Z, one grader run)

G1 pass, **G2 pass at all six sizes** (rows_differ 0, rows_other_experts
0, max_rel_err 0.0 at 1/8/32 and 127/1016/2048). Chained µs/layer
(ref / compiled / candidate): 1 row 68.7 / 58.0 / **46.9** (beats
compiled); 8 rows 106.2 / 84.5 / 300.0; 32 rows 106.7 / 90.9 / 297.2.
`beats_compiled` false. Baseline none, so no `beats_baseline`.

The exactness half of the bet won everywhere: attempt-2's scalar≡MMA
result extends to the two groupings it never tested — 8 scalar
partitions of 96 at 127 rows and the single serial accumulator over 48
chunks above 768 rows both reproduce the steel regimes bit for bit on
all graded inputs. Scalar partition accumulation inside attempt-1's
regime logic is therefore a full-G2 design, and the fastest at 1 row
(46.9 vs attempt-1's 54.9, same GEMV branch — the win there is the
removed MMA staging code around it, or run-to-run drift; the branch
itself is unchanged).

## Why the 8/32-row timings missed the prediction by >20%

Predicted 55/65/89, measured 46.9/300.0/297.2: the 1-row prediction
holds (−15%), the scalar rows are 4.6×/3.3× over. Analysis (no second
GPU run; this is code-level, not an isolated measurement):

- The scalar path is latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound. The candidate
  is flat 300→297 µs while rows quadruple (traffic 1.5→5.9 MB), where
  attempt-1 rose 91.4→114.8. Per row the path issues 60×768 = 46,080
  scalar `w_router` loads as one dependent FMA chain per
  (expert, partition) thread; the threads holding partition 31 chain
  272 dependent device loads, and at 8 rows only 64 warps (8
  threadgroups × 8) are resident across 16 GPU cores — too few to hide
  that chain. Attempt-1's MMA consumed 16 K values per hardware op
  after one cooperative stage per chunk; the scalar version pays a
  full load-to-FMA latency per product.
- The loads are also uncoalesced and bank-conflicted. A warp is one
  expert's 32 partitions, so lanes read `w_router` 16 floats (64 B)
  apart — 16 cache lines per load step — and read `xsh[p*16+k]` with
  all even partitions on the same threadgroup bank (`(p*16+k) mod 32`
  is `k` or `k+16`), a 16-way bank conflict on every product. The
  prediction assumed staging removal was pure profit; in fact
  attempt-1's per-chunk staging was also its coalescing mechanism.

Next change (one): keep the scalar sums and partition order, but stage
each partition's `w_router` block into threadgroup memory with
coalesced vector loads (as attempt-1 staged chunks) and sum from
threadgroup with a swizzled/padded `xsh` layout, so the scalar chain
reads conflict-free local memory instead of uncoalesced device memory.

  "output": "# Round-2 attempt 4 — builder-2-d, hardening of hyp-2-routing-exact

Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-3` (scalar
full-G2; chained 46.9/300.0/297.2 µs/layer vs compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9 —
latency-bound from uncoalesced device loads + `xsh` bank conflicts).
Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the compiled reference.

## The one main change

Stage each K-chunk's `w_router` block into threadgroup memory with
coalesced vector loads and sum from threadgroup with a padded `x`
layout, nothing else:

- Staging: chunks are staged 4 at a time (12 groups cover all 48
  BK=16 chunks). Each staged chunk is 60×16 floats, loaded as 240
  `float4` loads (consecutive threads cover one expert's 4 vectors,
  then the next expert) and stored transposed in `wsh[slot][k][expert]`
  with expert stride 64.
- Padded `x`: chunk `c` of `x` sits at `xpad[c*17 + k]` (one pad float
  per chunk), replacing attempt-3's flat `xsh[768]`.
- Scalar chain: expert-parallel lanes read `wsh` at consecutive expert
  banks (conflict-free) and `xpad` uniformly per `k` (broadcast).
  Partials live transposed in `parts[partition][expert]` (stride 64)
  and are resumed product-by-product in increasing `d` across staged
  groups, so each (expert, partition) partial is still one serial
  scalar sum in increasing `d`; partials are then summed sequentially
  in partition order. 24 barriers on the scalar path (2 per group).
- Threadgroup memory: (816 + 60 + 2048 + 4096) × 4 B = 28,080 B of
  32 KB. Same grid (`rows*256`), threadgroup (256) and one-kernel layout.

Kept verbatim from attempt-3: the regime branch on `rows` (GEMV only
at `rows == 1`; split-K while `rows <= 768`; regular above — the GEMV
branch is unchanged apart from reading the padded `x` layout), the
split-K partition formula (32 partitions at 8/32 rows, 8 of 96 at 127,
2 at 257–768, single partition above 768, last partition absorbing the
remainder chunks), the GEMV lane order and shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1,
MLX's verbatim sigmoid (`1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`),
the strictly-greater insertion top-4 (earliest index wins ties), and
`((w0+w1)+w2)+w3 + 1e-20`, divide, ×2.5 on unbiased scores.

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-routing-1` stays removed (same orders as attempt-3).
The target is attempt-3's diagnosed feeding cost (its notes: the
scalar chains read `w_router` uncoalesced — warp lanes 64 B apart,
16 cache lines per step — and `xsh[p*16+k]` with 16-way bank
conflicts on every product). Staging turns the device reads into
coalesced `float4` loads and the dependent chain's reads into
conflict-free threadgroup reads. The per-row `w_router` re-read
(`ineff-baseline-routing-4`) and the serial thread-0 scan are
untouched.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows

Anchor: attempt-3 measured 46.9/300.0/297.2, compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9
(same grader run). Traffic per row is unchanged at 184 KB of
`w_router` (0.9 µs at 200 GB/s), so floors are 0.9/7.4/29.5 µs; the
rest is chained-call latency and per-row work. Attempt-3's flat
~300 µs was the dependent device-load chain; the staged chain reads
threadgroup memory instead, at the cost of 24 barriers/row.

- 1 row: GEMV branch unchanged but for the padded index (a shift and
  mask per access) → ≈ attempt-3's 46.9 → **48**.
- 8 rows: fixed chained latency ≈ 40 µs (attempt-3's 1-row time less
  its small GEMV work) + traffic 7.4 + staged scalar work. The
  critical path is the last partition's 272 sequential threadgroup
  FMAs, overlapped across 8 threadgroups; allowance ≈ 20 µs →
  40 + 7.4 + 20 ≈ **67**.
- 32 rows: 40 + 29.5 + 25 (more threadgroups fill the GPU, critical
  path unchanged) ≈ **95**.

Prediction: **48 / 67 / 95 µs** — beats compiled (58.0/84.5/90.9) at
1 and 8 rows, near it at 32. G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes —
no accumulation order changes, only where operands are read from.

## Verdict (2026-11-04T03:56:12Z, one grader run)

G1 pass, **G2 pass at all six sizes** (rows_differ 0,
rows_other_experts 0, max_rel_err 0.0 at 1/8/32 and 127/1016/2048).
Chained µs/layer (ref / compiled / candidate): 1 row 71.1 / 60.7 /
**47.5**; 8 rows 102.9 / 84.9 / **69.1**; 32 rows 104.9 / 89.5 /
**72.9**. **`beats_compiled` true** — the first routing attempt to
beat the compiled reference at all three row counts. Baseline none,
so no `beats_baseline`. Vs attempt-3 (46.9/300.0/297.2): the staged
scalar path is 4.3×/4.1× faster at 8/32 rows; the 1-row GEMV branch

## Why the 32-row timing missed the prediction by >20%

Predicted 48/67/95, measured 47.5/69.1/72.9: 1 and 8 rows hold
(−1%/+3%), 32 rows is 23% under. The prediction added a fixed ~40 µs
chained latency, the full 29.5 µs traffic floor and a per-row work
allowance as if they were serial per layer call. They are not: at 32
rows, 32 threadgroups across 16 GPU cores overlap one threadgroup's
coalesced staging loads and barriers with other threadgroups' scalar

# attempt-4 (round 2): hardening — fused interleave gate/up (builder-1-d)

Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
`none`). Builds on the best attempt
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-1` (fused single kernel,
512 threads/pair, G2 pass all six, 104.3/193.3/535.7 µs/layer chained
vs compiled 77.6/235.7/791.6 — loses only at 1 row). This is the one
main change named by attempt-3's miss analysis
(`attempt-3/notes.md`, *Next change*): attempt-3 split into two
kernels and plateaued at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer at 1 row across three
packings, so group count is not the lever; the next lever is to
overlap the per-block serial K chain itself inside the fused kernel.

## The one main change

Stay in attempt-1's fused single kernel — same one kernel, same
512 threads per (row, expert-slot) pair, same grid `rows*2048`
threads = `rows*4` groups, same branch on `rows >= 60`, same
threadgroup buffers — and interleave gate and up in the decode
branch only:

- **Before (attempt-1):** simdgroup `b` (`b < 12`) ran
  `qvm_block(gate, block b)` to completion (24 strided K steps per
  lane: `k = lane, lane+32, ..., lane+744`; each step loads 4 weight
  words + scale/bias for that `k`, then accumulates 32 outputs),
  stored `tg_gate`, then ran `qvm_block(up, block b)` the same way
  and stored `tg_up`. The two blocks' K loops were fully sequential:
  up's first load waited for gate's last accumulate.
- **Now:** simdgroup `b` runs one merged loop,
  `qvm_gate_up_pair` (block-1). For each strided `k`, both blocks'
  loads are issued first — gate's 4 weight words, scale and bias,
  then up's 4 weight words, scale and bias (plus the shared
  `tg_x[k]`, read once) — and only then do the two accumulation
  passes run, gate's 32 terms then up's 32 terms, into separate
  accumulators `pg`/`pu`. The next `k`'s loads therefore sit behind
  twice the issued load traffic per step, and each block's load
  latency has the other block's loads/compute to hide behind
  (double-buffering the two blocks' weight/scale/x loads within
  the step). Lane 0 then stores both blocks in one loop:
  `tg_gate[b*32+j] = (bfloat)pg[j]`, `tg_up[b*32+j] = (bfloat)pu[j]`.

Everything else is copied, not redesigned:

- **Per-block bits unchanged.** In `qvm_gate_up_pair`, each block's
  adds run in exactly `qvm_block`'s order: the same strided `k`
  sequence, the same float32 dequant terms
  `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` /
  `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)` with `s1 = scale/16`, in the same
  per-output sequence; `pg` and `pu` are independent accumulators,
  so interleaving the two blocks cannot reorder either block's own
  adds. Each accumulator then gets the identical
  `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` `simd_sum` tree as `qvm_block`.
  Down still calls `qvm_block` verbatim (verified by diff against
  attempt-1: `qvm_block` and `qmm_accum` bodies byte-identical;
  block-0 differs only in the header comment and the decode
  gate/up call site).
- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`) unchanged.** Attempt-1's scalar
  `qmm_accum` (weight rounded to bfloat16 first,
  `float(bfloat(scale·q+bias))`, then K accumulated contiguously in
  `BK=32` tile order, one output per lane) is copied byte-identical
  for gate, up and down, and block-0's prefill branch is untouched —
  the interleaving does not touch the prefill arithmetic.
- Same four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden via the
  shared full-bfloat16 silu-mul, down — silu code byte-identical),
  fp32 accumulation, positional `y[r,j]` (`pair = r*4 + j`), and
  the same `rows >= 60` dispatch threshold from `x_shape[0]`, not
  the grader's bracketing sizes. No kernel split, no threadgroup
  count change, no new device-memory intermediate.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempts 1–3
  all plateau at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer at 1 row despite 4, 12+24 and
  48+96 threadgroups per call, so the binding cost past 4 groups is
  each block's serial K chain (24 + 24 + 12 strided
  load-accumulate steps, gate→up→down ordered by the hidden
  dependency) executed with only one block's loads in flight per
  simdgroup at a time. Interleaving gate and up — the two
  independent, equal-length (24-step) chains — puts both blocks'
  loads in flight in every step without touching any block's
  `simd_sum` order, the only lever attempt-3's analysis left inside
  the fused kernel. Down (12 steps) is left sequential: it cannot
  start before the silu barrier in any case.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
  attempt-1's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
  verbatim.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
  kept, as in attempts 1–3 — weight bytes per pair stay
  552,960 B; the interleaving changes load scheduling, not bytes.

## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)

512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 (spec unchanged, verified identical).
Threadgroup memory unchanged from attempt-1: `tg_x[768] +
tg_gate[384] + tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]` bfloat16 = **3,840 B** of
32,768 B, rows-independent. The only new state is register-local:
a second 32-float accumulator `pu[32]` beside `p[32]` and a second
4-word load buffer inside `qvm_gate_up_pair` — the register cost
is the risk noted below. Grid scales as `rows*4` groups, so the
kernel is valid at every `rows ≥ 1`, on both sides of 60.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)

Weight bytes per layer (552,960 B/pair, of which gate+up are
368,640 B = 2/3): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs.
Attempt-1 chained (this round's grader): 104.3 / 193.3 / 535.7
µs/layer = effective 21.2 / 91.5 / 132.1 GB/s; compiled (same run)
77.6 / 235.7 / 791.6.

- **1 row: 90.** Latency-bound (floor 2.21 MB ÷ 200 GB/s =
  11.1 µs). Gate+up are 48 of the 60 serial product steps and 2/3
  of the pair bytes, so ≈ 2/3 × 104.3 ≈ 69 µs of attempt-1's time
  is the gate/up chains (the rest: down's 12 steps, `tg_x` load,
  silu, barriers, chained launch/link). Issuing both blocks' loads
  before accumulating doubles the loads outstanding per step; if
  that hides ≈ 20% of the gate/up chain's exposed latency
  (0.20 × 69 ≈ 14 µs), the layer lands at ≈ **90 µs** — still
  above the compiled 77.6, closing about half the remaining gap.
  Risk: the second accumulator's register pressure could spill or
  cut resident groups and hand the saving back.

Only the arithmetic. Indexing, grid, threadgroup, inputs/outputs and the
final line `bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase]` are verbatim from the starting
point. The single-expression sum

```metal

```

which the compiler FP-contracts into FMAs (each product kept unrounded
into its add), becomes seven fma-free stepwise ops with explicit
rounding barriers:

```metal

volatile float p1 = float(y[ybase+768u]) * weights[wbase+1u];
volatile float p2 = float(y[ybase+1536u]) * weights[wbase+2u];
volatile float p3 = float(y[ybase+2304u]) * weights[wbase+3u];

volatile float acc = s012 + p3;                              // rounded to f32
```

Each `volatile` store materialises its f32 value, so no product can stay
