203|### D. Dequantization — `QuantizedBlockLoader` + `dequantize` (rounding point 1)
204|
205|- **Callers:** `affine_gather_qmm_rhs` with
206|  `QuantizedBlockLoader<T=bfloat16, BROWS=BK=32, BCOLS=BN=32,
207|  dst_ld=40, reduction_dim=0, tgp_size=64, group_size=32, bits=4>`
208|  (`quantized.h:2613-2621`); same loader family as `qmm_n`/`qmm_t`
209|  (§G).
210|- **Callees:** `load_unsafe`/`load_safe` (`quantized.h:736-770`) call
211|  `dequantize<T, pack_factor=2, bits=4>` (`quantized.h:557-663`,
212|  bits=4 at `:617-623`) per packed byte: with `s = float(scale)`,
213|  `b = float(bias)` it writes
214|  `w_local[2i] = (bfloat16)(s * (w[i] & 0x0f) + b)` and
215|  `w_local[2i+1] = (bfloat16)((s/16) * (w[i] & 0xf0) + b)` into
216|  threadgroup `Ws`. Scales: one `scale`/`bias` pair per thread from
217|  `scales + bi * N/32` (`:733-734`); `group_steps = 32/32 = 1`, so
218|  `next()` advances `scales/biases` by `32*N/32 = N` per K tile
219|  (`:772-790`) — exactly one scale group per `BN=32` output tile and
220|  per `BK=32` row of `K`, matching the `[E, K, N/32]` layout.
221|- **Data:** packed uint32 weights are viewed as bytes (`(device
222|  uint8_t*)w`); each byte yields 2 outputs (low/high nibble), each
223|  `BK×BN = 1,024`-element weight tile dequantized once per
224|  (row tile, K tile) visit into `Ws`, then read by the MMA (§E).
225|  `x` tiles by contrast are copied verbatim (bfloat16 → bfloat16,
226|  exact) by `BlockLoader` (`steel/gemm/loader.h:74-80`).
227|- **Neighbours:** this is the first of the two divergence points
228|  vs `qvm` (§F): the dequantized weight is **rounded to bfloat16
229|  before any multiply**. In `qvm` the same `scale*q + bias` value
230|  stays in float32 registers through the product.
231|- **Cost:** dequant element-ops per product per layer =
232|  `T × K × N` = `T × 294,912` (both products have `K·N = 294,912`):
233|  17.7M / 88.5M / 159.2M at the three prefill sizes (balanced `T`
234|  from §C), each a float mul+add, a float→bfloat round, and a
235|  threadgroup store+reload. This recompute-per-row-tile is the
236|  loader's design (no dequantized-weight cache exists; the full
237|  dequantized expert is 294,912 × 2 B = 590 KB, far above the
238|  32 KB threadgroup limit, so cross-tile reuse would need a device
239|  buffer and an extra kernel — not a free fix).
240|- **Invariants:** `scale`/`bias` themselves are bfloat16 values
241|  upcast to float exactly (bfloat→float is exact), identical to
242|  `qvm`'s inputs; the *only* added rounding is
243|  `static_cast<bfloat16>(s*q + b)`. Relative error up to half a
244|  bfloat ULP (≈2⁻⁹ ≈ 0.2%) per weight element, deterministic per
245|  `(expert, k, n)` — the same rounded weight is reused for all
246|  ≤16 rows of the tile, so errors are correlated across rows
247|  sharing an expert, unlike per-pair float weights.
248|
249|### E. Accumulation — `BlockLoader` + `BlockMMA` (rounding point 2)
250|
251|- **Callers:** `affine_gather_qmm_rhs` instantiates
252|  `BlockMMA<bfloat16, bfloat16, BM=16, BN=32, BK=32, WM=1, WN=2,
253|  false, transpose=false, ...>` (`quantized.h:2599-2610`) and
254|  `BlockLoader<bfloat16, BM=16, BK=32, dst_ld=40, reduction_dim=1,
255|  tgp_size=64>` for `x` (`:2611-2612`).
256|- **Callees:** `BlockMMA` (`steel/gemm/mma.h:439-537`) with
257|  `AccumType = float` by default (`mma.h:451`): accumulator
258|  fragments `Ctile` are `float` 8×8 `simdgroup_matrix` tiles
259|  (`TM = 16/(8·1) = 2`, `TN = 32/(8·2) = 2` frags per simdgroup).
260|  `mma()` (`mma.h:513-537`) steps `kk` over `BK` in 8-wide frags
261|  (4 steps per tile), each `tile_matmad` issuing
262|  `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate` (`mma.h:181-206, 406-427`).
263|  Operand fragments are loaded from threadgroup bfloat16 and
264|  widened to float (`BaseMMAFrag::load` casts, `mma.h:57-67`), so
265|  the multiply is float×float with float accumulate — but the
266|  weight operand is the already-bfloat-rounded value of §D, and
267|  the 8-term dot inside each frag is the hardware's tree order,
268|  not a serial FMA chain. `gemm_loop_*` then adds tile results
269|  sequentially over the 24/12 K tiles. Store:
270|  `store_result`/`store_result_safe` cast float → bfloat16 once
271|  (`mma.h:100-112, 540-592`; `quantized.h:2683, 2694`) — the same
272|  single final rounding as `qvm`.
273|- **Data:** `Xs` holds `16×32` bfloat16 activations per K tile
274|  (rows zero-padded by `load_safe` when `tgp_bm < 16`,
275|  `loader.h:83-128`); `Ws` holds the §D dequantized tile. Partial-row
276|  tiles take the `gemm_loop_unaligned<false, true, ...>` branch
277|  (`quantized.h:2687-2695`) — full MMA work on padded rows, results
278|  discarded.
279|- **Neighbours:** identical bfloat16 store boundary as `qvm`, so
280|  the downstream `swiglu` (gate/up) and down product see the same
281|  *kind* of rounding point — only the float value arriving at the
282|  cast differs.
283|- **Cost:** per product, MMA flops are `2·B_padded·K·N` with
284|  `B_padded = T·16` = 960 / 4,800 / 8,640 vs useful `B` = 508 /
285|  4,064 / 8,192 (padded fractions in `ineff-quantized-kernels-1`).
286|  At 5.2 TFLOPS peak (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:14`) the useful MMA
287|  floors at `2·B·K·N/5.2 TFLOPS` = 57.6 / 461.0 / 929.2 µs per
288|  layer-product (B = 508 / 4,064 / 8,192) if it ran at peak — it
289|  cannot, at `BM=16` tiles with two barriers per 32-K step
290|  (`quantized_utils.h:14-29`), so the path is
291|  overhead/latency-bound, not compute-bound; no measured prefill
292|  time exists to check this against (§A).
293|- **Invariants:** per-output accumulation grouping is
294|  **[contiguous 8-wide frag dots] sequentially over BK=32 tiles**,
295|  in increasing K. This is the second divergence from `qvm` (§F):
296|  even with bit-identical weight operands, regrouping a 768-term
297|  float sum this way rounds differently on generic data. Reproducing
298|  it with scalar FMAs is not bit-safe; reproducing it requires the
299|  same 8×8 `simdgroup_matrix` fragmentation (same `BK`, same
300|  frag step order) or a proof the hardware order coincides — none
301|  exists in the sources. Warp tiling `WM/WN` only partitions frags
302|  across simdgroups; it does not change a single output's add order.
303|
304|### F. Comparator — `qvm_impl` + `qouter` (what decode runs; delta only)
305|
306|Round 1 §A mapped this kernel fully; only the contrast is new.
307|
308|- **Callers/Callees:** `gather_qvm` host (`quantized.cpp:1462-1529`)
309|  → `affine_gather_qvm` (`quantized.h:2355-2416`) → `qvm_impl`
310|  (`quantized.h:1222-1330`): grid `(1, (N+63)/64, B)` threadgroups of
311|  64 threads; gate/up `(1, 6, B)`, down `(1, 12, B)`. Each lane owns
312|  one strided `K` element per 32-step (`x += block_size` with
313|  `block_size = 32`, `:1275-1287`) and accumulates 32 outputs in
314|  float registers via `qouter` (`quantized.h:452-553`, bits=4 at
315|  `:503-509`): `result += x * (scale*q + bias)` with
316|  `scale`/`bias`/`x` all float, **no bfloat16 rounding of the
317|  weight**, serial per-lane adds in strided-K order
318|  (`k = lane, lane+32, ...`), then one `simd_sum` tree over the 32
319|  lane partials (`:1317-1321`) and a single float→bfloat16 store
320|  (`:1324-1329`).
321|- **The two divergences, side by side:**
322|
323|  | aspect | `gather_qvm` (decode, rows < 60) | `gather_qmm_rhs` (prefill, rows ≥ 60) |
324|  |---|---|---|
325|  | weight value | `float(scale)·q + float(bias)` kept in float32 | same value rounded to bfloat16 in threadgroup (§D) |
326|  | K grouping | strided lanes: lane `l` sums `k≡l (mod 32)` serially, then `simd_sum` tree | contiguous: 8-wide frag dots, sequential over BK=32 tiles (§E) |
327|  | rows sharing work | none: one grid slice per pair | ≤16 sorted rows share each weight tile |
328|  | final rounding | float → bfloat16 once after `simd_sum` | float → bfloat16 once after MMA — identical point |
329|
330|  Either divergence alone breaks bit-equality (measured: 62.4–62.6%
331|  of experts outputs differ at all three prefill sizes, max
332|  43/65/110.5 ULP, `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-1/grade-exact-experts.json`;
333|  full statement in `ineff-baseline-experts-1`). A single arithmetic
334|  cannot match both kernels on generic inputs: pick any weight with
335|  `float(scale·q+bias)` not representable in bfloat16 and any
336|  `x ≠ 0` — the two references already disagree on that product
337|  before accumulation even starts. **Conclusion for builders: a
338|  size branch is required** — `qvm` arithmetic below 60 rows,
339|  `qmm_rhs` arithmetic (bfloat-rounded dequant tiles + 8-wide frag
340|  accumulation) at/above 60 rows — or a proof of coincidence that
341|  the 62% differ rate rules out empirically. The branch threshold
342|  must be the dispatch rule `rows >= 60` (pairs `>= 240`, `E=60`),
343|  not the grader's nearest tested sizes 32/127: rows 33–59 in the
344|  real model still run `qvm` (§A). Row *grouping* inside the
345|  prefill branch is free (§C invariant); per-row accumulation is
346|  not.
347|- **Cost:** decode cost is round 1's confirmed entry
348|  (`muse-spark/exploration/ineff-quantized-kernels-1`, confirmed;
349|  round-2 restatement `ineff-baseline-experts-3`): 51 MB read in
350|  0.92 ms at 1 row (55 GB/s), 908 MB in 14.67 ms at 32 rows
351|  (62 GB/s, 31% of peak). Not re-posted here.
352|- **Invariants:** both paths accumulate in float32 and round to
353|  bfloat16 exactly once per product; `silu(gate)·up` is computed on
354|  those bfloat16 values and rounded again before down (brief:
355|  `claude/muse-agent-brief.md:90`). Any candidate must keep all
356|  four bfloat16 points (gate, up, hidden, down) — matching only the
357|  final `y` rounding is insufficient, since 1-ULP hidden flips
358|  amplify through down (round 1
359|  `muse-spark/implementation/hyp-1-fused-experts.md:103-108`).
360|
361|### G. Never-run neighbours — `gather_qmm` / `qmm_n_impl` / `qmm_t_impl`
362|
363|- **Callers:** §A branch (2) needs `M >= 4`; MobileMoE always has
364|  `M=1`, so `affine_gather_qmm_n`/`_t` (`quantized.h:2418-2568`)
365|  with `qmm_n_impl` (`:1468-1595`) / `qmm_t_impl` (`:1341-1459`),
366|  all `BM=BN=BK=32, WM=WN=2`, never run in this model at any size.
367|  Documented so no one chases them for the prefill failure: the
368|  prefill kernel is `qmm_rhs` (§C), not these.
369|- **Callees/Data/Invariants:** they share §D's loader (bfloat-rounded
370|  weights) and §E's `BlockMMA` accumulation, so their per-output
371|  arithmetic would match `qmm_rhs`'s rounding family — but their
372|  grid is per `(N tile, M tile, pair-batch B)` via
373|  `adjust_matrix_offsets`, not offset tiles. Zero cost here; the
374|  only use is as evidence that MLX's matrix family consistently
375|  dequantizes to the element type before multiplying, while its
376|  vector family (`qvm`/`qmv`) does not.
377|
378|### H. NAX variant — `gather_qmm_rhs_nax` (not on this GPU)
379|
380|- **Callers:** §B's first gate only; false on the M1 Pro grader
381|  machine (§B). Tiles there are `bm=32` (or 64 when `M/E >= 64`),
382|  `bn=bk=64` with NAX matrix ops (`quantized_nax.h`). If the grader
383|  ever moved to an M3-class GPU, the prefill reference's frag size
384|  and K blocking would change with it, and a hard-coded `BK=32`
385|  replica would fail G2 there. On the current hardware this is a
386|  portability note, not a cost.

### attempt-2 (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-2`) — boundary-1 · 2026-11-04T03:45:19Z — **pass**

Checked against the Boundary above for what G2 cannot see. No defect found.

- **Row counts on each side of 60.** The branch is on the dispatch threshold itself, not the tested sizes: both kernels read `rows` from `inds_shape[0]` and take `qvm_block` below 60 and `qmm_block` at/above (`block-0.metal:11,26,49`; `block-1.metal:9,21,34`). This matches `B = rows*4 >= 240 ⇔ B/E >= 4` at exactly 60 rows; 33–59 therefore stay on `gather_qvm` and 60–126 on `gather_qmm_rhs`, as the Boundary requires. The sort threshold (rows ≥ 16) is correctly ignored — the kernel is positional in `inds` order (`block-0.metal:12-15`; `block-1.metal:10-11`), so reference-internal sorting cannot affect its bits at 16–59 rows either. Nothing in the kernel depends on the row count beyond this branch and the linear grids (`rows*1536` / `rows*3072` threads = `rows*48` / `rows*96` groups of 32, `spec.json:1`): pair/block decomposition (`tg/12`, `tg%12`; `tg/24`, `tg%24`) covers every `rows >= 1`, including untested 2–7, 9–31, 61–126, 128–1,015 and >2,048, and prefill chunks other than the first. Per-pair independence (no offsets, no cross-pair grouping) means chunk position and prompt length cannot change a row's arithmetic.
- **Unwritten threadgroup reads.** None. Decode: `tg_x[768]` is fully written (`i = lane; i < 768; i += 32`) and barriered before `qvm_block` reads it, and `tg_gate`/`tg_up[32]` are fully written by lane 0 and barriered before the silu read (`block-0.metal:19-21,27-48`); `tg_h[384]` likewise (`block-1.metal:16,22-25`). Prefill: each `BK=32` tile fully writes `Xs[256]` (row 0 = the pair's row, rows 1–7 zero — discarded padding in separate accumulators, as the Boundary allows) and `Ws[1024]` before the barrier, the MMA loads stay inside those extents, and `tmp[256]` is fully written by the four `simdgroup_store`s and barriered before `o32[j] = tmp[j]` reads row 0 (`block-2.metal:79-116`). The second `qmm_block` call re-writes `Xs`/`Ws` tile-by-tile behind the same barriers, so no stale or unwritten value is read. Device-side, `hidden` is written at every `(pair, block*32+lane)` (`block-0.metal:47-48,56-57`) before the down kernel reads it, and `y` at every output element in both branches (`block-1.metal:29-32,39`), so the uninitialised intermediate is never read.
- **Threadgroup memory vs the 32 KB limit.** Not close. Gate/up: `768*2 + 32*2 + 32*2 + 256*4 + 1024*4 + 256*4 = 7,808 B` (23.8% of 32,768 B; declarations at `block-0.metal:19-24`). Down: `384*2 + 256*4 + 1024*4 + 256*4 = 6,912 B` (21.1%; `block-1.metal:16-19`). The allocations are rows-independent, so this holds at every row count. (The prefill tiles are allocated in the decode branch too — a residency cost the builder's notes already record, not a limit risk: even so the decode group carries 7,808 B against a 32 KB cap.) The slot's baseline is `none` (this entry, line 11), so there is no `beats_baseline` bar; the bar is the compiled reference. Four round-1 conclusions are retired: the 1e-4 weight tolerance, expert-set (unordered) equality, the 1e-6 near-tie exemption, and "order of the 4 pairs is free". Everything else in round 1 — shapes/dtypes/layouts at decode sizes, the producer, the bias rule, the unbiased gather, the epsilon and the 2.5 scale, the GPU limits — holds as written, extended below where the size set grew.

28|### Inputs and outputs — extended to the prefill sizes (changed)
29|
30|Sources: the brief's routing table ([muse-agent-brief.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/muse-agent-brief.md:28)), `D, E, K = 768, 60, 4` ([slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:19)), [ref_routing](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:44) and the shape/dtype enforcement in [check_routing](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:107). All arrays stay row-contiguous ([muse-agent-brief.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/muse-agent-brief.md:24)). `rows` is now six graded values, not three: decode 1 / 8 / 32 and prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:272), [capture_prefill](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:214)).
31|
32|| | Name | Shape at decode 1 / 8 / 32 rows | Shape at prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [1,768] / [8,768] / [32,768] | [127,768] / [1016,768] / [2048,768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60,768] at all row counts | [60,768] at all row counts | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] at all row counts | [60] at all row counts | float32 |
37|| output | `inds` | [1,4] / [8,4] / [32,4] | [127,4] / [1016,4] / [2048,4] | uint32, each < 60 |
38|| output | `weights` | [1,4] / [8,4] / [32,4] | [127,4] / [1016,4] / [2048,4] | float32 |

40|`weights[r,j]` still belongs to `inds[r,j]` — now at the same position `j` as the reference, not merely as a pair (see *What must stay identical*).

42|### Before and after — the neighbour contract is narrowed, not moved (one line changed)
43|
44|- **Before (holds, at all six sizes).** The producer is unchanged: `x` is `post_attention_layernorm(h)` reshaped to flat `[rows,768]` ([mobilemoe.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:258), [slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:105)); `w_router` is `self.router.weight` and `bias` is `self.expert_bias.astype(float32)` ([slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:108)). The same `MoE.__call__` runs the prefill ([slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:217), [mobilemoe.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:217)), so the prefill sizes feed the slot through the identical path with larger `rows`. The slot still reads `x` as bfloat16; the reference casts to float32 itself ([mobilemoe.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:219)).
45|- **After (1), the experts call — round 1's "order is free" is retired.** `SwitchGLU` still gathers by index and, from `indices.size >= 64` (rows ≥ 16, so at every prefill size), sorts and unscatters internally so that `y[...,j,:]` corresponds to `inds[...,j]` ([switch_layers.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/switch_layers.py:181)). Functionally a permutation would still be gathered correctly, but it no longer satisfies the boundary: G2 compares `inds` in order ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:119), [ADR 0010](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:25)). The experts neighbour still expects 4 indices per row, each < 60 (checked at [check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:117)); distinctness follows from matching the reference's `argpartition` output, which is distinct by construction ([slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:46)).
46|- **After (2), combine — the pair order is now load-bearing.** Combine still computes `(y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(bfloat16) + shared` ([mobilemoe.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:231), [slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:51)), summing the 4 pairs in the emitted order, which is why the reference order is part of G2 ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:119)). Round 1's condition "`inds[r,j]` ↔ `weights[r,j]` pairing preserved, order free" is therefore insufficient: both the pairing and the position `j` must match the reference. The bfloat16 cast still happens in combine, outside the slot; the slot still outputs pure float32.
47|
48|Checklist delta (per [tracking.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/.agents/skills/muse-round/tracking.md:115)): producer — holds; `SwitchGLU` consumer — only the permutation line changed; combine consumer — only the order line changed. Callers, callees, data shapes/dtypes and costs are as in round 1, with `rows` extended as above.
49|
50|### What must stay identical — bit for bit at all six sizes (changed)
51|
52|G2 now passes only when a row is bitwise identical, in order: `differ = (inds != ref_inds).any(axis=1) | (w != ref_w).any(axis=1)` and `passes` requires `rows_differ == 0` ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:120), [check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:172)). `max_rel_err` is reported only over same-order rows as a diagnostic ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:122)); it cannot pass a differing row. The reference is [ref_routing](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:44):
53|
54|```python
55|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)
56|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=K - 1, axis=-1)[:, :K]
57|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)
58|return inds, w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * SCALE
59|```
60|
61|- **Rounding points (form holds, tolerance retired).** Everything inside the slot is still float32 after the exact bf16→f32 cast of `x`; there is still no bfloat16 rounding inside the slot ([slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:45), [mobilemoe.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:219)). Retired is round 1's "reduced precision anywhere … is allowed only if weights still land within 1e-4 relative … a different summation order is fine within that tolerance" ([hyp-2-fused-routing.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/implementation/hyp-2-fused-routing.md:49)): any last-bit difference in any of the 4 weights, at any of the six sizes, now fails the row.
62|- **The router product — three accumulation regimes, none of them serial (new).** The reference's MLX kernel, and with it the float32 accumulation order of `x.astype(f32) @ w_router.T`, changes with `rows` (MLX 0.32.4 `Matmul::eval_gpu`, M=rows, N=60, K=768; derivation in [territory-baseline-routing.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-baseline-routing.md:153) §3.1, confirmed in [ineff-baseline-routing-1.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/round-2/exploration/ineff-baseline-routing-1.md:24)):
63|
64|| `rows` | MLX kernel | float32 accumulation order |
65||---|---|---|
66|| 1 | GEMV (`gemv_float32_bm4_bn1_sm1_sn32_tm4_tn4`) | 32 lanes × serial 24 products (lane `l`: `d = i*128 + l*4 + 0..3`, `i=0..5`), then shuffle tree `sn = 16,8,4,2,1` |
67|| 8, 32, 127 | steel split-K GEMM | 32 K-partitions at 8/32 rows, 8 at 127; each partition: simdgroup 8×8 MMA over BK=16 chunks; partials summed sequentially in partition order |
68|| 1,016, 2,048 | regular steel GEMM | BM=64/BN=64/BK=16 tiles, K walked in BK=16 chunks, simdgroup MMA accumulation chunk after chunk |
69|
70|  A candidate must reproduce the regime that applies at the `rows` it is launched with — branching on `rows` generally (or one spec kernel per regime), not special-casing the six graded values: the dispatch is a function of `rows` (GEMV only at `rows = 1`; split-K while `768 >= rows`; regular GEMM above), and tile/partition counts vary inside the split-K regime. A serial reordering cannot reproduce the MMA regimes' rounding, since the 8-product accumulation inside each `simdgroup_float8x8` multiply-accumulate is the hardware's ([ineff-baseline-routing-1.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/round-2/exploration/ineff-baseline-routing-1.md:30)).
71|- **The sigmoid — MLX's formula verbatim (new).** The reference's `mx.sigmoid` is `y = 1 / (1 + metal::precise::exp(metal::abs(x)))`, returning `y` for `x < 0` and `1 - y` for `x >= 0` ([territory-baseline-routing.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-baseline-routing.md:213) §3.2, [ineff-baseline-routing-2.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/round-2/exploration/ineff-baseline-routing-2.md:15)). Any of `precise::exp` vs `exp`, the `|x|` argument, or the `1 - y` subtraction differing moves a score by 1 ULP and fails the row; this is independent of the product regime and both must be fixed.
72|- **Bias, gather and the 4-term normalise sum (arithmetic holds, now load-bearing).** The bias rule still holds: selection uses `scores + bias` (one f32 add), weights use the unbiased `scores` gathered at the selected indices ([mobilemoe.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:221), [slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:46)). The 4-term sum still holds and the starting point already matches it: `(((w0 + w1) + w2) + w3)` in `inds` order, then `+ 1e-20`, divide, `× 2.5` ([territory-baseline-routing.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-baseline-routing.md:247) §3.3, [slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:48)). What changed is only that this exact association is now required bit for bit, where round 1 allowed any order within tolerance; once the 4 selected scores are bit-equal and in the same order, the weights are bit-equal, so builders should not spend effort here.
73|- **Tie rule for the 4th and 5th expert, and the order of the 4 pairs (changed).** Retired is round 1's set equality with a 1e-6 near-tie exemption ([hyp-2-fused-routing.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/implementation/hyp-2-fused-routing.md:51)). The reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th biased scores, including exact ties, and the descending-biased-score order of positions 0..3 must be reproduced exactly at every size ([muse-agent-brief.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/muse-agent-brief.md:187), [check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:120)). No reordering of the 4 pairs is allowed (retires [hyp-2-fused-routing.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/implementation/hyp-2-fused-routing.md:52)); shapes, dtypes, the epsilon, the 2.5 scale and the unbiased-score rule still may not move.
74|- **Starting point against this boundary.** Checked line by line, [attempt-1](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:16) matches: the bf16→f32 cast ([block-0.metal](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:20)), the bias add ([block-0.metal](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:45)), the unbiased gather, the 4-term sum order with `+1e-20`, divide and `×2.5` ([block-0.metal](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:64)), and — on every graded input so far — the tie behaviour: the strictly-greater insertion scan (earliest index wins ties, descending biased order, [block-0.metal](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:44)) gives `rows_other_experts` 0 at all six sizes, so its tie rule must be preserved exactly (a `>=` compare or a differently-ordered parallel top-4 would break it). It does not match: the product, accumulated as one thread's serial 768-term chain ([block-0.metal](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:31)), and the sigmoid `1.0f / (1.0f + metal::exp(-acc))` ([block-0.metal](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:35)). Measured under the current grader it therefore fails G2 at every size while the experts and their order always match: rows differing 20/159/638 at decode 1/8/32 (100% / 99.4% / 99.7% of 20/160/640 rows over 20 layers) and 2,518/16,187/32,743 at prefill 127/1,016/2,048 (99.1% / 79.7% / 79.9%), max relative error 2.6e-06 at decode and 8.7e-06 at prefill ([territory-baseline-routing.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-baseline-routing.md:34)).

76|### What the grader checks, and what it can't see (changed)
77|
78|- **G1** compiles the Metal and runs it on all six sizes' inputs; `g1` is set only after every size's checks have run ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:267)).
79|- **G2** checks, per layer on all 20 layers: exact shapes/dtypes ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:107)), `inds < 60` ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:117)), and ordered bitwise equality of `inds` and `weights` ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:120)); `g2` requires every size to pass ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:308)). Decode inputs are captured from all 20 layers of one real decode step per row count ([slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:137)); prefill inputs are recorded live by `capture_prefill` with fixed seeds ([slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:240)). The G2 target is the uncompiled `ref_routing` ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:103)); `mx.compile` changes only the timing bar, not the target.
80|- **Piece timing (changed to chained).** Timing runs at decode 1 / 8 / 32 rows only, on the 20 layers' chained calls — each call data-dependent on the previous one through the `link` kernel ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:178)) — median of 30 repeats per layer ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:204)), and `beats_compiled` requires beating `mx.compile(ref_routing)` at all three row counts ([check_candidate.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/check_candidate.py:335)). The slot stops at the first attempt passing G1 and G2 and beating the compiled reference at all three row counts, or after 5 attempts ([muse-agent-brief.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/muse-agent-brief.md:201)).
81|- **What it can't see.** Row counts other than the six graded: any decode count from 1 to 32 ([muse-agent-brief.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/muse-agent-brief.md:24)) — 2–7 and 9–31 rows are ungraded, on both sides of the GEMV/split-K boundary at `rows = 1` — and prefill chunks of other sizes from other prompt counts or chunkings, on both sides of the split-K/regular boundary at `rows = 768` and of the tile/partition changes inside split-K; a kernel that hard-codes the six sizes passes G2 and breaks this boundary. Inputs other than the captured ones: other prompts, later decode steps, other layers' drift, unseen near-tie or exactly-tied 4th/5th biased scores (no graded row is a near-tie, so the tie rule is exercised only where the starting point already agrees), and score magnitudes that saturate the sigmoid differently. Threadgroup memory near the 32 KB limit: `slots.build` enforces only the 1,024-thread cap ([slots.py](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/bench/grader/slots.py:326)), so the 32 KB limit is unchecked by the grader. Reads of threadgroup memory that was never written, and any result that depends on thread timing or atomic order, which a single equality run per layer cannot expose. Prefill speed ([ADR 0010](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:42)), the end-to-end greedy-token check (24 tokens, plain MLX and vLLM) and G3 full-step timing, which the team runs after merging ([ADR 0010](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:32)). Boundary checks will probe exactly these.

Hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 16 cores, SIMD width 32, `bfloat` available in Metal ([muse-agent-brief.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/muse-agent-brief.md:99)). 166|  (matmul.cpp, `Matmul::eval_gpu`); the `gemv_wide` shortcut is skipped
167|  because the output is float32 (`gemv_wide_config` requires float16/bfloat16
168|  out). Dispatch picks `GEMVKernel<float, BM=4, BN=1, SM=1, SN=32, TM=4,
169|  TN=4>`: each output is accumulated by one simdgroup whose 32 lanes each
170|  serially sum 24 products — lane `l` takes `d = i*128 + l*4 + (0..3)` for
171|  `i = 0..5` (`kernels/gemv.h:162-182`) — and the 32 partials are then combined
172|  by a shuffle tree, `result += simd_shuffle_down(result, sn)` for
173|  sn = 16,8,4,2,1 (`gemv.h:202-208`). Grouping: 32 blocked partials + pairwise
174|  tree, not a serial chain.
175|- **rows = 8, 32, 127 → steel split-K GEMM.** In `steel_matmul_axpby` the
176|  split-K case fires when `_tm*_tn <= 2048` (this device's architecture string
177|  ends in `s`; brief:99 names it `applegpu_g13s`), `_tk = 768/16 = 48 >= 8`
178|  and `K >= max(M,N)` (matmul.cpp, Case 1). `steel_gemm_splitk_axpby` uses
179|  BM=16 (M<40) or 32, BN=32, BK=16, WM=WN=2 (steel/gemm split-K dispatch):
180|  partitions = min(max(2, next_pow2(48/(_tm*_tn))), 32) with
181|  `_tm=(M+31)/32, _tn=2` → **32 partitions at rows 8 and 32** (the last
182|  partition also absorbs the remaining 16 BK-iterations,
183|  `steel/gemm/kernels/steel_gemm_splitk.h:140-155`), **8 partitions at rows
184|  127**. Each partition accumulates its K-slice with simdgroup 8×8 matrix
185|  multiply-accumulate over BK=16 chunks in order (GEMMKernel/mma in
186|  `steel/gemm/gemm.h`, `mma.h`), writes a float32 partial, and
187|  `gemm_splitk_accum` sums the partials sequentially in partition order
188|  (`steel_gemm_splitk.h:186-189`).
189|- **rows = 1,016, 2,048 → regular steel GEMM.** Split-K no longer fires
190|  (768 < M), so `steel_matmul_regular_axpby` runs with the device tile from
191|  `GEMM_TPARAM_MACRO` (for an architecture ending in `s` the macro's fallback:
192|  BM=64, BN=64, BK=16, WM=2, WN=2): K is walked in BK=16 chunks staged through
193|  threadgroup memory, accumulated by simdgroup matrix ops chunk after chunk.
194|
195|So the reference has **three different float32 accumulation orders for the
196|same mathematical product, selected by `rows`** — and none of them is the
197|kernel's serial order. Every score therefore differs from the reference's in
198|the last bits with high probability, which is exactly the observed pattern:
199|~100% of decode rows and ~80–99% of prefill rows have at least one differing
200|weight, while no row picks different experts (the biased-score gaps at the
201|4th/5th place are far larger than 1-ULP score noise on these inputs).
202|The drop from ~100% (decode, GEMV/split-K regimes) to ~80% (1,016/2,048,
203|regular GEMM) is consistent with a per-regime last-bit flip rate; that last
204|step is an inference from the counts, not a measurement.
205|A scalar re-implementation cannot reproduce the steel regimes' rounding by
206|reordering a serial loop: within each 8×8 simdgroup matrix op the 8-product
207|accumulation is the hardware's. A bit-exact candidate must either reuse
208|`simdgroup_float8x8` multiply-accumulate with the same tiling/K-order per
209|regime (branching on `rows` inside the kernel, or one kernel per regime in
210|the spec), or find an accumulation that provably rounds identically — none
211|is known.
212|
213|#### 3.2 The sigmoid — DOES NOT MATCH (independent second cause)
214|
215|Kernel (`block-0.metal:35`): `1.0f / (1.0f + metal::exp(-acc))` — the fast
216|(non-`precise`) `exp`, applied to `-acc`, one division.
217|
218|Reference (`mx.sigmoid` → `Sigmoid` in
219|`mlx/backend/metal/kernels/unary_ops.h:308-314`, installed headers):
220|
221|```metal
222|auto y = 1 / (1 + metal::precise::exp(metal::abs(x)));
223|return (x < 0) ? y : 1 - y;
224|```
225|
226|Three differences, each able to move the result by 1 ULP: (a) `precise::exp`
227|vs `metal::exp`; (b) the argument is `|x|`, never negative; (c) for `x >= 0`
228|the result is `1 - y` (a subtraction that rounds) instead of the direct
229|division the kernel computes for all signs. Even a kernel whose matmul
230|matched bit for bit would still fail G2 on sigmoid alone for a large share
231|of scores. The fix is free in time: copy this formula verbatim.
232|
233|#### 3.3 Selection, gather, and the weight normalisation — MATCH
234|
235|- `scores + bias`: one f32 add in both (`block-0.metal:45`;
236|  `binary_ops.h:10-15`).
237|- Selection: the kernel's strictly-greater insertion scan emits descending
238|  biased order, earliest index winning ties (`block-0.metal:44-61`). The
239|  reference's argpartition is a full sort of `-(scores+bias)`
240|  (round-1 note, `ineff-runs-2.md:94-98`); on all six graded sizes the emitted
241|  sets *and* order agree (`rows_other_experts` 0, and the grader's worst-row
242|  examples show identical expert lists, grade-exact-routing.json). This is
243|  the part of Claude's round-1 reading ("the reference's order of
244|  operations … differ", round-2 README:39) that does **not** need fixing —
245|  but a builder must preserve the exact tie behaviour, since G2 now also
246|  compares order (`check_candidate.py:120`).
247|- The 4-term sum: the reference's `w.sum(axis=-1)` on a [rows,4] f32 array
248|  takes `row_reduce_small` (row_size 4 <= 64, MLX v0.32.4
249|  `mlx/backend/metal/reduce.cpp`, `row_reduce_general_dispatch` Case 1) in its
250|  per-thread branch (`non_row_reductions=1 < 32 && row_size <= 8`,
251|  `row_reduce_small` dispatch), i.e. `thread_reduce` with `N_READS=4`
252|  (`defines.h:12`): `total = (((0 + w0) + w1) + w2) + w3` in memory order —
253|  and `w`'s memory order is the `inds` order from argpartition, the same
254|  sequence the kernel sums as `s0 + s1 + s2 + s3` (`block-0.metal:64-68`;
255|  `kernels/reduction/reduce_row.h:164-181`). The kernel then adds `1e-20f`
256|  inside the same expression (`denom = s0+s1+s2+s3 + 1e-20f`), the reference
257|  as a separate add after the reduction (`slots.py:48`) — same association,
258|  and in float32 `sum + 1e-20` equals `sum` for any sum above ~1e-27, so the
259|  epsilon cannot be the cause either. Division and ×2.5 are the same single
260|  ops (`binary_ops.h:43-48,208-213`; `block-0.metal:74-77`).
261|  **Conclusion:** once the 4 selected scores are bit-equal and in the same
262|  order, the weights are bit-equal. Builders should spend their effort on
263|  3.1 and 3.2, not on the normalisation — the opposite emphasis to round 2
264|  README:39's example list, which names "the float32 sum order of
265|  `x @ w_router.T` and of `w.sum(...)`" as co-equal suspects.
266|

11|`routing`

13|## What happens
14|
15|The starting point (`muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:31-34`)
16|computes each of the 60 router scores as one thread's serial float32 chain,
17|`acc += xsh[d] * w_router[e*768 + d]` for d = 0..767 (compiler FMA contraction
18|does not change the left-to-right grouping). The reference,
19|`mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)` (`bench/grader/slots.py:45`),
20|never accumulates that way. In MLX 0.32.4's `Matmul::eval_gpu`
21|(`mlx/backend/metal/matmul.cpp`, tag v0.32.4) with M=rows, N=60, K=768,
22|A not transposed, B transposed, the accumulation order is chosen by `rows`:
23|
24|| rows | MLX kernel | float32 accumulation order |
25||---|---|---|
26|| 1 | GEMV `gemv_float32_bm4_bn1_sm1_sn32_tm4_tn4` (`min(M,N)==1` → `gemv`; `gemv_wide` skipped, f32 out) | 32 lanes × serial 24 products (lane l: d = i*128 + l*4 + 0..3, i=0..5, `kernels/gemv.h:162-182`), then shuffle tree sn=16,8,4,2,1 (`gemv.h:202-208`) |

29|
30|A serial scalar loop cannot reproduce the two MMA regimes' rounding by
31|reordering: the 8-product accumulation inside each `simdgroup_float8x8`
32|multiply-accumulate is the hardware's. Bit-exactness therefore needs either
33|the same simdgroup matrix ops with the same tiling and K-order per regime
34|(branch on `rows`, or separate spec kernels), or a proof that another order
35|rounds identically (none known). Full derivation:
36|`territory-baseline-routing.md` section 3.1.

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write a faster MobileMoE-S decode kernel
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*

8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
12|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
13|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
14|
15|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
16|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
17|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
18|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
19|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
20|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
21|
22|## The slots
23|
24|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the step: 1 to 32 in decode. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
25|
26|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
27|
28|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
29|
30|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
31||---|---|---|---|
32|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
33|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
34|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
35|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
36|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
37|
38|Reference:
39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
69|
70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.

177|## How each attempt is judged
178|
179|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only.
180|
181|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
182|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
183|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
184|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.

186|   At every size:
187|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.

199|**The piece timing** runs the slot on all 20 layers' captured decode inputs, at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and waits for the GPU once at the end. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. 4|starting point `muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4` (baseline: none;

6|kernels in list order, each branching on `rows` read from

8|from `territory-quantized-kernels` §A/§F, not the tested sizes):
9|
10|- `experts_gate_up` (block-0): one 32-thread threadgroup per
11|  (pair, 32-output block) — grid `rows*1536` threads = `rows*4*12`
12|  groups. Computes gate and up for its block, applies the silu-mul,
13|  writes `hidden[pair, block*32 + lane]`.
14|- `experts_down` (block-1): one 32-thread threadgroup per
15|  (pair, 32-output block) — grid `rows*3072` threads = `rows*4*24`
16|  groups. Reads `hidden`, writes its 32 outputs of `y`.
17|
18|Shared header (block-2): `qvm_block` copied byte-identically from
19|attempt-4, a new `qmm_block`, and attempt-4's full-bfloat16 silu.
20|
21|## What changed since attempt-4, and which inefficiency it removes
22|
23|1. **Prefill arithmetic (`ineff-baseline-experts-1`, the G2 gate).**
24|   Below 60 rows both kernels keep attempt-4's bit-exact `gather_qvm`
25|   arithmetic (float32 dequant through the product, strided lanes
26|   `k == lane (mod 32)` + `simd_sum`, full-bf16 silu). At 60 rows and
27|   above, `qmm_block` replicates `gather_qmm_rhs`: dequantized
28|   weights rounded to bfloat16 before the multiply
29|   (`dequantize` bits=4, `s` / `s/16` nibble form), then BK=32 tiles
30|   in increasing K order, each four sequential 8-wide
31|   `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate` steps on float fragments — the
32|   `BlockMMA` order. Row grouping is per-pair (fragment row 0, seven
33|   zero-padded rows in separate accumulators), which the boundary
34|   allows; per-row K order is unchanged. Gate/up/down each still
35|   round once from float32 to bfloat16, and the silu is shared.
36|2. **Chained 1-row latency (`ineff-baseline-experts-2`).** Attempt-4
37|   exposes 4 threadgroups per call at 1 row (one per pair) with
38|   barrier-serialised waves. Here a 1-row call exposes 48 (gate/up)
39|   + 96 (down) threadgroups, each computing exactly one 32-output
40|   block with the identical strided-lane + `simd_sum` order, so the
41|   GPU's 16 cores all have work while no block's bits change. Cost:
42|   a second launch per layer and one `hidden` round-trip (3 KB per
43|   pair); `x` is re-read from cache once per block (12x per pair,
44|   18 KB vs 369 KB of gate/up weights per pair).
45|3. `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair weight re-reads) is **not**
46|   removed: weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B, as in attempt-4.
47|   The 8/32-row chained wins must therefore be kept by occupancy,
48|   not by fewer bytes.
49|
50|Boundary kept: bit-exact accumulation order per size regime as
51|above; all four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden, down);
52|positional `y[r,j]` for any `inds` order; valid at every `rows`
53|(grid and block counts scale with `rows*4` pairs, branch only on
54|the 60-row dispatch threshold); 32 threads/group <= 1024;
55|threadgroup memory by hand (grader does not check 32 KB): GU
56|1536 + 128 + (256+1024+256)*4 = 7,808 B; Down 768 + 6,144 =
57|6,912 B.
58|

60|
61|Weight bytes per layer (552,960 B/pair): 2.21 / 17.7 / 70.8 MB at
62|4 / 32 / 128 pairs. Attempt-4 chained (round-2 exploration,
63|`console-chain.txt`): 132.9 / 175.9 / 587.6; reference chained
64|80.3 / 239.6 / 797.6.
65|
66|- 1 row: 144 small groups fill 16 cores; gate/up 1.47 MB + down
67|  0.74 MB at an assumed ~55 GB/s effective for 32-thread groups
68|  gives ~40 µs including the extra launch → **40 µs**
69|  (attempt-4 chained 132.9; reference 80.3).
70|- 8 rows: 384 + 768 groups, streaming regime; 17.7 MB at
71|  ~110 GB/s ≈ 160 µs → **165 µs** (attempt-4 175.9).
72|- 32 rows: 1,536 + 3,072 groups; 70.8 MB at ~115 GB/s ≈ 615 µs
73|  → **610 µs** (attempt-4 587.6; the 4% block-split tax is the
74|  risk to the kept win).
75|
76|G2: expect `differ == 0` at all six sizes. Decode reuses
77|attempt-4's proven per-block math unchanged; prefill depends on
78|the hardware's 8-wide fragment dot matching `BlockMMA`'s when fed
79|the same bfloat16-rounded operands in the same tile order.
80|
81|## Verdict
82|
83|G1 pass; **G2 pass — `differ` 0, `max_ulp` 0.0 at all six sizes**
84|(decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048). The prefill branch is
85|bit-exact: bfloat16-rounded dequantized weights plus BK=32 tiles of
86|four sequential 8-wide `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate` steps, fed a
87|single row per threadgroup, reproduce `gather_qmm_rhs` bit for bit
88|on every tested layer. `beats_compiled` false. Chained
89|µs/layer (candidate vs reference vs compiled, same run):
90|**103.6 / 326.8 / 887.6** vs 76.1 / 244.6 / 797.1 and
91|73.1 / 232.0 / 804.5. Baseline `none` — no
92|`wins_vs_baseline`/`beats_baseline`. The attempt is correct at
93|every size but slower than the compiled reference at all three
94|decode sizes, and slower than the starting point's chained times
95|(132.9 / 175.9 / 587.6, other harness) at 8/32 rows.
96|
97|## Miss analysis (prediction 40 / 165 / 610; all misses > 20%)
98|
99|Measured is 2.6x / 2.0x / 1.5x the prediction. Effective bandwidth
100|from 552,960 B/pair: 21 / 54 / 80 GB/s chained, against attempt-4's
101|chained 17 / 101 / 121 GB/s. The split helped exactly where group
102|count was the binding limit (1 row: 103.6 vs 132.9) and hurt
103|wherever streaming mattered. Two causes, both in the split shape,
104|not the arithmetic:
105|
106|1. **One simdgroup per group has too little memory parallelism.**
107|   Each 32-thread group runs its block's 24-step strided K loop
108|   alone; attempt-4 runs 8 such blocks concurrently per group, so
109|   one stalled load hides behind seven others. More groups only
110|   partly compensate: at 8/32 rows the GPU was already saturated
111|   with groups, and the per-group latency chain became the limit.
112|2. **Threadgroup memory caps residency in the decode branch too.**
113|   The qmm tiles (6,144 B of floats) are allocated in both kernels
114|   at every size, so a decode gate/up group carries 7,808 B where
115|   attempt-4 carries 3,840 B. Resident groups per core fall, and
116|   with 32-thread groups the resident thread count falls with
117|   them — the opposite of the occupancy the split was meant to add.
118|
119|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: exposing threadgroups is
120|not sufficient; a block-split kernel must keep several blocks in
121|flight per group (or per core) and keep decode threadgroup memory
122|near attempt-4's, e.g. 128-thread groups of 4 simdgroups each
123|owning one block (12 + 24 groups at 1 row), with the prefill tiles
124|overlaid on the decode buffers instead of added to them.
125|
126|**Next change:** rebuild the decode branch as 4-simdgroup groups
127|(4 blocks per group, qvm_block unchanged), overlay the qmm tile
128|memory on the decode threadgroup buffers, keep `qmm_block` as is.

# attempt-4: harden attempt-2 — 256 threads per pair (builder-1-d)

Single change on `../attempt-2` (direction b, one fused per-pair kernel):
256 threads per threadgroup (8 simdgroups) instead of 128 (4 simdgroups).
Grid goes from `rows*512` to `rows*1024` threads = still `rows*4` groups,
one per (row, expert-slot) pair. `block-1.metal` (qvm_block) is byte-identical
to attempt-2; only the wave structure in `block-0.metal` changed: gate/up 12
blocks in 2 waves of 8 (4 simds idle in wave 2, guarded by simd-uniform
`b < 12`), down 24 blocks in 3 waves of 8, x/silu strided loops step 256.

Removes the 1-row half of attempt-2's occupancy finding (its notes.md miss
analysis): at 1 row, 4 pairs x 128 threads = 512 threads on a 16-core GPU
streams at only ~20 GB/s effective (2.21 MB in 107.3 us), regressing 7.5%
vs eager (99.8 us). Doubling threads per pair doubles each group's in-flight
memory parallelism while keeping the proven-correct numerics untouched: same
qvm strided-lane accumulation + `simd_sum` per 32-output block (guard is
uniform inside each simd, so the reduction stays uniform), same full-bf16
silu lowering, same fp32 accumulation and bf16 rounding points. Gate/up/down
weight bytes per pair are unchanged (553 KB), so 8/32 rows — already
streaming at ~94-109 GB/s — should be unaffected.

Boundary kept: same as attempt-2 (boundary-1 pass): fp32 accumulation, all
four bf16 rounding points, positional `y[r,j]`, any `inds` order, valid for
all 1-32 rows (grid is `rows*4` groups, no rows-dependent indexing),
256 threads/group <= 1024, threadgroup memory unchanged at 3840 B (~12% of
32 KB).

## Predicted us per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows

- 1 row: occupancy-bound regime, threads 512 -> 1024. Effective bandwidth
  should roughly double from attempt-2's 20.6 GB/s (2.21 MB / 107.3 us):
  2.21 MB / 41 GB/s = 54 us + one launch ~7 us -> **60 us**
  (attempt-2 107.3; eager original 99.8; compiled 135.0). Beats eager.
- 8 rows: streaming regime already (17.7 MB in 188.4 us = 94 GB/s);
  same bytes, wider groups neutral -> **185 us**
  (attempt-2 188.4; original 218.7; compiled 216.9).
- 32 rows: same argument, full 70.8 MB at ~109 GB/s -> **650 us**
  (attempt-2 647.6; original 768.6; compiled 761.7).

G2: expect bit-exact (max_ulp 0.0) — every block's computation is identical
to attempt-2's v3, only the wave packing changed. beats_compiled: expect
true at all rows.

## Verdict

G1 pass; G2 pass with max_ulp 0.0 at all row counts (bit-exact vs reference,
as predicted); beats_compiled true. Piece timing us/layer (candidate vs
original vs compiled, this run): rows 1: 50.0 / 64.3 / 65.3; rows 8: 157.8 /
218.6 / 217.4; rows 32: 515.4 / 765.7 / 760.2. Beats BOTH the eager original
and the compiled reference at all rows (~22/28/33% over eager, ~23/27/32%
over compiled). The 1-row regression is fixed: 50.0 us vs attempt-2's 107.3
(2.1x), now beating eager's 64.3 by 22%.

Note: this run's 1-row baselines (64.3/65.3) are lower than attempt-2's run
(99.8/135.0) — the 1-row harness timing shifts between runs (attempt-1's
re-grade also saw 64.1/62.0), so cross-run candidate comparisons at 1 row
carry that caveat; within this run the candidate beats both baselines
cleanly. At 8/32 rows the baselines are stable across runs (218.6/217.4 vs
218.7/216.9; 765.7/760.2 vs 768.6/761.7), so the 8/32-row gains are real.

## Miss analysis (prediction 60 / 185 / 650)

Measured 50.0 / 157.8 / 515.4 — faster than predicted at all rows: -17% /
-15% / -21%. Only 32 rows exceeds the 20% bar, and on the fast side.

Why: the change did more than add 1-row occupancy. Eight blocks in flight
per wave per group (vs four) raised per-core memory-level parallelism in
EVERY regime: 32-row effective bandwidth went from attempt-2's ~109 GB/s
(70.8 MB / 647.6 us) to ~137 GB/s (70.8 MB / 515.4 us). Attempt-2 was mildly
MLP-bound even where it looked streaming-bound; the extra in-flight
weight/scale/bias loads per group hide more latency, and halving the wave
count halves barrier round-trips. Same mechanism explains the 8-row (-15%)
and 1-row (-17%) overshoots. Lesson for `ineff-quantized-kernels-1`: per-pair
qvm throughput scales with in-flight blocks per group up to at least 8
simds, not just with group count.

{"path":"muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-3/notes.md","content":"# attempt-3 (round 2): hardening — 4-block groups, scalar prefill (builder-1-c)

Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
`none`). Builds on the best attempt
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-1` (G2 pass all six,
104.3/193.3/535.7 µs/layer chained vs compiled 77.6/235.7/791.6 —
loses only at 1 row). Starting point for the decode arithmetic is
attempt-1's proven helpers; attempt-2's failure modes are the
constraint.

## The one main change

Split attempt-1's single fused per-pair kernel (4 threadgroups per
call at 1 row, 512 threads each) into two kernels with 4-block
threadgroups, exposing more threadgroups per call without
attempt-2's 1-simdgroup-per-group collapse:

- `experts_gate_up` (block-0): one 128-thread threadgroup (4
  simdgroups) owns 4 distinct 32-output blocks — simdgroup `s` of
  chunk `c = tg % 3` computes block `blk = c*4 + s` of pair
  `tg / 3` (12 blocks/pair ÷ 4 = 3 groups/pair). Grid
  `rows*1536` threads = `rows*12` groups: **12 groups at 1 row**
  (96 at 8, 384 at 32). Each simdgroup runs gate then up for its
  block, lane 0 (decode) or every lane (prefill) stores the
  bfloat16-rounded results to `tg_gate`/`tg_up`, one barrier, then
  every lane applies the shared full-bfloat16 silu-mul and writes
  `hidden[pair, blk*32 + lane]`.
- `experts_down` (block-1): same shape for the 24 down blocks —
  `blk = (tg % 6)*4 + simd`, pair `tg / 6` (24 ÷ 4 = 6 groups/pair).
  Grid `rows*3072` threads = `rows*24` groups: **24 groups at
  1 row** (192 at 8, 768 at 32).

Everything else is copied, not redesigned:

- **Decode (`rows < 60`):** `qvm_block` in block-2 is byte-identical
  to attempt-1's (verified by diff; itself attempt-4's proven
  helper) — strided lanes `k ≡ lane (mod 32)` serial in float32,
  float32 dequant `x·(scale·q+bias)`, `simd_sum` tree. Splitting
  blocks across threadgroups does not change any block's
  accumulation order, so decode bits are attempt-1's.
- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`):** `qmm_accum` in block-2 is
  byte-identical to attempt-1's scalar path (verified by diff) —
  weight rounded to bfloat16 first
  (`float(bfloat(scale·q+bias))`), then K accumulated contiguously
  in `BK=32` tile order by one thread per output, one output per
  lane. Attempt-2's MMA tiles (`qmm_block`,
  `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate`, 6,144 B of float tile buffers)
  are **not** used, so no tile memory is allocated in either branch
  and decode residency is not taxed for prefill.
- Same branch threshold (`rows >= 60` from `inds_shape[0]`, the
  `gather_qmm_rhs` dispatch threshold, not the tested sizes), same
  four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden via silu-mul,
  down — silu helper byte-identical to attempt-2's copy of
  attempt-4's full-bfloat16 lowering), fp32 accumulation, and
  positional `y[r,j]` (`pair = r*4 + j` throughout; `hidden` is
  indexed by the same flat pair).

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-1
  leaves 12 of 16 GPU cores idle per call (4 threadgroups). Here a
  1-row layer call exposes 12 (gate/up) then 24 (down)
  threadgroups, so up to 12/16 cores hold gate/up work and all 16
  hold down work, while each group keeps 4 blocks in flight —
  the in-group load overlap whose loss (1 block/group) cost
  attempt-2 its 8/32-row wins (326.8/887.6). Cost of the split:
  one extra launch per layer on the chain and a `hidden`
  round-trip (1.5 KB/pair written + re-read vs 552,960 B/pair of
  weights, 0.5%); `x` is re-read per chunk-group (3× per pair,
  4.5 KB vs 368 KB of gate/up weights).
- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
  attempt-1's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
  verbatim instead of attempt-2's MMA construction.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
  kept, as in attempt-1 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
  round-1 grouped evidence says removing them loses at this duty
  cycle.

## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)

128 threads/group ≤ 1,024. Threadgroup memory: gate/up
`tg_x[768] + tg_gate[128] + tg_up[128]` bfloat16 = **2,048 B**;
down `tg_h[384]` = **768 B** — both below attempt-1's 3,840 B and
far below the 32,768 B limit, at every row count (allocations are
rows-independent; no prefill-only buffers exist). Grids scale as
`rows*12` / `rows*24` groups, so the kernel is valid at every
`rows ≥ 1`, including untested counts on both sides of 60.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)

Weight bytes per layer (552,960 B/pair): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB
at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs. References: attempt-1 chained (this round's
grader) 104.3 / 193.3 / 535.7 (effective 21 / 92 / 132 GB/s);
attempt-2 chained 103.6 / 326.8 / 887.6 (21 / 54 / 80 GB/s);
compiled (attempt-1's run) 77.6 / 235.7 / 791.6.

- **1 row: 74.** Latency-bound, not byte-bound (floor 11.1 µs at
  peak). Attempt-1's 104.3 with 4 groups ≈ fixed cost (launch/link,
  `tg_x` load, barriers, lane-0 stores) + a wave-serial part only
  4 cores can work on. Gate/up now spreads over 12 groups and down
  over 24 (1.5 waves of 16), each group with 4 concurrent block
  K-chains instead of attempt-2's 1: assuming the serial part
  scales with cores busy (4 → 12) and adding ~6 µs for the second
  launch + `hidden` round-trip, 2.21 MB at ~33 GB/s effective
  (between attempt-2's 21 with 1 block/group and the 8-row
  streaming rate) ≈ 67 µs + ~7 µs fixed ≈ **74** — just under the
  compiled 77.6, with the launch overhead as the risk.
  Per step this is the ineff-2 headroom: (104.3 − 74) × 20 ≈
  0.61 ms/step recovered of the 1.05 ms gap.
- **8 rows: 162.** Streaming with 96 + 192 groups: resident groups
  per core are capped by 2,048/768 B threadgroup memory (vs
  attempt-2's 7,808/6,912 B), and each group hides loads behind
  4 blocks. 17.69 MB at ~115 GB/s (attempt-1's 92 GB/s at 32
  groups, raised by 3× the groups at lower memory) ≈ 154 µs +
  ~8 µs launch/hidden ≈ **162**, keeping attempt-1's win over
  compiled 235.7.
- **32 rows: 530.** 384 + 768 groups, already saturated:
  70.78 MB at ~135 GB/s (attempt-1 reached 132 GB/s with 128
  fused groups; the split's extra `x`/`hidden` traffic is <1% of
  weight bytes) ≈ 524 µs + ~6 µs ≈ **530**, keeping the win over
  compiled 791.6. Risk: if the second launch's serialization on
  the chain costs more than ~10 µs/layer at streaming sizes, this
  lands nearer attempt-1's 535.7 — still a win.

G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — decode
reuses attempt-1's per-block math unchanged (only the block→group
mapping moved), and prefill reuses attempt-1's `qmm_accum`
verbatim, which already matched `gather_qmm_rhs` bit for bit.

## Verdict

*(not yet graded)*

split kept attempt-1's bits in both regimes: per-block

scalar `qmm_accum` prefill path matched `gather_qmm_rhs` again.

(wins). `beats_compiled` false — the 1-row size still misses, as

77.6 → 86.9 compiled between runs, so treat 1 row as indicative):
109.5 vs 104.3 at 1 row (no gain), 195.0 vs 193.3 at 8 rows
(flat), 637.7 vs 535.7 at 32 rows (**+19% regression**). The
hardening did not beat the best attempt at any size.

## Miss analysis (prediction 74 / 162 / 530; all misses > 20%)

Measured 109.5 / 195.0 / 637.7 is **+48% / +20% / +20%** over
prediction. Effective bandwidth on pair bytes: 20 / 91 / 111 GB/s
— the 1- and 8-row rates are attempt-1's (21 / 92 GB/s), and the
32-row rate falls between attempt-2's 80 and attempt-1's 132 GB/s.
Three facts together locate the error in the prediction's model,
not in the arithmetic:

1. **Group count is not the 1-row binding limit past 4 groups.**
   Attempt-1 (4 groups × 512 threads), attempt-2 (48+96 groups ×
   32 threads) and this attempt (12+24 groups × 128 threads, 4
   blocks in flight per group, 2,048/768 B threadgroup memory) all
   land at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer chained at 1 row, across a 36×
   range of group counts. The prediction assumed attempt-1's
   serial part scales with cores busy (4 → 12); instead the
   ~100 µs plateau is invariant to how the blocks are packed. What
   does not shrink under any packing is each block's own serial
   K chain (24 strided load-accumulate steps per lane for gate,
   24 for up, 12 for down, gate→up→down ordered by the hidden
   dependency) plus the chained launch/link fixed cost — and this
   attempt *adds* a second launch and a `hidden` round-trip on
   that chain. Splitting exposes cores the critical path cannot
   use.
2. **At 32 rows the split tax is real and the fused kernel's
   in-group overlap was load-bearing.** 637.7 vs attempt-1's
   535.7: the two-kernel form pays 1,152 group dispatches (vs
   128), 3× duplicated `tg_x` loads and 6× duplicated `tg_h`
   loads, two extra barrier rounds per pair, and the `hidden`
   write+read — small bytes (<1% of weight traffic) but pure
   latency/occupancy overhead at streaming sizes, while a fused
   512-thread group keeps 16 blocks' loads in flight behind one
   barrier set. Restoring 4 blocks/group and low threadgroup
   memory recovered most of attempt-2's loss (80 → 111 GB/s) but
   not attempt-1's 132 GB/s.
3. **The 8-row rate confirms the mechanism:** 91 GB/s equals
   attempt-1's 92 GB/s — once enough groups exist to stream, the
   packing makes no difference, and the prediction's assumed
   residency gain (115 GB/s from lower threadgroup memory) did
   not appear; residency was not the cap.

Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: the 1-row lever is not
threadgroups per call (three packings, one plateau). The next
lever must shorten or overlap the per-block serial chain itself
— e.g. interleaving the independent gate and up K-loops so one's
loads hide the other's latency — or cut the chained fixed cost,
without touching any block's `simd_sum` order.

**Next change (one):** return to attempt-1's fused single kernel
and interleave gate/up: issue both blocks' K-loop loads per wave
before accumulating, keeping `qvm_block`'s per-block order and
all rounding points identical."}

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write a faster MobileMoE-S decode kernel
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.

7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
12|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
13|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
14|
15|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
16|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
17|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
18|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
19|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
20|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
21|
22|## The slots
23|
24|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the step: 1 to 32 in decode. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
25|
26|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
27|
28|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
29|
30|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
31||---|---|---|---|
32|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
33|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
34|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
35|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
36|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
37|
38|Reference:
39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
69|
70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.

182|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:

186|   At every size:
187|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
188|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
189|
190|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
191|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
192|3. **G3, faster.** The decode step's period is the median over 3 repeats in shuffled order, with 128-token prompts, at 1, 8 and 32 requests. It must be lower than both the original model's and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code. The gap must exceed the spread between repeats.
193|
194|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
195|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
196|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
197|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer`: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, and `beats_compiled`.
198|
199|**The piece timing** runs the slot on all 20 layers' captured decode inputs, at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and waits for the GPU once at the end. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row. It takes the median of 30 repeats, per layer. It is a guide; G3 decides.

201|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and beats the compiled reference in the piece timing at all three row counts, or after 5 attempts. 1|# Round-2 attempt 1 — builder-2-a, direction (a): faithful MLX-regime replica
2|
3|One fused Metal kernel, 256 threads (8 simdgroups) per row, branching on
4|`rows` in-Metal. Baseline: none. Builds on the starting point
5|`muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1` (kept: bf16->f32 cast, strictly-greater
6|insertion top-4 with earliest-index tie win, `((w0+w1)+w2)+w3 + 1e-20` then
7|`/ denom * 2.5` on unbiased scores).
8|
9|## What changed since the starting point
10|
11|- Product: serial 768-term chain replaced by the MLX regime for `rows`:
12|  rows==1 GEMV lane order (`d=i*128+lane*4+0..3`, i=0..5) + shuffle tree
13|  16,8,4,2,1; 1<rows<=768 split-K (BK=16 chunks, partitions from
14|  `next_pow2(48/((rows+31)/32*2))` clamped to [2,32], base `48/partitions`
15|  chunks, last partition to chunk 48, partials added in partition order);
16|  rows>768 BK=16 chunks in order. MMA regimes use `simdgroup_float8x8`
17|  multiply-accumulate, two 8-wide ops per BK=16 chunk; only A-tile row 0 is
18|  the real row, other rows staged zero, so per-element K order is steel's.
19|- Sigmoid: `1/(1+exp(-acc))` replaced by MLX verbatim
20|  `y=1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s))); (s<0)?y:1-y`, float32 throughout.
21|- Top-4/weights: unchanged from the starting point (see above).
22|
23|## Inefficiencies removed
24|
25|`ineff-baseline-routing-1` (three product accumulation orders), `-2`
26|(sigmoid formula), and the serial-dot part of `-3` (dots now lane- or
27|MMA-parallel; the serial thread-0 scan is kept deliberately to preserve
28|the tie rule bit for bit).
29|
30|## Predicted us per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows
31|
32|Starting point measured 28.5 / 23.6 / 41.8 us (its notes.md) against a
33|~24 us chained-harness floor; traffic per row is 184 KB (0.9 us at
34|200 GB/s) and body work is 92k FLOP/row. This kernel keeps one launch,
35|widens to 8 simdgroups/row (better 1-row occupancy) but the MMA path
36|stages 48 chunks x 2 barriers and wastes 7/8 of each 8x8 tile at decode
37|sizes, so I predict it lands near the starting point, not below the floor:
38|1 row ~ 24 floor + 0.9 traffic + ~2 MMA staging ~= **27 us**;
39|8 rows ~ 24 amortised + 7.4 traffic ~= **26 us**;
40|32 rows ~ 18 amortised + 29.5 traffic ~= **40 us**.
41|Compiled reference (starting point's run): 30.5 / 42.0 / 49.1 us, so a
42|chained win is plausible only if G2 passes.
43|
44|## Known limits (stated before grading)
45|
46|- MMA tile is 8 rows x 8 experts, not steel's BM=16/32 x BN=32 (split-K)
47|  or 64x64 (regular). Per-element K/chunk/partition order matches; if the
48|  hardware 8-product rounding depended on tile position it would still
49|  differ — no evidence it does, but this is the residual risk.
50|- GEMV per-lane products use the same `acc += x*w` form as MLX gemv.h;
51|  compiler FMA contraction is assumed to match MLX's build.
52|- The thread-0 top-4 scan remains serial (60 steps) by design for ties.
