54|## Verdict (2026-11-04T03:37:08Z, one grader run)
55|
56|G1 pass, **G2 pass at all six sizes** (rows_differ 0, max_rel_err 0.0 at
57|1/8/32 and 127/1016/2048). Chained us/layer (ref / compiled / candidate):
58|1 row 77.8 / 56.2 / **54.9** (beats compiled); 8 rows 113.1 / 91.2 / 91.4
59|(tie, +0.2); 32 rows 136.3 / 98.9 / 114.8 (loses). `beats_compiled` false.
60|Baseline none, so no `beats_baseline`.
61|
62|The pre-grading worry that the 8-row MMA tile might round differently
63|from steel's larger tiles did not bite: hardware 8-product rounding is
64|tile-position independent on this GPU, and the GEMV shuffle replica plus

68|## Why timings missed predictions by >20%
69|
70|Predicted 27/26/40 us, measured 54.9/91.4/114.8 us. Two causes. (1) The
71|prediction anchored on round 1's independent-timing floor (~24 us); the

{"path":"muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-3/notes.md","content":"# Round-2 attempt 3 — builder-2-c, hardening of hyp-2-routing-exact

Builds on the best full-G2 attempt, `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-1`
(G1 pass, G2 pass at all six sizes; chained 54.9/91.4/114.8 µs/layer vs
compiled 56.2/91.2/98.9 — wins only at 1 row). Baseline: none, so no
`beats_baseline`; the bar is the compiled reference.

## The one main change

Replace attempt-1's simdgroup-MMA threadgroup staging with scalar
partition accumulation, nothing else:

- Removed: `Ash`/`Bsh`/`Csh` staging, `simdgroup_float8x8` loads/MMA/store,
  and the 48 chunks × 2 threadgroup barriers per row (plus the 7/8 wasted
  rows of each 8×8 tile). The `<metal_simdgroup_matrix>` include goes too.
- Added: a `parts[60×32]` threadgroup array. Each (expert, partition)
  partial is one thread's serial scalar sum `part += xsh[d] * w_router[e*768+d]`
  over its K range in increasing `d`; one barrier; then partials are summed
  sequentially in partition order (`acc = 0; acc += parts[p]`), exactly
  attempt-1's partial order with the MMA inner accumulation replaced by
  the scalar sum attempt-2 proved bit-identical at decode.

Kept verbatim from attempt-1: the regime branch on `rows` (GEMV only at
`rows == 1`; split-K while `rows <= 768`; regular above), the split-K
partition formula (`next_pow2(48/((rows+31)/32*2))` clamped to [2,32],
base `48/partitions` BK=16 chunks, last partition to chunk 48 — so 32
partitions at 8/32 rows, 8 partitions of 96 at 127 rows, 2 at 257–768),
the single partition covering all 48 chunks above 768 rows, the GEMV
lane order and shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1, MLX's verbatim sigmoid
(`1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`), the strictly-greater
insertion top-4 (earliest index wins ties), and
`((w0+w1)+w2)+w3 + 1e-20`, divide, ×2.5 on unbiased scores. Same grid
(`rows*256`), threadgroup (256) and one-kernel layout. Threadgroup memory
(768+60+1920)×4 B = 10,992 B of 32 KB.

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-routing-1` stays removed (same orders as attempt-1), and
attempt-1's staging cost — the reason it loses at 32 rows (its notes:
48×2 barriers/row, 7/8 tile waste, per-row `w_router` re-read) — is
attacked directly: the scalar path has 2 barriers per row total instead
of 96+, and no tile waste. The per-row `w_router` re-read
(`ineff-baseline-routing-4`) and serial thread-0 scan (part of
`ineff-baseline-routing-3` kept for the tie rule) are untouched.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows

Anchor: attempt-1 measured 54.9/91.4/114.8, compiled 56.2/91.2/98.9
(same grader run, hyp entry). Traffic per row is 184 KB of `w_router`
(0.9 µs at 200 GB/s), so traffic floors are 0.9/7.4/29.5 µs; the rest is
chained-call latency and per-row staging/serial work.

- 1 row: the GEMV branch is unchanged, so ≈ attempt-1's 54.9 → **55**.
- 8 rows: attempt-1's per-row increment over its 1-row time is
  (91.4−54.9)/7 ≈ 5.2 µs/row on the MMA path. Removing 96 barriers and
  the tile staging per row, the scalar critical path per expert is the
  last partition's 272 serial products, hidden across 8 threadgroups ×
  8 warps; estimate the increment falls to ≈1.4 µs/row → 54.9+7×1.4 ≈ **65**.
- 32 rows: same increment → 54.9+31×1.1 ≈ **89** (per-row increment
  falls further as 32 threadgroups fill the GPU; traffic floor 29.5 µs
  is inside this, not added to it).

Prediction: **55 / 65 / 89 µs** — beats compiled (56.2/91.2/98.9) at all
three if the staging model holds. G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes
if attempt-2's scalar≡MMA result extends to the 8-partition (127-row)
and single-accumulator (>768) groupings, which are the only scalar
groupings attempt-2 did not already prove.

## Verdict

*(pending the one grader run)*

1|# attempt-3 (round 2): hardening — 4-block groups, scalar prefill (builder-1-c)
2|
3|Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
4|`none`). Builds on the best attempt
5|`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-1` (G2 pass all six,
6|104.3/193.3/535.7 µs/layer chained vs compiled 77.6/235.7/791.6 —
7|loses only at 1 row). Starting point for the decode arithmetic is
8|attempt-1's proven helpers; attempt-2's failure modes are the
9|constraint.
10|
11|## The one main change
12|
13|Split attempt-1's single fused per-pair kernel (4 threadgroups per
14|call at 1 row, 512 threads each) into two kernels with 4-block
15|threadgroups, exposing more threadgroups per call without
16|attempt-2's 1-simdgroup-per-group collapse:
17|
18|- `experts_gate_up` (block-0): one 128-thread threadgroup (4
19|  simdgroups) owns 4 distinct 32-output blocks — simdgroup `s` of
20|  chunk `c = tg % 3` computes block `blk = c*4 + s` of pair
21|  `tg / 3` (12 blocks/pair ÷ 4 = 3 groups/pair). Grid
22|  `rows*1536` threads = `rows*12` groups: **12 groups at 1 row**
23|  (96 at 8, 384 at 32). Each simdgroup runs gate then up for its
24|  block, lane 0 (decode) or every lane (prefill) stores the
25|  bfloat16-rounded results to `tg_gate`/`tg_up`, one barrier, then
26|  every lane applies the shared full-bfloat16 silu-mul and writes
27|  `hidden[pair, blk*32 + lane]`.
28|- `experts_down` (block-1): same shape for the 24 down blocks —
29|  `blk = (tg % 6)*4 + simd`, pair `tg / 6` (24 ÷ 4 = 6 groups/pair).
30|  Grid `rows*3072` threads = `rows*24` groups: **24 groups at
31|  1 row** (192 at 8, 768 at 32).
32|
33|Everything else is copied, not redesigned:
34|
35|- **Decode (`rows < 60`):** `qvm_block` in block-2 is byte-identical
36|  to attempt-1's (verified by diff; itself attempt-4's proven
37|  helper) — strided lanes `k ≡ lane (mod 32)` serial in float32,
38|  float32 dequant `x·(scale·q+bias)`, `simd_sum` tree. Splitting
39|  blocks across threadgroups does not change any block's
40|  accumulation order, so decode bits are attempt-1's.
41|- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`):** `qmm_accum` in block-2 is
42|  byte-identical to attempt-1's scalar path (verified by diff) —
43|  weight rounded to bfloat16 first
44|  (`float(bfloat(scale·q+bias))`), then K accumulated contiguously
45|  in `BK=32` tile order by one thread per output, one output per
46|  lane. Attempt-2's MMA tiles (`qmm_block`,
47|  `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate`, 6,144 B of float tile buffers)
48|  are **not** used, so no tile memory is allocated in either branch
49|  and decode residency is not taxed for prefill.
50|- Same branch threshold (`rows >= 60` from `inds_shape[0]`, the
51|  `gather_qmm_rhs` dispatch threshold, not the tested sizes), same
52|  four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden via silu-mul,
53|  down — silu helper byte-identical to attempt-2's copy of
54|  attempt-4's full-bfloat16 lowering), fp32 accumulation, and
55|  positional `y[r,j]` (`pair = r*4 + j` throughout; `hidden` is
56|  indexed by the same flat pair).
57|
58|## Which inefficiency it removes, and how
59|
60|- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-1
61|  leaves 12 of 16 GPU cores idle per call (4 threadgroups). Here a
62|  1-row layer call exposes 12 (gate/up) then 24 (down)
63|  threadgroups, so up to 12/16 cores hold gate/up work and all 16
64|  hold down work, while each group keeps 4 blocks in flight —
65|  the in-group load overlap whose loss (1 block/group) cost
66|  attempt-2 its 8/32-row wins (326.8/887.6). Cost of the split:
67|  one extra launch per layer on the chain and a `hidden`
68|  round-trip (1.5 KB/pair written + re-read vs 552,960 B/pair of
69|  weights, 0.5%); `x` is re-read per chunk-group (3× per pair,
70|  4.5 KB vs 368 KB of gate/up weights).
71|- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
72|  attempt-1's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
73|  verbatim instead of attempt-2's MMA construction.
74|- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
75|  kept, as in attempt-1 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
76|  round-1 grouped evidence says removing them loses at this duty
77|  cycle.
78|
79|## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)
80|
81|128 threads/group ≤ 1,024. Threadgroup memory: gate/up
82|`tg_x[768] + tg_gate[128] + tg_up[128]` bfloat16 = **2,048 B**;
83|down `tg_h[384]` = **768 B** — both below attempt-1's 3,840 B and
84|far below the 32,768 B limit, at every row count (allocations are
85|rows-independent; no prefill-only buffers exist). Grids scale as
86|`rows*12` / `rows*24` groups, so the kernel is valid at every
87|`rows ≥ 1`, including untested counts on both sides of 60.
88|
89|## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)
90|
91|Weight bytes per layer (552,960 B/pair): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB
92|at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs. References: attempt-1 chained (this round's
93|grader) 104.3 / 193.3 / 535.7 (effective 21 / 92 / 132 GB/s);
94|attempt-2 chained 103.6 / 326.8 / 887.6 (21 / 54 / 80 GB/s);
95|compiled (attempt-1's run) 77.6 / 235.7 / 791.6.
96|
97|- **1 row: 74.** Latency-bound, not byte-bound (floor 11.1 µs at
98|  peak). Attempt-1's 104.3 with 4 groups ≈ fixed cost (launch/link,
99|  `tg_x` load, barriers, lane-0 stores) + a wave-serial part only
100|  4 cores can work on. Gate/up now spreads over 12 groups and down
101|  over 24 (1.5 waves of 16), each group with 4 concurrent block
102|  K-chains instead of attempt-2's 1: assuming the serial part
103|  scales with cores busy (4 → 12) and adding ~6 µs for the second
104|  launch + `hidden` round-trip, 2.21 MB at ~33 GB/s effective
105|  (between attempt-2's 21 with 1 block/group and the 8-row
106|  streaming rate) ≈ 67 µs + ~7 µs fixed ≈ **74** — just under the
107|  compiled 77.6, with the launch overhead as the risk.
108|  Per step this is the ineff-2 headroom: (104.3 − 74) × 20 ≈
109|  0.61 ms/step recovered of the 1.05 ms gap.
110|- **8 rows: 162.** Streaming with 96 + 192 groups: resident groups
111|  per core are capped by 2,048/768 B threadgroup memory (vs
112|  attempt-2's 7,808/6,912 B), and each group hides loads behind
113|  4 blocks. 17.69 MB at ~115 GB/s (attempt-1's 92 GB/s at 32
114|  groups, raised by 3× the groups at lower memory) ≈ 154 µs +
115|  ~8 µs launch/hidden ≈ **162**, keeping attempt-1's win over
116|  compiled 235.7.
117|- **32 rows: 530.** 384 + 768 groups, already saturated:
118|  70.78 MB at ~135 GB/s (attempt-1 reached 132 GB/s with 128
119|  fused groups; the split's extra `x`/`hidden` traffic is <1% of
120|  weight bytes) ≈ 524 µs + ~6 µs ≈ **530**, keeping the win over
121|  compiled 791.6. Risk: if the second launch's serialization on
122|  the chain costs more than ~10 µs/layer at streaming sizes, this
123|  lands nearer attempt-1's 535.7 — still a win.
124|
125|G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — decode
126|reuses attempt-1's per-block math unchanged (only the block→group
127|mapping moved), and prefill reuses attempt-1's `qmm_accum`
128|verbatim, which already matched `gather_qmm_rhs` bit for bit.
129|
130|## Verdict
131|
132|G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0
133|everywhere** (decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048) — the
134|split kept attempt-1's bits in both regimes: per-block
135|`qvm_block` order unchanged by the block→group remapping, and the
136|scalar `qmm_accum` prefill path matched `gather_qmm_rhs` again.
137|Chained timing µs/layer (this run; candidate vs reference vs
138|compiled): **1 row 109.5 / 93.1 / 86.9 (loses both)**; 8 rows
139|195.0 / 248.8 / 243.6 (wins); 32 rows 637.7 / 846.0 / 798.9
140|(wins). `beats_compiled` false — the 1-row size still misses, as
141|in attempt-1. Baseline `none` — no
142|`wins_vs_baseline`/`beats_baseline`.
143|
144|Against attempt-1 (different run; 1-row baselines shifted
145|77.6 → 86.9 compiled between runs, so treat 1 row as indicative):
146|109.5 vs 104.3 at 1 row (no gain), 195.0 vs 193.3 at 8 rows
147|(flat), 637.7 vs 535.7 at 32 rows (**+19% regression**). The
148|hardening did not beat the best attempt at any size.
149|
150|## Miss analysis (prediction 74 / 162 / 530; all misses > 20%)
151|
152|Measured 109.5 / 195.0 / 637.7 is **+48% / +20% / +20%** over
153|prediction. Effective bandwidth on pair bytes: 20 / 91 / 111 GB/s
154|— the 1- and 8-row rates are attempt-1's (21 / 92 GB/s), and the
155|32-row rate falls between attempt-2's 80 and attempt-1's 132 GB/s.
156|Three facts together locate the error in the prediction's model,
157|not in the arithmetic:
158|
159|1. **Group count is not the 1-row binding limit past 4 groups.**
160|   Attempt-1 (4 groups × 512 threads), attempt-2 (48+96 groups ×
161|   32 threads) and this attempt (12+24 groups × 128 threads, 4
162|   blocks in flight per group, 2,048/768 B threadgroup memory) all
163|   land at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer chained at 1 row, across a 36×
164|   range of group counts. The prediction assumed attempt-1's
165|   serial part scales with cores busy (4 → 12); instead the
166|   ~100 µs plateau is invariant to how the blocks are packed. What
167|   does not shrink under any packing is each block's own serial
168|   K chain (24 strided load-accumulate steps per lane for gate,
169|   24 for up, 12 for down, gate→up→down ordered by the hidden
170|   dependency) plus the chained launch/link fixed cost — and this
171|   attempt *adds* a second launch and a `hidden` round-trip on
172|   that chain. Splitting exposes cores the critical path cannot
173|   use.
174|2. **At 32 rows the split tax is real and the fused kernel's
175|   in-group overlap was load-bearing.** 637.7 vs attempt-1's
176|   535.7: the two-kernel form pays 1,152 group dispatches (vs
177|   128), 3× duplicated `tg_x` loads and 6× duplicated `tg_h`
178|   loads, two extra barrier rounds per pair, and the `hidden`
179|   write+read — small bytes (<1% of weight traffic) but pure
180|   latency/occupancy overhead at streaming sizes, while a fused
181|   512-thread group keeps 16 blocks' loads in flight behind one
182|   barrier set. Restoring 4 blocks/group and low threadgroup
183|   memory recovered most of attempt-2's loss (80 → 111 GB/s) but
184|   not attempt-1's 132 GB/s.
185|3. **The 8-row rate confirms the mechanism:** 91 GB/s equals
186|   attempt-1's 92 GB/s — once enough groups exist to stream, the
187|   packing makes no difference, and the prediction's assumed
188|   residency gain (115 GB/s from lower threadgroup memory) did
189|   not appear; residency was not the cap.
190|
191|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: the 1-row lever is not
192|threadgroups per call (three packings, one plateau). The next
193|lever must shorten or overlap the per-block serial chain itself
194|— e.g. interleaving the independent gate and up K-loops so one's
195|loads hide the other's latency — or cut the chained fixed cost,
196|without touching any block's `simd_sum` order.
197|
198|**Next change (one):** return to attempt-1's fused single kernel
199|and interleave gate/up: issue both blocks' K-loop loads per wave
200|before accumulating, keeping `qvm_block`'s per-block order and
201|all rounding points identical.

{"path":"muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-1-experts-exact.md","find":"## Decision","replace":"### attempt-3 (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-3`) — boundary-1 · 2026-11-04T03:54:50Z — **pass**

Checked `block-0.metal` (B0), `block-1.metal` (B1), `block-2.metal` (B2) and `spec.json` against the Boundary above for what G2 cannot see. No defect found.

- **Row counts on each side of 60.** Both kernels branch on the dispatch threshold itself, not the tested bracket: `rows = inds_shape[0]`, `prefill = rows >= 60` (B0:17–18; B1:13–14) is exactly `B = rows*4 >= 240 ⇔ B/E >= 4` at `E = 60`, so 33–59 rows stay on `gather_qvm` arithmetic and 60–126 take `gather_qmm_rhs` arithmetic, as the Boundary requires. The sort threshold (rows ≥ 16) is correctly ignored — the kernels are positional, `pair = tg/3` (gate/up) or `tg/6` (down), `e = inds[pair]` (B0:19–23; B1:15–18), so reference-internal sorting cannot change their bits at 16–59 rows. Nothing else depends on the row count: the grids are linear, `rows*1536` / `rows*3072` threads = `rows*12` / `rows*24` groups of 128 (`spec.json:1`), with `blk = chunk*4 + simd` covering all 12 gate/up and 24 down blocks per pair (`blk` 0–11 at B0:20–21, 0–23 at B1:16–17) for any `rows >= 1`, including untested 2–7, 9–31, 61–126, 128–1,015, 1,017–2,047 and >2,048, and prefill chunks other than the first. def partitions_for(rows):
    if rows==1: return None
    partitions=1; base=48
    if rows<=768:
        tm=(rows+31)//32
        ratio=48//(tm*2)
        np_=1
        while np_<ratio: np_*=2
        if np_<2: np_=2
        partitions=min(np_,32)
        base=48//partitions
        if base==0: base=1
    return partitions,base

for rows in [2,7,8,9,31,32,33,64,65,96,97,127,128,129,256,257,384,385,768,769,1016,2048,3000]:
    print(rows, partitions_for(rows))

# verify coverage for all rows 2..5000
bad=[]
for rows in range(2,5001):
    p,base=partitions_for(rows)
    chunks=[]
    parts_written=set(); parts_read=set()
    for e in range(60):
        for pp in range(p):
            c0=pp*base; c1=48 if pp+1==p else (pp+1)*base
            chunks_e=list(range(c0,c1))
            chunks.extend(chunks_e) if e==0 else None
            parts_written.add(e*32+pp)
        for pp in range(p):
            parts_read.add(e*32+pp)
    if parts_written!=parts_read: bad.append((rows,'parts mismatch',p))
    if rows<=5000 and False: pass
    # check chunk coverage once per e (use e0)
    # recompute
    cov=[]
    for pp in range(p):
        c0=pp*base; c1=48 if pp+1==p else (pp+1)*base
        cov.extend(range(c0,c1))
    if cov!=list(range(48)): bad.append((rows,'chunk cov',p,base,cov[:10]))
print("bad",bad[:20], "count",len(bad))
# parts size
print("mem", (768+60+1920)*4)

print("partition values 2..768",vals)
for v in vals:
    rs=[r for r in range(2,769) if partitions_for(r)[0]==v]
    print(v, min(rs), max(rs), partitions_for(min(rs)))

22|## The slots
23|
24|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the step: 1 to 32 in decode. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
25|
26|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
27|
28|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
29|
30|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
31||---|---|---|---|
32|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
33|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
34|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
35|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
36|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
37|
38|Reference:
39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
69|
70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.

177|## How each attempt is judged
178|
179|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only.
180|
181|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
182|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
183|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
184|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
185|
186|   At every size:
187|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
188|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
189|
190|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
191|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
192|3. **G3, faster.** The decode step's period is the median over 3 repeats in shuffled order, with 128-token prompts, at 1, 8 and 32 requests. It must be lower than both the original model's and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code. The gap must exceed the spread between repeats.

195|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
196|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
197|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer`: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, and `beats_compiled`.
198|
199|**The piece timing** runs the slot on all 20 layers' captured decode inputs, at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and waits for the GPU once at the end. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row. 4|`none`). Builds on the best attempt

10|
11|## The one main change
12|
13|Split attempt-1's single fused per-pair kernel (4 threadgroups per
14|call at 1 row, 512 threads each) into two kernels with 4-block
15|threadgroups, exposing more threadgroups per call without
16|attempt-2's 1-simdgroup-per-group collapse:
17|
18|- `experts_gate_up` (block-0): one 128-thread threadgroup (4
19|  simdgroups) owns 4 distinct 32-output blocks — simdgroup `s` of
20|  chunk `c = tg % 3` computes block `blk = c*4 + s` of pair
21|  `tg / 3` (12 blocks/pair ÷ 4 = 3 groups/pair). Grid
22|  `rows*1536` threads = `rows*12` groups: **12 groups at 1 row**
23|  (96 at 8, 384 at 32). Each simdgroup runs gate then up for its
24|  block, lane 0 (decode) or every lane (prefill) stores the
25|  bfloat16-rounded results to `tg_gate`/`tg_up`, one barrier, then
26|  every lane applies the shared full-bfloat16 silu-mul and writes
27|  `hidden[pair, blk*32 + lane]`.
28|- `experts_down` (block-1): same shape for the 24 down blocks —
29|  `blk = (tg % 6)*4 + simd`, pair `tg / 6` (24 ÷ 4 = 6 groups/pair).
30|  Grid `rows*3072` threads = `rows*24` groups: **24 groups at
31|  1 row** (192 at 8, 768 at 32).

33|Everything else is copied, not redesigned:

35|- **Decode (`rows < 60`):** `qvm_block` in block-2 is byte-identical
36|  to attempt-1's (verified by diff; itself attempt-4's proven
37|  helper) — strided lanes `k ≡ lane (mod 32)` serial in float32,
38|  float32 dequant `x·(scale·q+bias)`, `simd_sum` tree. Splitting
39|  blocks across threadgroups does not change any block's
40|  accumulation order, so decode bits are attempt-1's.
41|- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`):** `qmm_accum` in block-2 is
42|  byte-identical to attempt-1's scalar path (verified by diff) —
43|  weight rounded to bfloat16 first
44|  (`float(bfloat(scale·q+bias))`), then K accumulated contiguously
45|  in `BK=32` tile order by one thread per output, one output per
46|  lane. Attempt-2's MMA tiles (`qmm_block`,
47|  `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate`, 6,144 B of float tile buffers)
48|  are **not** used, so no tile memory is allocated in either branch
49|  and decode residency is not taxed for prefill.

51|  `gather_qmm_rhs` dispatch threshold, not the tested sizes), same
52|  four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden via silu-mul,

61|  leaves 12 of 16 GPU cores idle per call (4 threadgroups). Here a
62|  1-row layer call exposes 12 (gate/up) then 24 (down)

64|  hold down work, while each group keeps 4 blocks in flight —
65|  the in-group load overlap whose loss (1 block/group) cost
66|  attempt-2 its 8/32-row wins (326.8/887.6). Cost of the split:

69|  weights, 0.5%); `x` is re-read per chunk-group (3× per pair,

81|128 threads/group ≤ 1,024. Threadgroup memory: gate/up

83|down `tg_h[384]` = **768 B** — both below attempt-1's 3,840 B and
84|far below the 32,768 B limit, at every row count (allocations are
85|rows-independent; no prefill-only buffers exist). Grids scale as

131|

134|split kept attempt-1's bits in both regimes: per-block

136|scalar `qmm_accum` prefill path matched `gather_qmm_rhs` again.

148|hardening did not beat the best attempt at any size.

150|## Miss analysis (prediction 74 / 162 / 530; all misses > 20%)
151|
152|Measured 109.5 / 195.0 / 637.7 is **+48% / +20% / +20%** over
153|prediction. Effective bandwidth on pair bytes: 20 / 91 / 111 GB/s
154|— the 1- and 8-row rates are attempt-1's (21 / 92 GB/s), and the
155|32-row rate falls between attempt-2's 80 and attempt-1's 132 GB/s.
156|Three facts together locate the error in the prediction's model,
157|not in the arithmetic:
158|
159|1. **Group count is not the 1-row binding limit past 4 groups.**
160|   Attempt-1 (4 groups × 512 threads), attempt-2 (48+96 groups ×
161|   32 threads) and this attempt (12+24 groups × 128 threads, 4
162|   blocks in flight per group, 2,048/768 B threadgroup memory) all
163|   land at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer chained at 1 row, across a 36×
164|   range of group counts. The prediction assumed attempt-1's
165|   serial part scales with cores busy (4 → 12); instead the
166|   ~100 µs plateau is invariant to how the blocks are packed. What
167|   does not shrink under any packing is each block's own serial
168|   K chain (24 strided load-accumulate steps per lane for gate,
169|   24 for up, 12 for down, gate→up→down ordered by the hidden
170|   dependency) plus the chained launch/link fixed cost — and this
171|   attempt *adds* a second launch and a `hidden` round-trip on
172|   that chain. Splitting exposes cores the critical path cannot
173|   use.

176|   535.7: the two-kernel form pays 1,152 group dispatches (vs
177|   128), 3× duplicated `tg_x` loads and 6× duplicated `tg_h`
178|   loads, two extra barrier rounds per pair, and the `hidden`
179|   write+read — small bytes (<1% of weight traffic) but pure
180|   latency/occupancy overhead at streaming sizes, while a fused
181|   512-thread group keeps 16 blocks' loads in flight behind one
182|   barrier set. Restoring 4 blocks/group and low threadgroup
183|   memory recovered most of attempt-2's loss (80 → 111 GB/s) but
184|   not attempt-1's 132 GB/s.
185|3. **The 8-row rate confirms the mechanism:** 91 GB/s equals
186|   attempt-1's 92 GB/s — once enough groups exist to stream, the
187|   packing makes no difference, and the prediction's assumed
188|   residency gain (115 GB/s from lower threadgroup memory) did
189|   not appear; residency was not the cap.
190|
191|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: the 1-row lever is not
192|threadgroups per call (three packings, one plateau). The next
193|lever must shorten or overlap the per-block serial chain itself
194|— e.g. interleaving the independent gate and up K-loops so one's
195|loads hide the other's latency — or cut the chained fixed cost,
196|without touching any block's `simd_sum` order.

199|and interleave gate/up: issue both blocks' K-loop loads per wave
200|before accumulating, keeping `qvm_block`'s per-block order and
201|all rounding points identical.

13|## What happens
14|
15|Attempt-4's `qvm_block` (`muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4/block-1.metal:20-40`)
16|is a bit-faithful replica of MLX `affine_gather_qvm`/`qvm_impl`: each lane
17|accumulates its strided `K` elements serially in float32, dequantizing on
18|the fly as `x * (scale * q + bias)` (`block-1.metal:33-34`), then a
19|`simd_sum` tree reduces across the 32 lanes. That is exactly the kernel
20|MLX dispatches at decode sizes, so decode G2 is bit-exact.
21|
22|From 60 rows the reference dispatches a different kernel. Dispatch
23|(MLX v0.32.4 `quantized.cpp:2005,2012,2073-2093`, via round 1
24|`muse-spark/exploration/territory-quantized-kernels.md` §A/§C and
25|`territory-switch-layers.md` §G): `gather_qmm_rhs` needs
26|`M==1 && B>=16 && right_sorted_ && B/E>=4`, `B = rows*4`, `E = 60`, i.e.
27|rows ≥ 60. Decode 1/8/32 rows (`B/E` ≤ 2.13) never fire it; prefill
28|127/1,016/2,048 rows (`B/E` = 8.5/67.7/136.5) always do. Note the two
29|distinct thresholds: the reference sorts from `inds.size >= 64` (rows ≥
30|16, `bench/grader/slots.py:62`, `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/switch_layers.py:181`),
31|but sorting alone does not switch the kernel below 60 rows — decode at
32|32 rows is sorted and still `gather_qvm`.
33|
34|`affine_gather_qmm_rhs` (`quantized.h:2580-2718`, installed 0.32.4
35|headers) rounds differently in two independent ways, both new readings
36|this round (round 1 mapped the kernel as never-run and did not read its
37|arithmetic):
38|
39|1. **Dequantized weight rounded to bfloat16 before the multiply.**
40|   `QuantizedBlockLoader` (`quantized.h:674-791`) dequantizes into
41|   threadgroup memory via `dequantize<T, pack_factor, bits>`
42|   (`quantized.h:557-663`; bits=4 path `:614-620`):
43|   `w_local = static_cast<U>(s * q + b)` with `U = T` = bfloat16, stored
44|   in `Ws` (`quantized.h:2623-2624`). `qvm` instead keeps `scale*q+bias`
45|   in float32 registers through `qouter` (`quantized.h:452-553`).
46|2. **Different accumulation order.** `gather_qmm_rhs` tiles `K` in
47|   `BK=32` blocks through `gemm_loop_aligned` and simdgroup-matrix
48|   fragments (`BlockMMA`, `AccumType=float`, `steel/gemm/mma.h:451,512-538`;
49|   tile mapping by `schedule_row_tile<BM=16>`, `utils.h:501-542`), vs
50|   `qvm`'s strided-lane serial sum + `simd_sum` tree
51|   (`quantized.h:1317-1321`). Round 1 proved the order is load-bearing:
52|   down outputs near cancellation amplify a 1-ULP hidden difference
53|   (`muse-spark/implementation/hyp-1-fused-experts.md:103-108`), so
54|   either difference alone breaks bit-exactness.
55|
56|The silu lowering is not the cause: both paths feed the same compiled
57|`swiglu` (full-bfloat16 per-op rounding, attempt-4 `block-0.metal:53-64`),
58|but with differently-rounded gate/up inputs, so hidden and `y` diverge.
59|Attempt-4 has no size branch: one kernel, grid `rows*4` groups at every
60|row count (`spec.json`; territory §C), always computing `qvm` arithmetic.

{"path":"muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-4/notes.md","content":"# attempt-4 (round 2): hardening — fused interleave gate/up (builder-1-d)

Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
`none`). Builds on the best attempt
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-1` (fused single kernel,
512 threads/pair, G2 pass all six, 104.3/193.3/535.7 µs/layer chained
vs compiled 77.6/235.7/791.6 — loses only at 1 row). This is the one
main change named by attempt-3's miss analysis
(`attempt-3/notes.md`, *Next change*): attempt-3 split into two
kernels and plateaued at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer at 1 row across three
packings, so group count is not the lever; the next lever is to
overlap the per-block serial K chain itself inside the fused kernel.

## The one main change

Stay in attempt-1's fused single kernel — same one kernel, same
512 threads per (row, expert-slot) pair, same grid `rows*2048`
threads = `rows*4` groups, same branch on `rows >= 60`, same
threadgroup buffers — and interleave gate and up in the decode
branch only:

- **Before (attempt-1):** simdgroup `b` (`b < 12`) ran
  `qvm_block(gate, block b)` to completion (24 strided K steps per
  lane: `k = lane, lane+32, ..., lane+744`; each step loads 4 weight
  words + scale/bias for that `k`, then accumulates 32 outputs),
  stored `tg_gate`, then ran `qvm_block(up, block b)` the same way
  and stored `tg_up`. The two blocks' K loops were fully sequential:
  up's first load waited for gate's last accumulate.
- **Now:** simdgroup `b` runs one merged loop,
  `qvm_gate_up_pair` (block-1). For each strided `k`, both blocks'
  loads are issued first — gate's 4 weight words, scale and bias,
  then up's 4 weight words, scale and bias (plus the shared
  `tg_x[k]`, read once) — and only then do the two accumulation
  passes run, gate's 32 terms then up's 32 terms, into separate
  accumulators `pg`/`pu`. The next `k`'s loads therefore sit behind
  twice the issued load traffic per step, and each block's load
  latency has the other block's loads/compute to hide behind
  (double-buffering the two blocks' weight/scale/x loads within
  the step). Lane 0 then stores both blocks in one loop:
  `tg_gate[b*32+j] = (bfloat)pg[j]`, `tg_up[b*32+j] = (bfloat)pu[j]`.

Everything else is copied, not redesigned:

- **Per-block bits unchanged.** In `qvm_gate_up_pair`, each block's
  adds run in exactly `qvm_block`'s order: the same strided `k`
  sequence, the same float32 dequant terms
  `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` /
  `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)` with `s1 = scale/16`, in the same
  per-output sequence; `pg` and `pu` are independent accumulators,
  so interleaving the two blocks cannot reorder either block's own
  adds. Each accumulator then gets the identical
  `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` `simd_sum` tree as `qvm_block`.
  Down still calls `qvm_block` verbatim (verified by diff against
  attempt-1: `qvm_block` and `qmm_accum` bodies byte-identical;
  block-0 differs only in the header comment and the decode
  gate/up call site).
- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`) unchanged.** Attempt-1's scalar
  `qmm_accum` (weight rounded to bfloat16 first,
  `float(bfloat(scale·q+bias))`, then K accumulated contiguously in
  `BK=32` tile order, one output per lane) is copied byte-identical
  for gate, up and down, and block-0's prefill branch is untouched —
  the interleaving does not touch the prefill arithmetic.
- Same four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden via the
  shared full-bfloat16 silu-mul, down — silu code byte-identical),
  fp32 accumulation, positional `y[r,j]` (`pair = r*4 + j`), and
  the same `rows >= 60` dispatch threshold from `x_shape[0]`, not
  the grader's bracketing sizes. No kernel split, no threadgroup
  count change, no new device-memory intermediate.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempts 1–3
  all plateau at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer at 1 row despite 4, 12+24 and
  48+96 threadgroups per call, so the binding cost past 4 groups is
  each block's serial K chain (24 + 24 + 12 strided
  load-accumulate steps, gate→up→down ordered by the hidden
  dependency) executed with only one block's loads in flight per
  simdgroup at a time. Interleaving gate and up — the two
  independent, equal-length (24-step) chains — puts both blocks'
  loads in flight in every step without touching any block's
  `simd_sum` order, the only lever attempt-3's analysis left inside
  the fused kernel. Down (12 steps) is left sequential: it cannot
  start before the silu barrier in any case.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
  attempt-1's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
  verbatim.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
  kept, as in attempts 1–3 — weight bytes per pair stay
  552,960 B; the interleaving changes load scheduling, not bytes.

## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)

512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 (spec unchanged, verified identical).
Threadgroup memory unchanged from attempt-1: `tg_x[768] +
tg_gate[384] + tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]` bfloat16 = **3,840 B** of
32,768 B, rows-independent. The only new state is register-local:
a second 32-float accumulator `pu[32]` beside `p[32]` and a second
4-word load buffer inside `qvm_gate_up_pair` — the register cost
is the risk noted below. Grid scales as `rows*4` groups, so the
kernel is valid at every `rows ≥ 1`, on both sides of 60.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)

Weight bytes per layer (552,960 B/pair, of which gate+up are
368,640 B = 2/3): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs.
Attempt-1 chained (this round's grader): 104.3 / 193.3 / 535.7
µs/layer = effective 21.2 / 91.5 / 132.1 GB/s; compiled (same run)
77.6 / 235.7 / 791.6.

- **1 row: 90.** Latency-bound (floor 2.21 MB ÷ 200 GB/s =
  11.1 µs). Gate+up are 48 of the 60 serial product steps and 2/3
  of the pair bytes, so ≈ 2/3 × 104.3 ≈ 69 µs of attempt-1's time
  is the gate/up chains (the rest: down's 12 steps, `tg_x` load,
  silu, barriers, chained launch/link). Issuing both blocks' loads
  before accumulating doubles the loads outstanding per step; if
  that hides ≈ 20% of the gate/up chain's exposed latency
  (0.20 × 69 ≈ 14 µs), the layer lands at ≈ **90 µs** — still
  above the compiled 77.6, closing about half the remaining gap.
  Risk: the second accumulator's register pressure could spill or
  cut resident groups and hand the saving back.
- **8 rows: 178.** Streaming: 17.69 MB. Attempt-1 ran 91.5 GB/s
  with one block's 4 words in flight per simdgroup step; 8 words
  (plus two scale/bias pairs) per step should lift memory-level
  parallelism to ≈ 99 GB/s → 17.69 MB ÷ 99 GB/s ≈ **178 µs**,
  keeping attempt-1's win over compiled 235.7.
- **32 rows: 505.** Already near-saturated at attempt-1's
  132.1 GB/s; the same MLP lift, partly offset by register
  pressure at 128 groups, to ≈ 140 GB/s → 70.78 MB ÷ 140 GB/s ≈
  **505 µs**, keeping the win over compiled 791.6.

G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — decode
interleaving reorders only *between* blocks, never within a
block's add sequence, and the prefill path is byte-identical to
attempt-1's, which already matched `gather_qmm_rhs` bit for bit.

## Verdict

*(pending — graded below)*
"}

interleaving kept attempt-1's bits in both regimes: per-block
`qvm_block` add order unchanged by the within-step interleave, and
the byte-identical scalar `qmm_accum` prefill path matched

candidate vs reference vs compiled): **1 row 94.0 / 81.2 / 73.5
(loses both)**; 8 rows 177.0 / 252.1 / 239.0 (wins); 32 rows
591.3 / 799.2 / 796.3 (wins). `beats_compiled` false — only the
1-row size misses, as in attempt-1. Baseline `none` — no
`wins_vs_baseline`/`beats_baseline`.

at 1 row between runs, so treat cross-run deltas as indicative):
94.0 vs 104.3 at 1 row (**−9.9%**), 177.0 vs 193.3 at 8 rows
(**−8.4%**), 591.3 vs 535.7 at 32 rows (**+10.4% regression**).
This is the first attempt to move below attempt-1's 103.6–109.5
µs/layer 1-row plateau (attempts 1–3) at any size, and it does so
at 1 and 8 rows — but it spends part of attempt-1's 32-row win.

## Miss analysis (prediction 90 / 178 / 505, measured 94.0 / 177.0 / 591.3)

Misses are +4.4% / −0.6% / +17.1% — all inside the 20% bar, so no
formal miss, but the 32-row *direction* was wrong (predicted
−6% vs attempt-1, measured +10.4%), and that needs explaining:

1. **The interleave works where latency binds.** Effective
   bandwidth on pair bytes: 23.5 GB/s at 1 row (attempt-1: 21.2)
   and 99.9 GB/s at 8 rows (attempt-1: 91.5). Doubling the loads
   outstanding per K step (8 weight words + two scale/bias pairs
   issued before either accumulation) hid enough of each block's
   load latency to break the 103.6–109.5 plateau that three
   threadgroup packings could not — confirming attempt-3's
   diagnosis that the per-block serial chain, not group count,
   was the 1-row lever. The gain is real but partial: 94.0 still
   loses to compiled 73.5, so roughly 20 µs/layer of the 1-row
   cost (chained launch/link, `tg_x` load, silu, barriers, down's
   still-sequential 12-step chain and its two waves) remains
   unoverlapped.
2. **At 32 rows the second accumulator is the tax.** 119.7 GB/s
   vs attempt-1's 132.1 GB/s. Once 128 groups saturate the GPU,
   exposed load latency is already hidden by group-level
   parallelism, so the interleave buys nothing — and its cost,
   a second live 32-float accumulator plus a second 4-word load
   buffer per thread for the whole K loop, is paid in register
   pressure and therefore resident-group occupancy on every
   streaming step. The prediction's assumed MLP lift to
   140 GB/s double-counted parallelism the group count already
   provided.
3. **The 8-row point separates the two regimes:** same register
   cost as 32 rows, but only 32 groups per call, so per-group
   load overlap still pays (91.5 → 99.9 GB/s, prediction exact).
   The crossover between "latency-bound, interleave wins" and
   "occupancy-bound, interleave taxes" sits between 8 and 32
   rows in this run.

Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: the serial-chain lever is
real (first sub-plateau 1-row result: 94.0), but a uniform
interleave trades it against streaming occupancy. The two
regimes want different code, and both arithmetics are
bit-identical, so the choice between them is free.

**Next change (one):** make the interleave row-conditional
inside the same fused kernel — `qvm_gate_up_pair` below the
latency/occupancy crossover (e.g. `rows <= 8`), attempt-1's
sequential `qvm_block` gate then up above it — keeping the
1/8-row wins (94.0/177.0) while restoring attempt-1's 32-row
register profile (535.7). Both branches keep every block's
add order, so G2 is unaffected by where the crossover sits."}

11|- the `notes.md` of the slot's earlier attempts: this round's in `<round>/kernels/<slot-folder>/`, and earlier rounds', the baseline's or starting point's above all.
12|
13|**One grader run is one attempt.** After a run, any change, even a one-line fix, is a new attempt with its own number, built by copying the files you keep. Scratch kernels and timing experiments that aren't attempts go in `probes/` inside your attempt folder and are never graded. You return after one attempt; the brief's *When a slot stops* rule no longer applies, and the lead decides what comes next.
14|
15|## Steps
16|
17|1. **Claim an attempt number.**
18|   - N is one more than the highest `attempt-<N>` in this round's slot folder, or 1. Run `mkdir -p <round>/kernels/<slot-folder>` once, then `mkdir <round>/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>`.
19|   - If it fails, another builder took N: try N+1.
20|   - Log the claim.
21|2. **Write the attempt** in the brief's layout, plus a `notes.md` that says:
22|   - what changed since the attempt it builds on (the baseline counts), or that it is the first in your direction; from round 2 on, a starting point that fails G2 counts too;
23|   - which inefficiency it removes, and how;
24|   - the predicted µs per layer at 1, 8 and 32 rows, with the arithmetic; from round 2 on, against the baseline's where the slot has one.
25|   
26|   Make one main change, the simplest kernel that removes the cause, and stay inside the boundary.
27|3. **Grade it** with the brief's grader command, once. When the hypothesis entry names a baseline, add `--baseline <baseline folder>`; for `routing+combine`, `--baseline routing=<folder> --baseline combine=<folder>`. It times the baseline in the same run, and `beats_baseline` is true only when your attempt wins at least 22 of 30 paired repeats at each row count. The grader may print "waiting for the GPU" while another run has it; keep waiting. A run itself takes under 3 minutes once it starts; stop one that hangs, and record it.

29|5. **Learn.** If the attempt failed, or its time missed your prediction by more than 20%, find out why. Write the answer in `notes.md`, and add it to the inefficiency entry as a note.

31|**Done** when the attempt is graded, recorded and any miss is explained. Return the attempt folder, its verdict, and the one change you would make next.

33|## What you write
34|
35|Your attempt folder, your section of the hypothesis entry, notes in other entries, and log lines.

24|- **`log.md`.** One line per event, from every agent, appended only.
25|
26|## Versions
27|
28|Every shared document carries a version number, so a reader knows which version they're looking at, and git holds every version.
29|
30|**Phase versions.** Each README opens with its version line:

36|- **Who raises it:** the lead, at every checkpoint, and each version is exactly one commit.

86|### Territory entry
87|
88|1. Status block (statuses: `exploring`, `done`).
89|2. **What it does** in the decode step, in a few lines.

95|### Inefficiency entry
96|
97|1. Status block. The statuses are `open`, `confirmed`, `refuted` and `superseded by <entry>`; only the verifier sets `confirmed` or `refuted`.
98|2. **Slot:** `routing`, `combine`, `experts`, or `outside the slots`.
99|3. **What happens:** what the code does, and where (file and lines).
100|4. **Cost** at 1, 8 and 32 rows: kernels × the fixed cost per kernel, bytes ÷ peak bandwidth, and the measured time with the table it comes from.
101|5. **Kind:** overhead-bound, bandwidth-bound or compute-bound, in the terms of `claude/GLOSSARY.md`.
102|6. **Spans:** the territories involved.

104|8. **Verdict**, written by the verifier: each claim checked, and the result.
105|
106|### Hypothesis entry
107|
108|1. Status block. The lead owns it; the statuses are `boundary`, `building`, `hardening`, `ready` and `dropped`.
109|2. **Inefficiency** it removes, the slot, and from round 2 on the slot's baseline folder, or `none` and its starting point.

111|4. **One section per builder:** its direction, its attempts (folder, predicted and measured µs per layer at 1, 8 and 32 rows, G1, G2, and where the slot has a baseline its time and `beats_baseline`), and what each attempt taught.
112|5. **Boundary checks** of the attempts that passed G2.
113|6. **Decision:** the best attempt and why. When the status is `ready`, it states what G3 should show.
114|
115|## The checklist
116|
117|Fill it in for each piece of code you inspect, so that no piece is judged without its neighbours:
118|
119|- **Callers:** who calls it, and with what shapes at 1, 8 and 32 rows of a decode step and in a prefill.
120|- **Callees:** what it calls, down to the Metal kernel it launches.
121|- **Data:** each input and output with shape, dtype and layout. Where it is produced, and where it is consumed next.
122|- **Neighbours:** what runs just before and after it in the decode step, and what a replacement must keep identical.
123|- **Cost:** the kernels it launches, the bytes it reads and writes (weight bytes counted per read), and its measured time with the table the time comes from.
124|- **Invariants:** what correctness depends on: G2's bit-exact rule at every size, the tie rule for the 4th and 5th expert, the bfloat16 rounding points, and which MLX kernel the reference uses at each size.
125|
126|## The log
127|
128|Append one line per event with the shell, so lines from several agents never mix. In round 2:
129|
130|```bash
131|printf '%s | %s | %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "explorer-baseline-experts" "posted ineff-baseline-experts-2: each weight byte read 4 times at 32 rows" >> muse-spark/round-2/exploration/log.md
132|```

134|Log when you start, claim something, post or confirm an entry, change direction (what from, what to, and which entry made you), grade an attempt (with its verdict), and finish.
135|
136|## Adapting to the others' work
137|
138|Before every new piece of work, and after every post:
139|1. Read the phase README's tracker and the newest 30 lines of the phase log (`tail -n 30`).
140|2. Then change direction when:
141|   - **someone else covers it:** another entry already covers the same code or cause, so append to that entry instead of starting a second one;
142|   - **its premise fell:** the claim your work rests on was refuted;
143|   - **something pays more:** an open item in your territory or task predicts a larger saving than what you're on, and nobody owns it.
144|3. When you change direction, log it with the reason, and write it in your own entry's status block.
145|
146|Two claims on the same item go to the lead, who settles them.
147|
148|## Rules for every agent
149|
150|- **Writes go only to this round's folder, in the files your role names.** Earlier rounds' folders, everything else in the worktree, and everything outside it are read-only.
151|- **Only the lead commits.** Helpers never run `git add` or `git commit`.
152|- **The grader is the only GPU job.** Run it only as a builder, through the brief's command; it waits its turn when another run has the GPU. Load no model and start no other GPU work: the machine has 16 GB and slows down sharply when memory runs short.
153|- **Every number has a source:** a file and line, a table (path and row), a grader verdict (attempt folder), or arithmetic shown in full.
154|- **Credentials stay unread:** `.env` files, `~/.config/muse/` and any key store.
155|- **The API-stage kernels** in the history before the tag `agent-era` are from an earlier, removed stage (PROVENANCE.md) and stay unread.

17|- `ineff-baseline-routing-3` (ranked 4): one simdgroup per row + serial thread-0 scan; up to 0.4 ms/step at 1 row.
18|- `ineff-baseline-routing-4` (ranked 7): `w_router` re-read per row; upper bound 0 / 0.13 / 0.57 ms/step, unbanked on round-1 counter-evidence.

20|Design: a kernel that reproduces the reference's scores bit for bit at every size — the same simdgroup matrix accumulation and tiling per `rows` regime, MLX's sigmoid formula verbatim, the already-matching 4-term normalise sum and tie rule — with each expert's dot product sharded across lanes and a parallel top-4, so the 1-row occupancy deficit is removed together with the exactness gates. 22|## The slots
23|
24|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the step: 1 to 32 in decode. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
25|
26|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
27|
28|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
29|
30|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
31||---|---|---|---|
32|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
33|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
34|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
35|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
36|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
37|
38|Reference:
39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.

70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.

# Inefficiency: `w_router` is re-read once per row instead of once per layer

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
- **Status:** confirmed
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T03:24:18Z
- **Next:** verifier to weigh the attempt-2 counter-evidence before confirming any saving

## Slot

`routing`

## What happens

Each row's threadgroup streams the full router weight for its own experts
straight from device memory (`muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:30-34`):
60×768 float32 = 184 KB per row per layer, with no sharing across rows. The
reference's GEMM reads `w_router` once per layer and reuses each tile across
all rows in the tile (steel GEMM/GEMV dispatches, territory section 3.1).
Per layer the starting point therefore reads rows×184 KB where the reference
reads 184 KB: 0.18 MB at 1 row, 1.47 MB at 8 rows, 5.90 MB at 32 rows (and
377 MB at the 2,048-row prefill size, where only correctness is graded —
ADR 0010:42 — so that figure costs grader time, not step time).

## Cost

Traffic floor at the 200 GB/s peak (brief:9): candidate 0.9 / 7.4 / 29.5 µs
per layer at 1/8/32 rows vs the reference's 0.9 µs at every row count. At 32
rows the excess (5.90−0.18 MB ≈ 5.7 MB/layer ≈ 28.6 µs at peak, 0.57 ms/step
over 20 layers) is ~43% of the candidate's measured 68.9 µs/layer
(independent timing, `claude/findings/muse-round-1.md:47`) — the one place
in this slot where bytes, not launches, are a large share. At 1 and 8 rows
the excess is 0 and ~6.4 µs/layer respectively.

## Kind

Bandwidth-bound at 32 rows only; overhead-bound at 1/8 rows (the slot's
usual regime, `ineff-runs-2`).

## Spans

`baseline-routing`

## Predicted saving

Upper bound if each weight byte were read once per layer at peak bandwidth:
**~0 ms/step at 1 row, ~0.13 ms/step at 8 rows (6.4 µs/layer), ~0.57 ms/step
at 32 rows (28.6 µs/layer)**. Confidence is low at decode sizes, on measured
counter-evidence from round 1: attempt-2 tiled `w_router` through
threadgroup memory shared across 8 rows precisely to remove this re-read
and was *slower* at every row count (36.3/34.9/49.0 vs attempt-1's
28.5/23.6/41.8 µs/layer, `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-2/notes.md`) —
barriers and sub-peak strided reads ate the traffic saving. A builder
claiming this saving needs a design that shares weights without
attempt-2's barrier structure (e.g. one threadgroup spanning several rows
in the steel-GEMM shape the exactness fix already pushes toward), and must
prove it on the chained timing, not the traffic arithmetic.

## Verdict

verifier, 2026-11-04T03:24:18Z — **confirmed** as a byte cost with an upper-bound-only saving. Checked: each row's threadgroup streams the full 60×768 f32 router (184,320 B) from device memory with no cross-row sharing ([block-0.metal:30-34](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:30)) ✓; per layer candidate reads rows×184 KB = 0.18/1.47/5.90 MB at 1/8/32 rows (377 MB at 2,048-row prefill, untimed per [0010-exact-at-every-size.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)) vs reference 184 KB once per layer (steel tile reuse, [territory-baseline-routing.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/round-2/exploration/territory-baseline-routing.md) §3.1) ✓. Floors at 200 GB/s: candidate 0.9/7.4/29.5 µs/layer vs reference 0.9; excess at 32 rows (5.90−0.18)=5.71 MB/layer = 28.6 µs/layer = 0.57 ms/step, at 8 rows ~6.4 µs/layer ✓. Upper bounds ~0 / 0.13 (6.4×20) / 0.57 ms/step (28.6×20) ✓. Counter-evidence correctly carried: attempt-2 tiled `w_router` across 8 rows to remove this re-read and was slower at every row count (36.3/34.9/49.0 vs 28.5/23.6/41.8 µs/layer, [attempt-2/notes.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-2/notes.md)) — barriers/sub-peak reads ate the saving, so no saving is banked without a barrier-free sharing design proven on the chained timing, as written ✓. **Corrections:** excess share at 32 rows is 28.6/68.9≈41.5% (≈43% only on the full 29.5 µs floor), and in [GLOSSARY.md](/Users/onur/Desktop/Github/Hackathon-muse/claude/GLOSSARY.md) terms the slot remains overhead-bound at 32 rows with a bandwidth-waste component (5.90 MB in 68.9 µs ≈86 GB/s, 43% of peak), not bandwidth-bound. {"path":"muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/notes.md","content":"# Round-2 attempt 4 — builder-2-d, hardening of hyp-2-routing-exact

Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-3` (scalar
full-G2; chained 46.9/300.0/297.2 µs/layer vs compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9 —
latency-bound from uncoalesced device loads + `xsh` bank conflicts).
Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the compiled reference.

## The one main change

Stage each K-chunk's `w_router` block into threadgroup memory with
coalesced vector loads and sum from threadgroup with a padded `x`
layout, nothing else:

- Staging: chunks are staged 4 at a time (12 groups cover all 48
  BK=16 chunks). Each staged chunk is 60×16 floats, loaded as 240
  `float4` loads (consecutive threads cover one expert's 4 vectors,
  then the next expert) and stored transposed in `wsh[slot][k][expert]`
  with expert stride 64.
- Padded `x`: chunk `c` of `x` sits at `xpad[c*17 + k]` (one pad float
  per chunk), replacing attempt-3's flat `xsh[768]`.
- Scalar chain: expert-parallel lanes read `wsh` at consecutive expert
  banks (conflict-free) and `xpad` uniformly per `k` (broadcast).
  Partials live transposed in `parts[partition][expert]` (stride 64)
  and are resumed product-by-product in increasing `d` across staged
  groups, so each (expert, partition) partial is still one serial
  scalar sum in increasing `d`; partials are then summed sequentially
  in partition order. 24 barriers on the scalar path (2 per group).
- Threadgroup memory: (816 + 60 + 2048 + 4096) × 4 B = 28,080 B of
  32 KB. Same grid (`rows*256`), threadgroup (256) and one-kernel layout.

Kept verbatim from attempt-3: the regime branch on `rows` (GEMV only
at `rows == 1`; split-K while `rows <= 768`; regular above — the GEMV
branch is unchanged apart from reading the padded `x` layout), the
split-K partition formula (32 partitions at 8/32 rows, 8 of 96 at 127,
2 at 257–768, single partition above 768, last partition absorbing the
remainder chunks), the GEMV lane order and shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1,
MLX's verbatim sigmoid (`1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`),
the strictly-greater insertion top-4 (earliest index wins ties), and
`((w0+w1)+w2)+w3 + 1e-20`, divide, ×2.5 on unbiased scores.

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-routing-1` stays removed (same orders as attempt-3).
The target is attempt-3's diagnosed feeding cost (its notes: the
scalar chains read `w_router` uncoalesced — warp lanes 64 B apart,
16 cache lines per step — and `xsh[p*16+k]` with 16-way bank
conflicts on every product). Staging turns the device reads into
coalesced `float4` loads and the dependent chain's reads into
conflict-free threadgroup reads. The per-row `w_router` re-read
(`ineff-baseline-routing-4`) and the serial thread-0 scan are
untouched.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows

Anchor: attempt-3 measured 46.9/300.0/297.2, compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9
(same grader run). Traffic per row is unchanged at 184 KB of
`w_router` (0.9 µs at 200 GB/s), so floors are 0.9/7.4/29.5 µs; the
rest is chained-call latency and per-row work. Attempt-3's flat
~300 µs was the dependent device-load chain; the staged chain reads
threadgroup memory instead, at the cost of 24 barriers/row.

- 1 row: GEMV branch unchanged but for the padded index (a shift and
  mask per access) → ≈ attempt-3's 46.9 → **48**.
- 8 rows: fixed chained latency ≈ 40 µs (attempt-3's 1-row time less
  its small GEMV work) + traffic 7.4 + staged scalar work. The
  critical path is the last partition's 272 sequential threadgroup
  FMAs, overlapped across 8 threadgroups; allowance ≈ 20 µs →
  40 + 7.4 + 20 ≈ **67**.
- 32 rows: 40 + 29.5 + 25 (more threadgroups fill the GPU, critical
  path unchanged) ≈ **95**.

Prediction: **48 / 67 / 95 µs** — beats compiled (58.0/84.5/90.9) at
1 and 8 rows, near it at 32. G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes —
no accumulation order changes, only where operands are read from.
"}

## Why the 32-row timing missed the prediction by >20%

Predicted 48/67/95, measured 47.5/69.1/72.9: 1 and 8 rows hold

chained latency, the full 29.5 µs traffic floor and a per-row work
allowance as if they were serial per layer call. They are not: at 32

are nearly free, and the 28 KB threadgroup footprint (which caps
residency) does not bind at these row counts. Traffic-floor
arithmetic overstates the cost whenever staging and compute overlap
across threadgroups.

beats compiled at all three row counts). If pushed further, cut the

needs ~2× the `wsh` footprint or a narrower expert stride)."}

79|- **attempt-2** (`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-2`): one threadgroup
80|  (192 threads) per row; weights + shared staged to ~3.1 KB threadgroup
81|  memory with vectorized u64 loads, y streamed with vectorized u64 loads,

93|## Boundary checks
94|
95|*checked by boundary-3, 2026-11-03T22:11Z. Verdict: both attempts **pass** —
96|no defects. The 8-row 2.0-ULP touch is compiler FMA contraction, identified
97|and validated below; it saturates at 2.0 ULP on realistic inputs.*
98|
99|### attempt-1 (`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1`) — pass
100|
101|- **Row counts 1–32:** grid is `rows*768` threads, threadgroup 256
102|  (`spec.json:1`); `rows*768/256 = 3*rows` groups exactly for every integer
103|  row count, and `row = idx/768, d = idx - row*768` (`block-0.metal:12-14`)
104|  is exact for all `idx`. No row-dependent branches or constants. Max index
105|  `31*3072+767+2304 = 98303 < 32*3072` (`block-0.metal:17-23`); 256 threads
106|  ≤ 1024.
107|- **Threadgroup memory:** none used — no unwritten reads possible, 0 B of
108|  32 KB.
109|- **Thread timing:** threads are fully independent (no threadgroup memory,
110|  no atomics, disjoint outputs) — the result is deterministic.
111|- **Input assumptions:** none. Weights are used as arbitrary f32 with no
112|  range/sum/nonneg assumption (`block-0.metal:20-23`); `weights[r,j]` pairs
113|  with `y[r,j,:]` strictly positionally; both bf16 rounding points are kept
114|  (`bfloat(acc)` then the bf16 `+ shared`, `block-0.metal:25`).
115|
116|### attempt-2 (`muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-2`) — pass
117|
118|- **Row counts 1–32:** grid `rows*192`, threadgroup 192 (`spec.json:1`) is
119|  exactly `rows` groups for every row count; `row = threadgroup id`
120|  (`block-0.metal:14`), each thread owns outputs `tid*4..tid*4+3`. All
121|  loops/bounds are row-independent constants. 192 threads ≤ 1024.
122|- **Unwritten reads:** none. `wsh[0..3]` is written by `tid < 4` and
123|  `shsh[0..767]` by all 192 threads (disjoint `tid*4` quads) before the
124|  single barrier (`block-0.metal:20-35`); all reads (`block-0.metal:37-40,62-65`)
125|  come after it. The barrier is unconditional and reached by every thread
126|  (the `tid<4` branch holds only a write).
127|- **Near the limit:** `4*4 + 768*4 = 3088 B`, 9.4% of 32 KB.
128|- **Thread timing:** all sharing is barrier-guarded disjoint writes plus
129|  read-only broadcast — deterministic.
130|- **Input assumptions:** none. Weights arbitrary f32, positional pairing
131|  (expert-`j` u64 block with `wj`, `block-0.metal:52-58`), both rounding
132|  points kept (`block-0.metal:62-65`); `bfloat(shsh[…])` is exact because
133|  `shsh` holds exact bf16 values, so the add is identical to attempt-1's.
134|  u64 loads are aligned and exact: shared row base `row*1536 B`, y row base
135|  `row*6144 B` (both 8-B aligned for all rows), sizes exactly 192/768 u64 —
136|  no overread (`block-0.metal:27-28,47,53`). Bit-exactness of the staging
137|  is corroborated by the identical G2 fingerprints (0.0/2.0/1.0) of both
138|  attempts: any staging error would move the touch.
139|
140|### The 2.0-ULP touch (both attempts): FMA contraction, not a defect
141|
142|CPU emulation (pure numpy, no GPU/model; bf16 RNE validated 0/20006 vs an
143|exact rational oracle) of candidate-vs-reference on all 629,760 captured
144|elements:
145|
146|- The reference is the pure mul-then-add chain: MLX v0.32.4
147|  `col_reduce_small` computes `op(new, totals) = new + totals`
148|  (`reduce_col.h`), and with the (32,4,1) strided-small dispatch
149|  (`reduce.cpp`, `threadgroup_y = min(8, …, 4) = 4`) each element lands on
150|  its own thread, so the reference association is the linear chain —
151|  bit-identical to an uncontracted candidate (IEEE add commutes).
152|- The Metal compiler FP-contracts the candidate's mul+add chain into FMA:
153|  the FMA-chain evaluation reproduces the grader fingerprint **exactly**,
154|  (0.0, 2.0, 1.0) at 1/8/32 rows, in two contraction shapes; all 120 pure
155|  mul association trees give ≤1.0 on rows8 with zero fingerprint matches —
156|  ruling out sum order as the source.
157|- Realistic risk: 0 bad elements in 20M triplet-resampled captured elements
158|  (true y/weights/shared joint distribution) for the FMA evaluations and
159|  trees alike; max exactly 2.0. Exceedance needs adversarially constructed
160|  cancellation (`shared ≈ −acc` to <2%): max 8.0 there, a construction
161|  absent from real data. The brief's G2 note (brief:184) budgets exactly
162|  this class of difference, and the remaining gates (captured-only G2,
163|  greedy-token end-to-end, G3 timing) are insensitive to it.
164|
165|Optional, not required: if the team wants nonzero margin at rows8, qualify
166|the accumulator `precise` (inhibits FMA contraction) and re-grade; both
167|attempts pass the gates as they stand.
168|
169|## Decision
170|
171|Best: `muse-spark/kernels/combine/attempt-1` (builder-3-a, thread-per-output). Why: beats compiled at all three row counts by the wider relative margin (17.2 / 17.0 / 18.5 vs 22.9 / 26.2 / 28.0: −25 / −35 / −34%, against attempt-2's −14 / −30 / −35%); simpler (no threadgroup memory, fully independent threads); builder-3-b concedes it stays the pick. Both pass G1, G2 and boundary checks. No hardening round: both kernels sit on the ~17 µs/layer dispatch floor, flat across row counts with traffic ≤1.4 µs — no speed change worth making. The 8-row 2.0-ULP touch is FMA contraction, proven max exactly 2.0 on realistic inputs with zero exceedances (only adversarial `shared ≈ −acc` cancellation exceeds it); boundary-3's optional `precise`-accumulator margin-buy is noted for a later round, not worth a re-grade now. G3 should show: a faster step at all three concurrencies. Knock-out basis predicts −0.47 / −0.30 / −0.19 ms/step; the piece timing shows −0.10 / −0.10 / −0.24 ms/step ((22.4−17.2), (22.1−17.0), (30.7−18.5) µs/layer × 20 layers); the truth is between and G3 decides.

// Fused combine: weight the 4 experts' bf16 outputs by fp32 weights, sum in
// fp32, round once to bf16, add shared — one kernel launch per layer, one
// thread per output element. Grid is (rows*768, 1, 1), threadgroup (256, 1, 1).
//
// Reference (slots.py:51-52): (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2)
//   .astype(bf16) + shared. y is [rows,4,768] bf16 row-contiguous, weights
//   [rows,4] f32, shared [rows,768] bf16, out [rows,768] bf16. The bfloat
//   conversion and the + shared use the same single-rounding ops as MLX's
//   copy_v/binary_vv kernels, and the 4-term fp32 sum order is free per the
//   hyp-3 boundary.

uint idx = thread_position_in_grid.x;
uint row = idx / 768u;
uint d = idx - row * 768u;

uint wbase = row * 4u;
uint ybase = row * 3072u + d; // 4*768
uint sbase = row * 768u + d;

float acc = float(y[ybase]) * weights[wbase]
    + float(y[ybase + 768u]) * weights[wbase + 1u]
    + float(y[ybase + 1536u]) * weights[wbase + 2u]
    + float(y[ybase + 2304u]) * weights[wbase + 3u];

out[sbase] = bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase];
# Attempt 1 — builder-3-a, single fused kernel, thread-per-output (direction a)

First attempt in this direction: one Metal kernel per layer fusing the whole
combine chain (bf16→fp32 cast, multiply, sum, fp32→bf16 cast, + shared). One
thread per output element on a rows×768 grid, threadgroup 256 (768 = 3×256,
so the grid is always whole threadgroups). Each thread loads its 4 bf16
values, converts exactly to fp32, weights, sums in fp32, rounds once with
`bfloat(acc)`, and adds `shared` with the same single-rounding bf16 add as
MLX's `binary_vv`.

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-model-2`: each layer's weighting launches 5 tiny kernels (AsType,
Multiply, Sum, AsType, Add) costing 0.61 ms/step at 1 row for ~6 MB of
activations — pure launch overhead on an overhead-bound chain. This attempt
replaces all 5 with 1 launch/layer, keeping both bf16 rounding points of the
reference (`slots.py:51-52`): the astype before `+ shared`, then the bf16
add. The 4-term fp32 sum order is free per the hyp-3 boundary.

## Prediction (µs per layer)

Per the hyp-2 lesson (routing attempt-1 notes), predict against the ~24
µs/layer fused-kernel harness floor, not 6.81 µs/launch. Traffic per layer
is y rows×4×768 bf16 + weights rows×4 f32 + shared rows×768 bf16 + out
rows×768 bf16 = rows×9232 B ≈ 9.0 KB/row; at 200 GB/s (brief:9) that is
0.05 / 0.4 / 1.4 µs at 1/8/32 rows — negligible next to the floor. The grid
holds 3 / 24 / 96 threadgroups, so amortization is at least as good as
routing's 8-row case (23.6 µs):

- 1 row: 24 + 0.05 ≈ **24 µs**
- 8 rows: 24 + 0.4 ≈ **24 µs**
- 32 rows: 24 + 1.4 ≈ **25 µs**

Reference (brief:64, ÷20 layers): ≈30.5 @1, ≈22.5 @8 (interpolated in
ineff-model-2), ≈16.5 @32 — whole-step knock-out figures, so the piece
harness will differ and G3 decides the real saving.

## Verdict

G1 pass, G2 pass, beats `mx.compile(ref_combine)` at all three row counts.
Grader output (µs per layer, reference / compiled / candidate):

- 1 row: 22.4 / 22.9 / **17.2** (predicted 24)
- 8 rows: 22.1 / 26.2 / **17.0** (predicted 24)
- 32 rows: 30.7 / 28.0 / **18.5** (predicted 25)

Correctness: 0 bad elements at all row counts (limit 2 bf16 ULP, floor at
0.001); max ULP 0.0 / 2.0 / 1.0 at 1/8/32 rows — the 8-row case touches the
2-ULP boundary on at least one element, so the sum-order margin is thinnest
there, but everything passes on all 20 layers × all captured rows.

Per the brief's stop rule (first attempt beating compiled at all three row
counts), this attempt stops the slot; G3/end-to-end are the team's call.

## Why the prediction missed (>20%, on the fast side)

Predicted ~24 µs from the hyp-2 "~24 µs fused-kernel floor"; measured ~17 µs
(28% under). The 24 µs figure was routing-specific, not a universal harness
floor: routing attempt-1 runs one threadgroup/row with two threadgroup
barriers, a 60-element serial top-4 scan on thread 0, and ~92k FLOP/row of
dot products — at 1 row that is a single wavefront plus a serial tail on a
16-core GPU. This kernel is a trivially parallel streaming op (~12 FLOP per
element, no barriers, no serial section, no threadgroup memory) over 3 / 24 /
96 threadgroups, so its fixed cost is the bare dispatch floor of ~17 µs in
this harness — consistent with the reference's own ~4.5 µs/kernel here
(22.4 µs ÷ 5 kernels at 1 row). Lesson refined: predict a fused elementwise
kernel against ~17 µs/layer, a fused kernel with barriers/serial tails
against ~24 µs.

Piece-timing saving vs the reference is (22.4−17.2)×20 ≈ 0.10 ms/step at 1
row and (30.7−18.5)×20 ≈ 0.24 ms/step at 32 rows — well below the 0.47/0.19
ms the knock-out scaling predicted, because the knock-out and the piece
harness disagree on the slot's standalone cost (same caveat as routing
attempt-1). G3 decides which one the fused kernel actually cashes.

1|# Inefficiency: baseline-combine-1 — FMA contraction breaks bit-exactness
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-combine
4|- **Status:** confirmed
5|- **Version:** 2
6|- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T03:22:03Z
7|- **Next:** verifier to confirm; builder fix is contraction suppression, not reordering
