1|# attempt-5 (round 2): hardening — parallel block stores (builder-1-e)
2|
3|Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
4|`none`). Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-4`
5|(interleaved gate/up, fused single kernel, 512 threads/pair, G2 pass
6|all six, 94.0 / 177.0 / 591.3 µs/layer chained vs compiled
7|73.5 / 239.0 / 796.3 — loses only at 1 row).
8|
9|## The one main change
10|
11|Parallelize the block stores, decode branch only. Nothing else
12|changes: same `qvm_block` / `qvm_gate_up_pair` / `qmm_accum` bodies
13|(`block-1.metal` byte-identical to attempt-4, verified by diff),
14|same interleaved gate/up K loop, same silu, same prefill branch,
15|same grids and `spec.json` (byte-identical).
16|
17|- **Before (attempt-4):** after each block's `simd_sum`, lane 0 alone
18|  stored the block: `for (j = 0..31) tg_gate[b*32+j] = p[j]` and
19|  likewise `tg_up`, and for down `y[pair*768 + b*32 + j] = p[j]`.
20|  That is 48 blocks per pair (12 gate + 12 up + 24 down) × 32 serial
21|  stores, all on the 16 lanes-0 of the pair's threadgroup (12 active
22|  in gate/up, up to 16 per down wave), while the other 31 lanes of
23|  each simdgroup idle at the following barrier / next wave.
24|- **Now:** after each `simd_sum` every lane holds the full reduced
25|  32-vector (`p[j] = simd_sum(p[j])` for all `j` in `block-1.metal`,
26|  so each lane's `p[0..31]` is the whole block output). Lane `j`
27|  stores element `j` — one store per lane, 32-way parallel:
28|  `tg_gate[b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`,
29|  `tg_up[b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)pu[lane]`, and for down
30|  `y[pair*768 + b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]` (still inside the
31|  `b < 24` guard, so idle simdgroups store nothing). The
32|  `(bfloat)` rounding at the store is unchanged, so the bfloat16
33|  rounding points are identical.
34|- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`) untouched:** it already stores one output
35|  per lane (`tg_gate[b*32 + lane]`, `y[... + lane]`), so there is no
36|  serial store to parallelize there.
37|
38|Correctness rests on `simd_sum` being a broadcast reduction: if any
39|lane held only its own partial, the parallel store would write
40|partials and G2 would fail loudly with large `differ` at decode
41|sizes. That is the intended check.
42|
43|## Which inefficiency it removes, and how
44|
45|- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-4's
46|  miss analysis left the still-sequential tails — chained fixed
47|  cost, `tg_x` load, silu, barriers and the down chain — plus these
48|  serial stores on the critical path. On the per-pair critical path
49|  the serial stores are: gate/up phase, 64 threadgroup stores by
50|  each active simdgroup's lane 0 (32 gate + 32 up, 12 simdgroups
51|  concurrent) before the silu barrier; down, 32 device stores per
52|  wave × 2 waves. That is ~128 serial store issues (plus their loop
53|  control) that every other lane waits on. Parallel stores cut that
54|  to 4 parallel store steps (gate 1, up 1, down 1 per wave),
55|  removing ~124 serial issues from the path without touching any
56|  accumulation order, so decode bits are attempt-4's by construction
57|  if the broadcast premise holds.
58|- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
59|  attempt-4's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
60|  verbatim.
61|- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
62|  kept, as in attempts 1–4 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
63|  the store bytes are tiny beside them (`y` 1,536 B/pair = 0.28%).
64|
65|## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)
66|
67|512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 and threadgroup memory unchanged at
68|3,840 B (`tg_x[768] + tg_gate[384] + tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]`
69|bfloat16) of 32,768 B, rows-independent (`spec.json` identical to
70|attempt-4). No new state: `p[lane]` reads the existing per-thread
71|accumulator. Valid at every `rows ≥ 1` on both sides of 60; decode
72|stores cover every `(pair, block, lane)` exactly once, as before
73|(gate/up: 12 simdgroups × 32 lanes; down: 24 blocks × 32 lanes over
74|2 waves).
75|
76|## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)
77|
78|Attempt-4 (other run): 94.0 / 177.0 / 591.3 vs compiled
79|73.5 / 239.0 / 796.3. Baseline `none`, so no
80|`wins_vs_baseline` / `beats_baseline`.
81|
82|- **1 row: 91.** Latency-bound. ~124 serial store issues leave the
83|  critical path; at ~20 exposed cycles each (single-lane store
84|  pipeline plus 32-iteration loop overhead, GPU ≈ 1.3 GHz) that is
85|  124 × 20 / 1.3e9 ≈ 1.9 µs, plus the down device stores' extra
86|  latency on lane 0, ≈ 3 µs total → 94.0 − 3 ≈ **91 µs**. Still
87|  above compiled 73.5 — this trims a tail, it does not close the
88|  remaining down-chain / fixed-cost gap.
89|- **8 rows: 175.** 32 groups per call partly hide one group's store
90|  tail behind other groups' K loops, so roughly half the 1-row
91|  saving survives: 177.0 − 2 ≈ **175 µs**, keeping the win over
92|  compiled 239.0.
93|- **32 rows: 589.** Streaming-bound (attempt-4: 119.7 GB/s on pair
94|  bytes). Store bytes are 0.28% of pair traffic and group-level
95|  parallelism already hides the store latency, so the change is
96|  ~neutral: 591.3 − 2 ≈ **589 µs**, keeping the win over compiled
97|  796.3. Risk: none structural — no register or threadgroup change;
98|  the only risk is the broadcast premise, which G2 tests directly.
99|
100|G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — the
101|parallel store writes the same `(bfloat)p[j]` values attempt-4's
102|lane 0 wrote, just from lane `j` instead of lane 0, and the prefill
103|path is byte-identical to attempt-4's.
104|
105|## Verdict
106|
107|G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0
108|everywhere** (decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048) — the
109|broadcast premise holds: every lane's `p[0..31]` after `simd_sum`
110|is the full reduced block, so lane `j` storing `p[j]` reproduces
111|attempt-4's serial lane-0 stores bit for bit, for gate, up and
112|down alike. Chained timing µs/layer (this run; candidate vs
113|reference vs compiled): **1 row 92.1 / 95.7 / 75.9 (loses to
114|compiled, beats reference)**; 8 rows 162.0 / 232.4 / 234.6 (wins);
115|32 rows 534.8 / 802.3 / 798.2 (wins). `beats_compiled` false —
116|only the 1-row size misses, as in attempt-4. Baseline `none` — no
117|`wins_vs_baseline`/`beats_baseline`.
118|
119|Against attempt-4 (different run; compiled shifted 73.5 → 75.9 at
120|1 row and reference 81.2 → 95.7 between runs, so treat cross-run
121|deltas as indicative): 92.1 vs 94.0 at 1 row (**−2.0%**), 162.0
122|vs 177.0 at 8 rows (**−8.5%**), 534.8 vs 591.3 at 32 rows
123|(**−9.6%**). Effective bandwidth on pair bytes: 24.0 / 109.2 /
124|132.3 GB/s (attempt-4: 23.5 / 99.9 / 119.7). The 32-row rate is
125|back at attempt-1's 132.1 GB/s level while keeping the
126|interleave's 1/8-row wins — attempt-5 dominates attempt-4 at
127|every size and matches the best previous 32-row time (attempt-1:
128|535.7).
129|
130|## Miss analysis (prediction 91 / 175 / 589, measured 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8)
131|
132|Misses are +1.2% / −7.4% / −9.2% — all inside the 20% bar, so no
133|formal miss, but the size pattern was inverted versus the
134|prediction (smallest gain at 1 row, largest at 32 rows) and that
135|needs explaining:
136|
137|1. **At 1 row the serial stores were a small tail, as the
138|   arithmetic said, but the fixed remainder is larger than the
139|   store tail.** Removing ~124 serial issues bought only ~2 µs of
140|   the predicted ~3; the remaining ~16 µs gap to compiled (92.1 vs
141|   75.9) is the still-sequential down chain (12 strided steps × 2
142|   waves behind the silu barrier), the `tg_x` load, silu, barriers
143|   and the chained launch/link cost — none of which this change
144|   touches.
145|2. **At 8/32 rows the serial device stores cost more than pure
146|   latency.** Lane 0's 32 serial stores to `y` per down block are
147|   32 separate single-lane transactions to consecutive addresses;
148|   32 lanes storing in parallel coalesce into full transactions.
149|   Paid per block (24 per pair) on every streaming step, that
150|   inefficiency — plus the serial threadgroup stores delaying the
151|   silu barrier — taxed attempt-4 by ~9% at 32 rows, which the
152|   latency-only prediction (store bytes = 0.28% of pair traffic)
153|   missed. Parallel stores removed it, which is also why the
154|   interleave's 32-row register tax (attempt-4 notes) no longer
155|   shows: 534.8 ≈ attempt-1's non-interleaved 535.7.
156|
157|Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: a serial lane-0 store
158|after a broadcast reduction is never free — at latency sizes it
159|is a barrier tail, at streaming sizes the uncoalesced device
160|stores tax every block. Any future block kernel should store
161|from all 32 lanes by default.
162|
163|## Next change
164|
165|Make the down product's two waves overlap like gate/up: one
166|simdgroup computes two down blocks in one interleaved K loop
167|(separate accumulators, per-block `qvm_block` order and the new
168|parallel store kept), attacking the still-sequential 12-step
169|down chain that is now the largest named remainder at 1 row.
170|The row-conditional interleave attempt-4 proposed is moot —
171|attempt-5 already restored attempt-1's 32-row rate (534.8 vs
172|535.7) with the interleave kept.

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write a faster MobileMoE-S decode kernel
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
12|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
13|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
14|
15|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
16|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
17|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
18|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
19|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
20|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
21|
22|## The slots
23|
24|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the step: 1 to 32 in decode. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
25|
26|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
27|
28|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
29|
30|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
31||---|---|---|---|
32|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
33|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
34|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
35|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
36|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
37|
38|Reference:
39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
69|
70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
93|
94|## Tools and limits
95|
96|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
97|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
98|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes; stop one that hangs.
99|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.
100|
101|## Rules of this session
102|
103|These keep your work apart from everyone else's. Git hooks and an audit script enforce them, and a commit that breaks them is refused.
104|

# Hypothesis 1: experts kernel exact at every size, faster chained at 1 row

- **Owner:** lead
- **Status:** hardening
- **Version:** 7
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T04:04:00Z
- **Next:** hardening from attempt-5: interleaved down block pair

## Inefficiency

Slot `experts`. Baseline: `none` (no earlier attempt passes the current G2). Starting point: `muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4`.

One combined fix for three confirmed entries (savings do not add; the gate must be removed before any timing counts):

- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (gate, ranked 8): starting point matches `gather_qvm` but prefill runs `gather_qmm_rhs` — prefill differ 62.4–62.6%, up to 110.5 ULP; 0 µs saving, blocks all timing.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (ranked 2, mean 7.4%): chained 1-row latency 132.9 vs 80.3 µs/layer (+52.6, 1.05 ms/step); 4 threadgroups with wave/barrier serialisation.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (ranked 3, mean 3.7% floors): per-pair re-reads persist — 908 vs 443 MB at 32 rows, 2.33 ms floor, 0 banked on round-1 grouped evidence.

Design: a kernel (or size-branched kernels) that is bit-exact at decode sizes (matching `gather_qvm`: float32 dequant `x·(scale·q+bias)`, strided-lane accumulation + `simd_sum`, full-bfloat16 silu) and at prefill sizes (matching `gather_qmm_rhs`: bfloat16-rounded dequantized tiles, `BK=32` MMA-order accumulation), while exposing more concurrent threadgroups per call at 1 row so the chained latency falls to or below the reference's, without spending the 8/32-row chained wins (63.7 / 210.0 µs/layer ahead). Must keep the G2 boundary (bit-exact at all six sizes, fp32 accumulation, bfloat16 rounding points).

## Boundary

(written by boundary-1; delta only — every line carries its source)

**Cited boundary, checked line by line.** Round 1's boundary for this slot is
[`muse-spark/implementation/hyp-1-fused-experts.md`](../../implementation/hyp-1-fused-experts.md)
*Boundary* (inputs/outputs table, neighbours A/B, identical-math, grader,
GPU limits). I checked each line against the starting point
`muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4` (`block-0.metal`, `block-1.metal`,
`spec.json`) and against the current G2
(`claude/muse-agent-brief.md:179,182-188`; `claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:22-29`;

Still holding, not rewritten below: input/output names, dtypes, layouts and
weight shapes/bytes; `y[r,j]` positional in `inds` order; neighbour
contracts; the four bfloat16 rounding points in kind; launch-spec surface;
GPU limits. Baseline is `none` — no earlier attempt passes the current G2
(this entry, *Inefficiency*; `claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:38`).
Only what changed follows.

### Inputs and outputs — changed: prefill row counts added

Unchanged shapes now also run at prefill sizes. `rows` is still read from
the first slot input's `shape[0]` (`bench/grader/slots.py:323`); the grader
adds prefill `127 / 1,016 / 2,048` rows (1/8/32 requests × 128-token
prompts, first chunk; `bench/grader/slots.py:211,214-220,240-254`;
`bench/grader/check_candidate.py:272-276`):

| Name | Shape at 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows | Dtype |
|---|---|---|
| `x` | [127,768] / [1016,768] / [2048,768] | bfloat16 (`claude/muse-agent-brief.md:74`) |
| `inds` | [127,4] / [1016,4] / [2048,4] | uint32 (`claude/muse-agent-brief.md:75`) |

This covers untested 2–7, 9–31, 61–126, 128–1,015, 1,017–2,047 and >2,048 rows, and prefill chunks other than the first: each pair is computed independently (no offsets, no cross-pair grouping, no chunk state), and the per-output K order in both branches — strided `k = lane, lane+32, …` in decode (B1:82), contiguous `BK=32` tiles in prefill (B1:146–153) — is rows-independent, so chunk position and prompt length cannot change a row's arithmetic. A short later chunk of <60 rows correctly falls back to the `qvm` branch, matching the reference's per-call dispatch.
- **Unwritten threadgroup reads.** None. `tg_x[768]` is written exactly once by `for (i = tid; i < 768; i += 512)` (B0:29–31) and barriered (B0:32) before any `qvm_gate_up_pair`/`qvm_block`/`qmm_accum` read of it (B0:47–49,61,67; B1:83). `tg_gate`/`tg_up[384]` are fully covered before the barrier at B0:71 and the silu reads at B0:76,82: in decode, simdgroups 0–11 each have lane 0 store their block's 32 gate and 32 up outputs (B0:44–55); in prefill, each lane stores one output, `b*32 + lane` (B0:59–68) — 12 blocks × 32 = 384 either way. `tg_h[384]` is written exactly once by tids 0–383 in the silu loop (B0:75–82) and barriered (B0:84) before the down reads (B0:91,104). The new helper zero-initialises both accumulators before accumulating (B1:78–81) and fully writes its private `w4g`/`w4u[4]` load buffers before reading them (B1:89–101); idle simdgroups (12–15 in gate/up; wave-2 `b >= 24` in down, B0:88–97,101–106) write nothing and their never-initialised `p`/`pu` is never stored — every store sits inside the same `simd < 12` / `lane == 0` / `b < 24` guard as the compute, and `qvm_block` re-zeroes `p` on entry (B1:27–29). Device-side, `y` is written at every output element in both branches (decode by lane 0 per block, B0:92–95; prefill per lane, B0:105) — 24 blocks × 32 = 768 per pair — and the fused kernel has no device-memory intermediate, so nothing uninitialised is read.
- **Threadgroup memory vs the 32 KB limit.** Not close, unchanged from attempt-1. `tg_x[768] + tg_gate[384] + tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]` = 1,920 bfloat16 = 3,840 B (B0:24–27), 11.7% of the 32,768 B limit, rows-independent so it holds at every row count. The interleave's second 32-float accumulator `pu[32]` and second 4-word load buffer (B0:46; B1:89–101) are register-local, not threadgroup memory — an occupancy cost the builder's notes record, not a limit risk. Threads per threadgroup are 512 ≤ 1,024 (`spec.json:1`).
- **Thread-timing dependence.** None found. All cross-thread sharing is ordered by `threadgroup_barrier` between write and read (B0:32,71,84), and all three barriers sit outside any lane- or simd-divergent control flow — `prefill` (B0:22) is uniform across the group, so every thread reaches each barrier. The interleave itself cannot reorder a block's bits with timing: for each strided `k` both blocks' loads are issued (B1:84–101), then gate's 32 adds run (B1:102–106), then up's (B1:107–111), into separate accumulators `pg`/`pu`, so each block's per-output add sequence is the fixed `k = lane, lane+32, …` order of `qvm_block` regardless of load scheduling, and the two fixed `simd_sum` trees run sequentially afterwards (B1:113–120). Both reductions are entered only under simd-uniform guards (`simd < 12` at B0:44,59,65; `b = v*16 + simd < 24` at B0:90,103), so a simdgroup always reduces wholly or skips wholly. Each threadgroup writes a disjoint `y` slice (unique `pair`; B0:94,105), each `tg_gate`/`tg_up`/`tg_h` element is written exactly once (previous bullet), `atomic_outputs` is false and no atomics are used (`spec.json:1`), and the prefill accumulation is a fixed-order serial `BK=32` loop in a single thread per output (B1:146–154).
- **Captured-input assumptions.** None beyond the slot contract. The decode helper `qvm_block` and prefill helper `qmm_accum` are body-identical to attempt-1's proven copies (verified by diff; only the header comment and the inserted `qvm_gate_up_pair` differ in B1), keeping float32 dequant `x·(scale·q + bias)` with the strided-lane order and `simd_sum` (B1:30–50) and rounding every prefill weight to bfloat16 before the multiply, `(bfloat)(scale·q + bias)` (B1:151–152); the silu is the starting point's full-bfloat16 lowering shared by both branches (B0:73–82) and the down product still calls `qvm_block` verbatim (B0:91). In `qvm_gate_up_pair` each block keeps `qvm_block`'s exact terms — `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` / `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)` with `s1 = scale/16` (B1:104–105,109–110) — reading the shared `tg_x[k]` once per `k` (B1:83), the same float value the sequential pair of calls read twice, so gate and up bits are attempt-1's by construction. Hard-coded constants are the model's fixed slot dimensions (768/384 widths, 12/24 output blocks, `G = 12/24`, `Ww = 48/96`, per-expert strides 36864/9216, 4-bit nibble dequant), not properties of the captured arrays. The kernel assumes only what the Boundary guarantees — `inds` values in [0,60), flat row-major `[rows,768]` `x` and `[rows,4]` `inds`, contiguous weights — and no property of the captured distributions: `e = inds[pair]` is used directly per pair (B0:21), so any expert order, duplicates, skewed popularity (including an expert absent or chosen by every row), near-tie ids on either side, and later prefill chunks all take the same path, with no value-based early exits. Residual, not a defect (carried from the attempt-1 check): `qmm_accum` reproduces `BlockMMA`'s 8-wide fragment dots with a single thread's serial adds in `BK=32` order (B1:146–154) rather than by construction with `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate` as attempt-2 does, so its equality rests on the G2 evidence (differ 0 at 127/1,016/2,048 rows over all 20 layers) plus the shared full-bfloat16 silu residual; since the prefill path is byte-identical to attempt-1's and the per-output order is independent of row count and expert distribution, other row counts add no risk to it, but an unseen activation value cannot be ruled out from source alone.

# attempt-5 (round 2): hardening — parallel block stores (builder-1-e)

Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
`none`). Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-4`
(interleaved gate/up, fused single kernel, 512 threads/pair, G2 pass
all six, 94.0 / 177.0 / 591.3 µs/layer chained vs compiled
73.5 / 239.0 / 796.3 — loses only at 1 row).

## The one main change

Parallelize the block stores, decode branch only. Nothing else
changes: same `qvm_block` / `qvm_gate_up_pair` / `qmm_accum` bodies
(`block-1.metal` byte-identical to attempt-4, verified by diff),
same interleaved gate/up K loop, same silu, same prefill branch,
same grids and `spec.json` (byte-identical).

- **Before (attempt-4):** after each block's `simd_sum`, lane 0 alone
  stored the block: `for (j = 0..31) tg_gate[b*32+j] = p[j]` and
  likewise `tg_up`, and for down `y[pair*768 + b*32 + j] = p[j]`.
  That is 48 blocks per pair (12 gate + 12 up + 24 down) × 32 serial
  stores, all on the 16 lanes-0 of the pair's threadgroup (12 active
  in gate/up, up to 16 per down wave), while the other 31 lanes of
  each simdgroup idle at the following barrier / next wave.
- **Now:** after each `simd_sum` every lane holds the full reduced
  32-vector (`p[j] = simd_sum(p[j])` for all `j` in `block-1.metal`,
  so each lane's `p[0..31]` is the whole block output). Lane `j`
  stores element `j` — one store per lane, 32-way parallel:
  `tg_gate[b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`,
  `tg_up[b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)pu[lane]`, and for down
  `y[pair*768 + b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]` (still inside the
  `b < 24` guard, so idle simdgroups store nothing). The
  `(bfloat)` rounding at the store is unchanged, so the bfloat16
  rounding points are identical.
- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`) untouched:** it already stores one output
  per lane (`tg_gate[b*32 + lane]`, `y[... + lane]`), so there is no
  serial store to parallelize there.

Correctness rests on `simd_sum` being a broadcast reduction: if any
lane held only its own partial, the parallel store would write
partials and G2 would fail loudly with large `differ` at decode
sizes. That is the intended check.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-4's
  miss analysis left the still-sequential tails — chained fixed
  cost, `tg_x` load, silu, barriers and the down chain — plus these
  serial stores on the critical path. On the per-pair critical path
  the serial stores are: gate/up phase, 64 threadgroup stores by
  each active simdgroup's lane 0 (32 gate + 32 up, 12 simdgroups
  concurrent) before the silu barrier; down, 32 device stores per
  wave × 2 waves. That is ~128 serial store issues (plus their loop
  control) that every other lane waits on. Parallel stores cut that
  to 4 parallel store steps (gate 1, up 1, down 1 per wave),
  removing ~124 serial issues from the path without touching any
  accumulation order, so decode bits are attempt-4's by construction
  if the broadcast premise holds.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
  attempt-4's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
  verbatim.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
  kept, as in attempts 1–4 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
  the store bytes are tiny beside them (`y` 1,536 B/pair = 0.28%).

## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)

512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 and threadgroup memory unchanged at
3,840 B (`tg_x[768] + tg_gate[384] + tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]`
bfloat16) of 32,768 B, rows-independent (`spec.json` identical to
attempt-4). No new state: `p[lane]` reads the existing per-thread
accumulator. Valid at every `rows ≥ 1` on both sides of 60; decode
stores cover every `(pair, block, lane)` exactly once, as before
(gate/up: 12 simdgroups × 32 lanes; down: 24 blocks × 32 lanes over
2 waves).

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)

Attempt-4 (other run): 94.0 / 177.0 / 591.3 vs compiled
73.5 / 239.0 / 796.3. Baseline `none`, so no
`wins_vs_baseline` / `beats_baseline`.

- **1 row: 91.** Latency-bound. ~124 serial store issues leave the
  critical path; at ~20 exposed cycles each (single-lane store
  pipeline plus 32-iteration loop overhead, GPU ≈ 1.3 GHz) that is
  124 × 20 / 1.3e9 ≈ 1.9 µs, plus the down device stores' extra
  latency on lane 0, ≈ 3 µs total → 94.0 − 3 ≈ **91 µs**. Still
  above compiled 73.5 — this trims a tail, it does not close the
  remaining down-chain / fixed-cost gap.
- **8 rows: 175.** 32 groups per call partly hide one group's store
  tail behind other groups' K loops, so roughly half the 1-row
  saving survives: 177.0 − 2 ≈ **175 µs**, keeping the win over
  compiled 239.0.
- **32 rows: 589.** Streaming-bound (attempt-4: 119.7 GB/s on pair
  bytes). Store bytes are 0.28% of pair traffic and group-level
  parallelism already hides the store latency, so the change is
  ~neutral: 591.3 − 2 ≈ **589 µs**, keeping the win over compiled
  796.3. Risk: none structural — no register or threadgroup change;
  the only risk is the broadcast premise, which G2 tests directly.

G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — the
parallel store writes the same `(bfloat)p[j]` values attempt-4's
lane 0 wrote, just from lane `j` instead of lane 0, and the prefill
path is byte-identical to attempt-4's.

## Verdict

G1 pass; **G2 pass at all six sizes, differ 0 / max_ulp 0.0
everywhere** (decode 1/8/32 and prefill 127/1,016/2,048) — the
broadcast premise holds: every lane's `p[0..31]` after `simd_sum`
is the full reduced block, so lane `j` storing `p[j]` reproduces
attempt-4's serial lane-0 stores bit for bit, for gate, up and
down alike. Chained timing µs/layer (this run; candidate vs
reference vs compiled): **1 row 92.1 / 95.7 / 75.9 (loses to
compiled, beats reference)**; 8 rows 162.0 / 232.4 / 234.6 (wins);
32 rows 534.8 / 802.3 / 798.2 (wins). `beats_compiled` false —
only the 1-row size misses, as in attempt-4. Baseline `none` — no
`wins_vs_baseline`/`beats_baseline`.

Against attempt-4 (different run; compiled shifted 73.5 → 75.9 at
1 row and reference 81.2 → 95.7 between runs, so treat cross-run
deltas as indicative): 92.1 vs 94.0 at 1 row (**−2.0%**), 162.0
vs 177.0 at 8 rows (**−8.5%**), 534.8 vs 591.3 at 32 rows
(**−9.6%**). Effective bandwidth on pair bytes: 24.0 / 109.2 /
132.3 GB/s (attempt-4: 23.5 / 99.9 / 119.7). The 32-row rate is
back at attempt-1's 132.1 GB/s level while keeping the
interleave's 1/8-row wins — attempt-5 dominates attempt-4 at
every size and matches the best previous 32-row time (attempt-1:
535.7).

## Miss analysis (prediction 91 / 175 / 589, measured 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8)

Misses are +1.2% / −7.4% / −9.2% — all inside the 20% bar, so no
formal miss, but the size pattern was inverted versus the
prediction (smallest gain at 1 row, largest at 32 rows) and that
needs explaining:

1. **At 1 row the serial stores were a small tail, as the
   arithmetic said, but the fixed remainder is larger than the
   store tail.** Removing ~124 serial issues bought only ~2 µs of
   the predicted ~3; the remaining ~16 µs gap to compiled (92.1 vs
   75.9) is the still-sequential down chain (12 strided steps × 2
   waves behind the silu barrier), the `tg_x` load, silu, barriers
   and the chained launch/link cost — none of which this change
   touches.
2. **At 8/32 rows the serial device stores cost more than pure
   latency.** Lane 0's 32 serial stores to `y` per down block are
   32 separate single-lane transactions to consecutive addresses;
   32 lanes storing in parallel coalesce into full transactions.
   Paid per block (24 per pair) on every streaming step, that
   inefficiency — plus the serial threadgroup stores delaying the
   silu barrier — taxed attempt-4 by ~9% at 32 rows, which the
   latency-only prediction (store bytes = 0.28% of pair traffic)
   missed. Parallel stores removed it, which is also why the
   interleave's 32-row register tax (attempt-4 notes) no longer
   shows: 534.8 ≈ attempt-1's non-interleaved 535.7.

Lesson for `ineff-baseline-experts-2`: a serial lane-0 store
after a broadcast reduction is never free — at latency sizes it
is a barrier tail, at streaming sizes the uncoalesced device
stores tax every block. Any future block kernel should store
from all 32 lanes by default.

## Next change

Make the down product's two waves overlap like gate/up: one
simdgroup computes two down blocks in one interleaved K loop
(separate accumulators, per-block `qvm_block` order and the new
parallel store kept), attacking the still-sequential 12-step
down chain that is now the largest named remainder at 1 row.
The row-conditional interleave attempt-4 proposed is moot —
attempt-5 already restored attempt-1's 32-row rate (534.8 vs
535.7) with the interleave kept.

# attempt-4 (round 2): hardening — fused interleave gate/up (builder-1-d)

Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
`none`). Builds on the best attempt
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-1` (fused single kernel,
512 threads/pair, G2 pass all six, 104.3/193.3/535.7 µs/layer chained
vs compiled 77.6/235.7/791.6 — loses only at 1 row). This is the one
main change named by attempt-3's miss analysis
(`attempt-3/notes.md`, *Next change*): attempt-3 split into two
kernels and plateaued at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer at 1 row across three
packings, so group count is not the lever; the next lever is to
overlap the per-block serial K chain itself inside the fused kernel.

## The one main change

Stay in attempt-1's fused single kernel — same one kernel, same
512 threads per (row, expert-slot) pair, same grid `rows*2048`
threads = `rows*4` groups, same branch on `rows >= 60`, same
threadgroup buffers — and interleave gate and up in the decode
branch only:

- **Before (attempt-1):** simdgroup `b` (`b < 12`) ran
  `qvm_block(gate, block b)` to completion (24 strided K steps per
  lane: `k = lane, lane+32, ..., lane+744`; each step loads 4 weight
  words + scale/bias for that `k`, then accumulates 32 outputs),
  stored `tg_gate`, then ran `qvm_block(up, block b)` the same way
  and stored `tg_up`. The two blocks' K loops were fully sequential:
  up's first load waited for gate's last accumulate.
- **Now:** simdgroup `b` runs one merged loop,
  `qvm_gate_up_pair` (block-1). For each strided `k`, both blocks'
  loads are issued first — gate's 4 weight words, scale and bias,
  then up's 4 weight words, scale and bias (plus the shared
  `tg_x[k]`, read once) — and only then do the two accumulation
  passes run, gate's 32 terms then up's 32 terms, into separate
  accumulators `pg`/`pu`. The next `k`'s loads therefore sit behind
  twice the issued load traffic per step, and each block's load
  latency has the other block's loads/compute to hide behind
  (double-buffering the two blocks' weight/scale/x loads within
  the step). Lane 0 then stores both blocks in one loop:
  `tg_gate[b*32+j] = (bfloat)pg[j]`, `tg_up[b*32+j] = (bfloat)pu[j]`.

Everything else is copied, not redesigned:

- **Per-block bits unchanged.** In `qvm_gate_up_pair`, each block's
  adds run in exactly `qvm_block`'s order: the same strided `k`
  sequence, the same float32 dequant terms
  `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` /
  `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)` with `s1 = scale/16`, in the same
  per-output sequence; `pg` and `pu` are independent accumulators,
  so interleaving the two blocks cannot reorder either block's own
  adds. Each accumulator then gets the identical
  `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` `simd_sum` tree as `qvm_block`.
  Down still calls `qvm_block` verbatim (verified by diff against
  attempt-1: `qvm_block` and `qmm_accum` bodies byte-identical;
  block-0 differs only in the header comment and the decode
  gate/up call site).
- **Prefill (`rows >= 60`) unchanged.** Attempt-1's scalar
  `qmm_accum` (weight rounded to bfloat16 first,
  `float(bfloat(scale·q+bias))`, then K accumulated contiguously in
  `BK=32` tile order, one output per lane) is copied byte-identical
  for gate, up and down, and block-0's prefill branch is untouched —
  the interleaving does not touch the prefill arithmetic.
- Same four bfloat16 rounding points (gate, up, hidden via the
  shared full-bfloat16 silu-mul, down — silu code byte-identical),
  fp32 accumulation, positional `y[r,j]` (`pair = r*4 + j`), and
  the same `rows >= 60` dispatch threshold from `x_shape[0]`, not
  the grader's bracketing sizes. No kernel split, no threadgroup
  count change, no new device-memory intermediate.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempts 1–3
  all plateau at 103.6–109.5 µs/layer at 1 row despite 4, 12+24 and
  48+96 threadgroups per call, so the binding cost past 4 groups is
  each block's serial K chain (24 + 24 + 12 strided
  load-accumulate steps, gate→up→down ordered by the hidden
  dependency) executed with only one block's loads in flight per
  simdgroup at a time. Interleaving gate and up — the two
  independent, equal-length (24-step) chains — puts both blocks'
  loads in flight in every step without touching any block's
  `simd_sum` order, the only lever attempt-3's analysis left inside
  the fused kernel. Down (12 steps) is left sequential: it cannot
  start before the silu barrier in any case.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
  attempt-1's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
  verbatim.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
  kept, as in attempts 1–3 — weight bytes per pair stay
  552,960 B; the interleaving changes load scheduling, not bytes.

## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)

512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 (spec unchanged, verified identical).
Threadgroup memory unchanged from attempt-1: `tg_x[768] +
tg_gate[384] + tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]` bfloat16 = **3,840 B** of
32,768 B, rows-independent. The only new state is register-local:
a second 32-float accumulator `pu[32]` beside `p[32]` and a second
4-word load buffer inside `qvm_gate_up_pair` — the register cost
is the risk noted below. Grid scales as `rows*4` groups, so the
kernel is valid at every `rows ≥ 1`, on both sides of 60.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)

Weight bytes per layer (552,960 B/pair, of which gate+up are
368,640 B = 2/3): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs.
Attempt-1 chained (this round's grader): 104.3 / 193.3 / 535.7
µs/layer = effective 21.2 / 91.5 / 132.1 GB/s; compiled (same run)
77.6 / 235.7 / 791.6.

- **1 row: 90.** Latency-bound (floor 2.21 MB ÷ 200 GB/s =
  11.1 µs). Gate+up are 48 of the 60 serial product steps and 2/3
  of the pair bytes, so ≈ 2/3 × 104.3 ≈ 69 µs of attempt-1's time
  is the gate/up chains (the rest: down's 12 steps, `tg_x` load,
  silu, barriers, chained launch/link). Issuing both blocks' loads
  before accumulating doubles the loads outstanding per step; if
  that hides ≈ 20% of the gate/up chain's exposed latency
  (0.20 × 69 ≈ 14 µs), the layer lands at ≈ **90 µs** — still

{"path":"muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-6/notes.md","content":"# attempt-6 (round 2): hardening — interleaved down block pair (builder-1-f)

Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
`none`). Builds on the best attempt
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-5` (fused single kernel,
512 threads/pair, interleaved gate/up + parallel block stores, G2 pass
all six, 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8 µs/layer chained vs compiled
75.9 / 234.6 / 798.2 — loses only at 1 row by 16.2 µs). This is the
one main change named in attempt-5's notes (*Next change*): make the
down product's two waves overlap like gate/up.

## The one main change

Interleave the down product like gate/up, decode branch only.
Everything else is copied from attempt-5, not redesigned
(`spec.json` byte-identical; `block-1.metal` helpers `qvm_block`,
`qvm_gate_up_pair`, `qmm_accum` bodies byte-identical by diff;
`block-0.metal` gate/up, silu and prefill branches byte-identical):

- **Before (attempt-5):** down ran 24 blocks of 32 outputs in 2
  sequential waves of 16 simdgroups (`b = v*16 + simd`, `b < 24`):
  wave 0 computed blocks 0–15, wave 1 blocks 16–23 (simdgroups
  8–15 idle), each block a separate `qvm_block` call — 12 strided
  K steps per lane (`k = lane, lane+32, …, lane+352` over `K=384`),
  then `simd_sum` and the parallel store
  `y[pair*768 + b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`. The second wave's
  first load waited for the first wave's last accumulate.
- **Now:** one simdgroup computes two down blocks in one merged K
  loop (`qvm_down_pair`, block-1). Simdgroup `s < 12` owns the
  consecutive pair `b0 = 2s`, `b1 = 2s+1` (12 pairs, one wave;
  simdgroups 12–15 idle, as in gate/up). For each strided `k` both
  blocks' loads are issued before either accumulates — block 0's
  scale/bias and 4 weight words, then block 1's scale/bias and 4
  weight words (plus the shared `tg_h[k]`, read once) — and only
  then do the two accumulation passes run, block 0's 32 terms then
  block 1's, into separate accumulators `p`/`q`. The 24 down blocks
  therefore run as 12 interleaved pairs instead of 2 sequential
  waves.

Everything else is kept identical, as the task requires:

- **Per-block bits unchanged.** In `qvm_down_pair` each block's adds
  run in exactly `qvm_block`'s order: the same strided `k` sequence,
  the same float32 dequant terms
  `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` / `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)`
  with `s1 = scale/16`, in the same per-output sequence; `p` and
  `q` are independent accumulators, so interleaving cannot reorder
  either block's own adds. Each accumulator then gets the identical
  `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` `simd_sum` tree as `qvm_block`.
  The `(bfloat)` rounding at the store is unchanged.
- **Parallel lane stores kept.** After the two `simd_sum`s every
  lane holds both blocks' full reduced 32-vectors, so lane `j`
  stores element `j` of each block — one store per lane per block:
  `y[pair*768 + b0*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`,
  `y[pair*768 + b1*32 + lane] = (bfloat)q[lane]`.
- **Gate/up interleave, silu, prefill scalar branch, grids and
  rounding points identical.** Gate/up still calls
  `qvm_gate_up_pair` verbatim with attempt-5's parallel
  `tg_gate`/`tg_up` stores; the full-bfloat16 silu-mul is
  byte-identical; the `rows >= 60` prefill branch still uses the
  scalar `qmm_accum` (bfloat16-rounded dequant, contiguous `BK=32`
  order) for gate, up and down, with the same `x_shape[0] >= 60`
  dispatch threshold; `spec.json` (one kernel, `rows*2048` threads
  = `rows*4` groups of 512) is byte-identical. No kernel split, no
  new device-memory intermediate, same four bfloat16 rounding
  points and positional `y[r,j]`.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-5's
  miss analysis left the still-sequential down chain as the largest
  named remainder at 1 row — 12 strided steps × 2 waves behind the
  silu barrier, plus the `tg_x` load, silu, barriers and chained
  fixed cost. Attempts 1–3 showed threadgroup count past 4 is not
  the lever and attempt-4/5 showed overlapping the per-block serial
  K chain is. The down product was the last product still running
  its blocks in fully sequential waves with only one block's loads
  in flight per simdgroup; merging two blocks per simdgroup puts
  both blocks' loads (8 weight words + 2 scales/biases per step)
  in flight in every step, so each block's load latency has the
  other block's loads/compute to hide behind, without touching
  any block's `simd_sum` order.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
  attempt-5's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
  verbatim — the interleave does not touch prefill arithmetic.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
  kept, as in attempts 1–5 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
  the interleave changes load scheduling, not bytes.

## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)

512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 (`spec.json` identical to attempt-5).
Threadgroup memory unchanged: `tg_x[768] + tg_gate[384] +
tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]` bfloat16 = **3,840 B** of 32,768 B,
rows-independent. The only new state is register-local: a second
32-float accumulator `q[32]` beside `p[32]` and a second 4-word
load buffer inside `qvm_down_pair` — the register cost is the risk
noted below. Grid scales as `rows*4` groups, so the kernel is
valid at every `rows ≥ 1`, on both sides of 60. Decode coverage:
12 simdgroups × 2 blocks × 32 lanes = 768 outputs per pair, each
written exactly once, as before.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)

Attempt-5 (other run): 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8 µs/layer vs compiled
75.9 / 234.6 / 798.2 and reference 95.7 / 232.4 / 802.3. Baseline
`none`, so no `wins_vs_baseline` / `beats_baseline`. Weight bytes
per layer (552,960 B/pair): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB at 4 / 32 /
128 pairs; bandwidth floors at 200 GB/s: 11.1 / 88.5 / 353.9 µs.
Attempt-5 effective: 24.0 / 109.2 / 132.3 GB/s.

Down arithmetic: `K = 384` → 12 strided steps per lane per block.
Attempt-5 pays 2 waves × 12 steps sequentially after the silu
barrier; attempt-6 pays 12 merged steps. A merged step issues
twice the loads (8 weight words, 2 scales) for twice the
accumulate work, so it costs more than a single-block step but
less than two — the gate/up precedent (attempt-4) hid ≈ 20% of
the merged chain's exposed latency at 1 row.

- **1 row: 85.** Latency-bound (floor 11.1 µs). The down phase
  sits alone behind the silu barrier; at attempt-5's 92.1 µs the
  product chains (gate/up merged 24 steps + down 2×12 steps)
  dominate, so the down waves are roughly a third of the layer
  (≈ 30 µs). Collapsing 24 sequential steps into 12 merged ones
  at ≈ 1.3× the per-step cost (8 loads share the `tg_h[k]` read
  and the loop control) cuts the down phase to ≈ 23 µs, saving
  ≈ 7 µs → 92.1 − 7 ≈ **85 µs**. Still above compiled 75.9 — the
  `tg_x` load, silu, barriers and chained launch/link cost
  remain untouched — but it should roughly halve the 16.2 µs gap.
- **8 rows: 156.** 32 groups per call partly hide one group's
  down tail behind other groups' K loops (attempt-5 already at
  109.2 GB/s), so only part of the 1-row saving survives:
  162.0 − 6 ≈ **156 µs**, keeping the win over compiled 234.6.
- **32 rows: 540.** Streaming-bound (attempt-5: 132.3 GB/s).
  Group parallelism already hides load latency, so the merged
  loop buys nothing; the risk is the second live 32-float
  accumulator taxing occupancy, as the gate/up interleave did in
  attempt-4 before attempt-5's store fix (+10.4%). With the
  parallel stores already in place that tax measured ≈ 0 for
  gate/up (534.8 ≈ attempt-1's 535.7), so the down interleave is
  predicted ≈ neutral: 534.8 + 5 ≈ **540 µs**, keeping the win
  over compiled 798.2. Register spill remains the failure mode
  to watch.

G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — each
down block's dequant terms, add order and `simd_sum` are
attempt-5's by construction (separate accumulators), gate/up and
prefill are byte-identical to attempt-5's, and the parallel store
writes the same `(bfloat)p[j]` values, just one merged loop
earlier.

## Verdict

*(to be filled after the grader run)*

## Next change

*(to be filled after the grader run)*
"}

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write a faster MobileMoE-S decode kernel
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
12|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
13|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
14|
15|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
16|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
17|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
18|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
19|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
20|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
21|
22|## The slots
23|
24|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the step: 1 to 32 in decode. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
25|
26|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
27|
28|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
29|
30|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
31||---|---|---|---|
32|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
33|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
34|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
35|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
36|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
37|
38|Reference:
39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
69|
70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
93|
94|## Tools and limits
95|
96|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
97|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
98|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes; stop one that hangs.
99|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.
100|
101|## Rules of this session
102|
103|These keep your work apart from everyone else's. Git hooks and an audit script enforce them, and a commit that breaks them is refused.
104|
105|- **Write only inside `muse-spark/`.** Never change `bench/`, `claude/`, `results/`, `tools/`, `third_party/`, or any other file. A copy of the grader you edit is never used.
106|- **Commit only on `muse-agent`,** with the co-author trailer your settings add: `Co-Authored-By: Muse Spark (Meta Model API) <muse-spark@meta-model-api.invalid>`. Start each subject with `Muse Spark:`. No other co-author.
107|- **Never push, merge, rebase, change git config, or skip hooks.**
108|- **Don't read `.env`** or any credentials file.
109|- One commit per attempt, after you've run the grader on it, so the history shows every attempt in order.
110|
111|## Your files
112|
113|```
114|muse-spark/
115|  strategy.md                                your choice and design, ending with the targets JSON
116|  kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>/
117|    block-0.metal, block-1.metal, ...        Metal kernel bodies (and headers), numbered from 0
118|    spec.json                                the launch spec
119|    notes.md                                 optional: what you tried and why
120|  summary.md                                 your final attempt per slot
121|```
122|
123|`<slot-folder>` is `routing`, `combine`, `routing-combine` or `experts`. Grade an attempt with:
124|
125|```bash
126|.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_candidate.py muse-spark/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N> <slot>
127|```
128|
129|where `<slot>` is `routing`, `combine`, `routing+combine` or `experts`.
130|
131|**The targets JSON** at the end of `strategy.md`:
132|
133|```json
134|{
135|  "targets": [
136|    {"slot": "routing+combine", "why": "...", "expected_saving_ms": {"rows_1": 0.0, "rows_32": 0.0}, "design": "..."}
137|  ]
138|}
139|```
140|
141|List one or two targets, in the order you work on them.
142|
143|**The launch spec** (`spec.json`):
144|
145|```json
146|{
147|  "kernels": [
148|    {
149|      "name": "fused_routing",
150|      "source_block": 0,
151|      "header_block": null,
152|      "inputs": ["x", "w_router", "bias"],
153|      "outputs": [
154|        {"name": "inds", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "uint32"},
155|        {"name": "weights", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "float32"}
156|      ],
157|      "grid": ["rows*32", 1, 1],
158|      "threadgroup": [32, 1, 1],
159|      "template": {"T": "bfloat16"},
160|      "init_value": null,
161|      "atomic_outputs": false
162|    }
163|  ],
164|  "slot_outputs": {"inds": "inds", "weights": "weights"}
165|}
166|```
167|
168|- **`source_block` and `header_block`** are the numbers of your `block-N.metal` files.
169|- **Kernels run in list order.** A kernel's `inputs` may name slot inputs or outputs of earlier kernels.
170|- **`slot_outputs`** maps each output of the slot to the kernel output that provides it.
171|- **For `routing+combine`,** `spec.json` holds two specs, each in the format above for its own slot: `{"routing": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}, "combine": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}}`. The original experts and shared expert run between the two parts. The grader tests each part on its own, and the combine part receives the reference routing weights.
172|- **Shape and grid entries** are integers, or products of integers and the names `rows`, `D`, `E`, `K` and `H`, such as `"rows*32"`. Nothing else is evaluated.
173|- **dtypes** are `float32`, `bfloat16`, `float16`, `uint32` or `int32`.
174|- **Template values** are one of those dtypes, an integer or a boolean.
175|- **`grid`** counts threads, not threadgroups, as in `mx.fast.metal_kernel`.
176|
177|## How each attempt is judged
178|
179|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only.
180|
181|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
182|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
183|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
184|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
185|
186|   At every size:
187|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
188|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
189|
190|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
191|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
192|3. **G3, faster.** The decode step's period is the median over 3 repeats in shuffled order, with 128-token prompts, at 1, 8 and 32 requests. It must be lower than both the original model's and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code. The gap must exceed the spread between repeats.
193|
194|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
195|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
196|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
197|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer`: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, and `beats_compiled`.
198|
199|**The piece timing** runs the slot on all 20 layers' captured decode inputs, at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and waits for the GPU once at the end. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row. It takes the median of 30 repeats, per layer. It is a guide; G3 decides.
200|
201|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and beats the compiled reference in the piece timing at all three row counts, or after 5 attempts. Name your final attempt per slot in `muse-spark/summary.md`; it goes to the end-to-end and G3 checks, which surucuonur's team runs after merging your branch.

181|register/thread storage, which Metal folds into that limit. The
182|inferred cause (from the code, not a register dump — no second GPU
183|job was run to measure it): attempt-5 has two distinct 32-float
184|thread arrays (`p[32]` at kernel scope, `pu[32]` scoped to the
185|gate/up branch; down reuses `p` alone), while attempt-6 has three

200|the launch itself becomes illegal. Peak live floats per phase did
201|not grow (gate/up already held 64), but distinct-array count did,
202|and that is what the compiler charged for.

{"path":"muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/notes.md","content":"# attempt-7 (round 2): hardening — interleaved down, shared second accumulator (builder-1-g)

Hardening attempt for `hyp-1-experts-exact` (slot `experts`, baseline
`none`). Builds on the best attempt
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-5` (fused single kernel,
512 threads/pair, interleaved gate/up + parallel block stores, G2 pass
all six, 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8 µs/layer chained vs compiled
75.9 / 234.6 / 798.2 — loses only at 1 row by 16.2 µs) with the
down-interleave `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-6` tried
(one simdgroup, two down blocks, merged K loop), made to compile
within the pipeline threadgroup limit. Attempt-6 failed G1:
`Thread group size (512) is greater than the maximum allowed
threads per threadgroup (448)` — its compiled pipeline's
`maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` fell to 448 for the identical
512-thread launch.

## The one main change

Attempt-6's merged down loop, with the second accumulator's storage
shared so the kernel compiles at 512 threads. Everything else is
copied from attempt-5/6, not redesigned (`spec.json` byte-identical
to attempt-5/6; `block-1.metal` helpers `qvm_block`,
`qvm_gate_up_pair`, `qvm_down_pair`, `qmm_accum` bodies byte-identical
to attempt-6 by diff; `block-0.metal` gate/up, silu and prefill
branches otherwise byte-identical):

- **Before (attempt-5):** down ran 24 blocks of 32 outputs in 2
  sequential waves of 16 simdgroups (`b = v*16 + simd`, `b < 24`):
  wave 0 computed blocks 0–15, wave 1 blocks 16–23 (simdgroups
  8–15 idle), each block a separate `qvm_block` call — 12 strided
  K steps per lane (`k = lane, lane+32, …, lane+352` over `K=384`),
  then `simd_sum` and the parallel store
  `y[pair*768 + b*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`. The second wave's
  first load waited for the first wave's last accumulate.
- **Attempt-6's down change (kept):** one simdgroup computes two
  down blocks in one merged K loop (`qvm_down_pair`, block-1).
  Simdgroup `s < 12` owns the consecutive pair `b0 = 2s`,
  `b1 = 2s+1` (12 pairs, one wave; simdgroups 12–15 idle, as in
  gate/up). For each strided `k` both blocks' loads are issued
  before either accumulates — block 0's scale/bias and 4 weight
  words, then block 1's scale/bias and 4 weight words (plus the
  shared `tg_h[k]`, read once) — and only then do the two
  accumulation passes run, block 0's 32 terms then block 1's, into
  separate accumulators. The 24 down blocks therefore run as 12
  interleaved pairs instead of 2 sequential waves.
- **This attempt's fix vs attempt-6:** attempt-6 declared three
  distinct 32-float thread arrays — kernel-scope `p[32]`, a
  gate/up-scoped `pu[32]` and a down-scoped `q[32]` — and the
  compiler charged all three against the per-threadgroup budget
  (`maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` 448 < 512) even though `pu` and
  `q` are live in disjoint phases. Attempt-7 hoists the second
  accumulator to kernel scope: `float p[32]; float q[32];` beside
  the existing buffers in `block-0`, and passes the same `q` as
  gate/up's second accumulator (`qvm_gate_up_pair(..., p, q)`) and
  as down's second accumulator (`qvm_down_pair(..., p, q)`),
  deleting both scoped declarations. The kernel again has two
  distinct 32-float thread arrays, exactly attempt-5's footprint,
  at unchanged 512 threads.

Everything else is kept identical, as the task requires:

- **Per-block bits unchanged.** In `qvm_down_pair` each block's adds
  run in exactly `qvm_block`'s order: the same strided `k` sequence,
  the same float32 dequant terms
  `x * (s0 * (by & 0x0f) + bias)` / `x * (s1 * (by & 0xf0) + bias)`
  with `s1 = scale/16`, in the same per-output sequence; the two
  accumulators are independent, so interleaving cannot reorder
  either block's own adds. Each accumulator then gets the identical
  `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` `simd_sum` tree as `qvm_block`.
  The `(bfloat)` rounding at the store is unchanged.
- **Sharing is a pure storage rename.** Gate/up and down run in
  disjoint phases separated by two `threadgroup_barrier`s (after
  gate/up and after silu): gate/up's `q` values are stored to
  `tg_up` before the first barrier, silu consumes only
  `tg_gate`/`tg_up`/`tg_h`, and `qvm_down_pair` re-zeroes both
  `p[0..31]` and `q[0..31]` on entry (as `qvm_gate_up_pair` does),
  so no value can leak across the barrier through the shared array.
  Peak live floats per phase is unchanged (64 in gate/up, 64 in
  down); only the distinct-array count charged by the compiler
  drops from three to two.
- **Parallel lane stores kept.** After the two `simd_sum`s every
  lane holds both blocks' full reduced 32-vectors, so lane `j`
  stores element `j` of each block — one store per lane per block:
  `y[pair*768 + b0*32 + lane] = (bfloat)p[lane]`,
  `y[pair*768 + b1*32 + lane] = (bfloat)q[lane]`.
- **Gate/up interleave, silu, prefill scalar branch, grids and
  rounding points identical.** Gate/up still calls
  `qvm_gate_up_pair` with attempt-5's parallel `tg_gate`/`tg_up`
  stores; the full-bfloat16 silu-mul is byte-identical; the
  `rows >= 60` prefill branch still uses the scalar `qmm_accum`
  (bfloat16-rounded dequant, contiguous `BK=32` order) for gate,
  up and down, with the same `x_shape[0] >= 60` dispatch
  threshold; `spec.json` (one kernel, `rows*2048` threads =
  `rows*4` groups of 512) is byte-identical. No kernel split, no
  new device-memory intermediate, same four bfloat16 rounding
  points and positional `y[r,j]`.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

- `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (chained 1-row latency): attempt-5's
  miss analysis left the still-sequential down chain as the
  largest named remainder at 1 row — 12 strided steps × 2 waves
  behind the silu barrier, plus the `tg_x` load, silu, barriers
  and chained fixed cost. Attempts 1–3 showed threadgroup count
  past 4 is not the lever and attempt-4/5 showed overlapping the
  per-block serial K chain is. The down product was the last
  product still running its blocks in fully sequential waves with
  only one block's loads in flight per simdgroup; merging two
  blocks per simdgroup puts both blocks' loads (8 weight words +
  2 scales/biases per step) in flight in every step, so each
  block's load latency has the other block's loads/compute to
  hide behind, without touching any block's `simd_sum` order.
  The shared-`q` fix is what lets this merged loop launch at all:
  attempt-6 proved the three-array form exceeds the pipeline
  threadgroup budget at 512 threads.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (prefill G2 gate): already removed by
  attempt-5's branch; kept by reusing its scalar `qmm_accum`
  verbatim — the interleave does not touch prefill arithmetic.
- `ineff-baseline-experts-3` (per-pair re-reads): deliberately
  kept, as in attempts 1–6 — weight bytes per pair stay 552,960 B;
  the interleave changes load scheduling, not bytes.

## Limits (by hand; the grader does not check the 32 KB cap)

512 threads/group ≤ 1,024 (`spec.json` identical to attempt-5/6).
Threadgroup memory unchanged: `tg_x[768] + tg_gate[384] +
tg_up[384] + tg_h[384]` bfloat16 = **3,840 B** of 32,768 B,
rows-independent. Distinct thread arrays are two 32-float
accumulators (`p`, shared `q`) — attempt-5's count, one fewer than
attempt-6's three. Grid scales as `rows*4` groups, so the kernel
is valid at every `rows ≥ 1`, on both sides of 60. Decode coverage:
12 simdgroups × 2 blocks × 32 lanes = 768 outputs per pair, each
written exactly once, as before.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (chained, grader timing)

Attempt-5 (other run): 92.1 / 162.0 / 534.8 µs/layer vs compiled
75.9 / 234.6 / 798.2 and reference 95.7 / 232.4 / 802.3. Attempt-6
predicted 85 / 156 / 540 but never launched, so that prediction is
untested, not missed. Baseline `none`, so no
`wins_vs_baseline` / `beats_baseline`. Weight bytes per layer
(552,960 B/pair): 2.21 / 17.69 / 70.78 MB at 4 / 32 / 128 pairs;
bandwidth floors at 200 GB/s: 11.1 / 88.5 / 353.9 µs.
Attempt-5 effective: 24.0 / 109.2 / 132.3 GB/s.

Down arithmetic: `K = 384` → 12 strided steps per lane per block.
Attempt-5 pays 2 waves × 12 steps sequentially after the silu
barrier; this attempt pays 12 merged steps. A merged step issues
twice the loads (8 weight words, 2 scales) for twice the
accumulate work, so it costs more than a single-block step but
less than two — the gate/up precedent (attempt-4) hid ≈ 20% of
the merged chain's exposed latency at 1 row.

- **1 row: 85.** Latency-bound (floor 11.1 µs). The down phase
  sits alone behind the silu barrier; at attempt-5's 92.1 µs the
  product chains (gate/up merged 24 steps + down 2×12 steps)
  dominate, so the down waves are roughly a third of the layer
  (≈ 30 µs). Collapsing 24 sequential steps into 12 merged ones
  at ≈ 1.3× the per-step cost (8 loads share the `tg_h[k]` read
  and the loop control) cuts the down phase to ≈ 23 µs, saving
  ≈ 7 µs → 92.1 − 7 ≈ **85 µs**. Still above compiled 75.9 — the
  `tg_x` load, silu, barriers and chained launch/link cost
  remain untouched — but it should roughly halve the 16.2 µs gap.
  The shared `q` itself is arithmetic-neutral; its only timing
  effect is restoring a legal 512-thread pipeline.
- **8 rows: 156.** 32 groups per call partly hide one group's
  down tail behind other groups' K loops (attempt-5 already at
  109.2 GB/s), so only part of the 1-row saving survives:
  162.0 − 6 ≈ **156 µs**, keeping the win over compiled 234.6.
- **32 rows: 540.** Streaming-bound (attempt-5: 132.3 GB/s).
  Group parallelism already hides load latency, so the merged
  loop buys nothing; the peak live accumulator count is the same
  64 floats gate/up already held in attempt-5, so no new spill
  tax is expected beyond attempt-6's identical merged step:
  534.8 + 5 ≈ **540 µs**, keeping the win over compiled 798.2.

G1 prediction: pass — the launch is attempt-5's (512 threads,
3,840 B threadgroup memory) and the only change from attempt-5's
register footprint is that down now also holds a second live
accumulator, which gate/up already held in the same kernel that
launched at 512; the distinct-array count is attempt-5's two,
not attempt-6's three.
G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes with `differ == 0` — each
down block's dequant terms, add order and `simd_sum` are
attempt-5's by construction (separate logical accumulators,
shared storage re-zeroed per call), gate/up and prefill are
byte-identical to attempt-5's, and the parallel store writes the
same `(bfloat)p[j]` values, just one merged loop earlier.

## Verdict
